If a workflow scenario isn't covered here, the rules in CLAUDE.md (per-project) and the global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (Kai's defaults) are authoritative — this handbook is the friendly summary.

docs.title: First week: the essentials
docs.text:
New to git/GitHub entirely? Read the 10-minute primer first — it defines every term this page uses (commit, push, branch, markdown, repo).

Audience: anyone joining a kai-team-claude project as a co-author or PhD student. Read this once. ~15 minutes. Last substantive revision: 2026-05-21.

Why this page. Citations are the single highest-friction shared resource on a paper — two people adding the same reference under different keys is how bibliographies break for everyone. Getting the citekey rule and the bib flow right in week one prevents that, which is why this page leads with them.

This doc covers what you need to know in the first week. No Claude Code, no Zotero, no Python required — all of those are optional. The only pieces everything else depends on are GitHub, Dropbox, Overleaf (where applicable), and a shared citekey format — get these consistent and the rest is flexible.

Manual or with Claude — your choice, per task. Every git step on this page can be done by hand (see the manual workflow) or by asking Claude Code in plain language. Pick whichever you prefer for each task; the rules are the same either way.

docs.title: What you need to know on day one
The repo lives in Dropbox (and usually GitHub)
docs.text:
Each paper has two homes: - Dropbox folder — always present. Holds data, large files (PDFs, figures), working notes, and the project's CLAUDE.md. Every project co-author needs to be on Dropbox — project_management/zotero_todo.md and the PDF mirror flow through it. Ask whoever manages the project for access. - GitHub repo — present for most projects. What is canonical (paper text in git vs in Overleaf) depends on the project's mode (declared in the project's CLAUDE.md under ## Project mode). The four modes are defined in principles/project-structure-canonical.md — read that first to understand what you can commit/push from your sessions.

Quick mode summary: - Overleaf-mastered (e.g., Virality): Overleaf is canonical. Paper drafts live as date-stamped PDFs in the Dropbox folder under paper/. The Overleaf admin applies final changes manually in Overleaf. - Git-mastered (e.g., Sor4d): GitHub is canonical. paper/paper.tex and paper/references.bib are the editable source. Drafting happens there directly.

See principles/project-structure-canonical.md for the full layout (every project, every mode).

docs.title: How citations work
docs.text:
The paper's references.bib is split into two zones by anchor tokens. Entries live inside the START/END pair:

% <<<SYNC-BIB:ZOTERO-START>>>
% Auto-generated from Zotero. Do not edit here — overwritten on /sync-bib.

@article{smith2024corruption, ... }
@techreport{jones2024growth, ... }

% <<<SYNC-BIB:ZOTERO-END>>>

% <<<SYNC-BIB:MANUAL-START>>>
% Hand-edited entries. Preserved across /sync-bib runs.

@unpublished{schmidt2024draft, ... }

% <<<SYNC-BIB:MANUAL-END>>>

You have three ways to add a citation. Pick whichever fits how you work.

Default to Path 1. Use Path 2 only when you have full metadata in front of you and want the citation to resolve immediately (e.g., before a deadline). Use Path 3 only if you're already a Zotero user or want to invest the setup time.

docs.title: Path 1 — You just type the citation in .tex (citation-only)
docs.text:
Easiest. No setup needed.

  1. In your .tex file, write \citep{authorYEARkeyword} — e.g., \citep{jones2024corruption}.
  2. Don't touch references.bib.
  3. Record and share the change:
  4. Overleaf-mastered project: nothing more to do — Overleaf saves it.
  5. Git-mastered project, no terminal: open GitHub Desktop (free, https://desktop.github.com), which lists your changed .tex; type a one-line summary, click Commit, then Push origin. (Commit = record a snapshot; push = upload it so co-authors see it.)
  6. Terminal users: git add / git commit / git push per the handbook §2.3.

Whoever next runs /sync-bib will see your new citation surface as a "pending orphan" in project_management/zotero_todo.md. They'll source the paper into Zotero. Your \citep{...} will resolve in the next compile.

In the meantime, your compiled PDF will show [??] for the unresolved citation. That's expected — it'll resolve when the bib gets updated. Don't try to "fix" it yourself unless you're under a deadline (then use Path 2 below).

Before inventing a new citekey, search (Ctrl-F) references.bib AND project_management/zotero_todo.md for the first-author surname. Avoids the case where the paper is already pending under a slightly different key.

Disambiguation when Overleaf autocomplete suggests an existing key: pick a more specific keyword (gehring2025narrative already taken → use gehring2025refugees, gehring2025wartime, whatever the new paper is about). If you genuinely can't distinguish: letter suffix (smith2024a, smith2024b) is the fallback.

In long-form workflow doc, this is Workflow D.

docs.title: Path 2 — You write a bib entry by hand (manual bib edit)
docs.text:
For LaTeX-fluent people who'd rather add an entry directly:

  1. Open references.bib. Scroll to the MANUAL zone — do not edit the ZOTERO zone, those entries are auto-generated and your edits will be erased.
  2. Inside the MANUAL zone (between % <<<SYNC-BIB:MANUAL-START>>> and % <<<SYNC-BIB:MANUAL-END>>>), add your entry. Use the format described in principles/citation-style.md:
  3. @article for papers published in a journal
  4. @techreport for working papers (NBER, CEPR, IZA, SSRN, arXiv)
  5. @unpublished for circulated drafts / mimeo / unpublished manuscripts
  6. Before adding, search (Ctrl-F) the MANUAL zone for the first-author surname to avoid silent duplicates (the case where another co-author already added the same paper under a different citekey on a parallel branch).
  7. Get the core fields right (author, title, year, journal/institution + DOI if known). Style polish (Chicago title case, full author names, exact page-range format) gets normalized later by /fix-bib-in-zotero. Follow citation-style.md from the start if you can — it saves the bib_keeper time later.
  8. Commit and push.

Your entry survives indefinitely. Someone will eventually promote it to Zotero via /fix-bib-in-zotero. Until then, your bib entry is the source of truth.

In long-form workflow doc, this is Workflow E.

docs.title: Path 3 — You use Zotero
docs.text:
If you already have Zotero installed and use the browser Connector:

  1. In your browser, click the Zotero Connector button on the paper's page. Zotero saves the metadata + PDF.
  2. Ask whoever manages the Zotero library which group the project uses — they'll add you.
  3. After adding a few papers, run /sync-bib (if you have Claude Code) or wait for someone else to run it. New entries appear in the ZOTERO zone of references.bib.

If you want to run /sync-bib yourself, you'll need: - Zotero desktop running - Zotero Connector browser extension - Better BibTeX installed and configured (see install/install-better-bibtex.md) - Zotero MCP authenticated (see install/mcp-add-zotero.md)

This is optional. Path 1 or Path 2 work fine without any of this.

In long-form workflow doc, this is Workflow A.

docs.title: Choosing a citekey strategy (Path 3 users only)
docs.text:
Important constraint: Better BibTeX's citekey-generation formula is global per Zotero install — not per project, not per library. If you work on multiple papers with different citekey conventions (very common for active academics), you cannot satisfy all of them at once by changing the BBT formula.

The project's CLAUDE.md records a formula_mode to handle this:

Mode What it means Who picks this bib-canonical (recommended default) Treat the bib as source of truth. /sync-bib runs hygiene checks (orphans, collisions) but does NOT fetch new entries from BBT. To add a citation: hand-edit MANUAL zone of references.bib, or use a future /add-cite-from-zotero helper. Multi-project academics — the typical case formula-aligned Change your global BBT formula to match the project's. /sync-bib then fetches new entries from BBT and regenerates the ZOTERO zone. WARNING: affects every other project you cite from this Zotero install. Single-project users, or users whose projects all share one convention per-project-export Advanced. Configure BBT to auto-export a project-specific .bib with the project's formula. /sync-bib reads that file instead of querying BBT. Power users who set up per-project BBT auto-export

Check the project's CLAUDE.md zotero.formula_mode to see which mode is recorded. If you're not the bib_keeper, you don't need to change anything — just follow Path 1 (citation-only) or Path 2 (manual bib edit) and the bib_keeper handles the rest.

Switching modes mid-project: edit formula_mode in CLAUDE.md, commit, ask co-authors to do the same. Don't toggle frequently — pick a stable mode once and stick.

docs.title: The one convention worth keeping consistent
docs.text:
Citekey format: authorYEARkeyword — lowercase, no separators.

  • gehring2025narrative ✓
  • acemoglu2001colonial ✓
  • vanderberg2022growth ✓ (particles like "van der" join the surname; no spaces)
  • smith2024a / smith2024b ✓ (letter-suffix disambiguation as fallback)
  • Gehring_2025_Narrative ✗ (no underscores, no capitals)
  • Gehring2025 ✗ (missing keyword)

If you make up a citekey when adding a citation in Path 1, follow this format. The person who sources the paper into Zotero will use the same format, so your \citep{jones2024corruption} will resolve cleanly.

Year unknown at first citation? Use \cite{TODO_smith_corruption} — the TODO_ prefix tells /sync-bib to skip orphan detection for this key. Resolve later.

Special cases (single-name authors like Aristotle, institutional authors like World Bank, Asian names, Spanish double surnames, joint first authors): see citation-style.md §2.

Once a citekey appears in a shared PDF (referee version, JMP, working-paper distribution), it doesn't change. The bib_keeper sets draft_state: shared in CLAUDE.md when first sending the paper out — this mechanically protects all keys from being rewritten by /sync-bib.

docs.title: Habits that quietly break the bib for everyone
docs.text:
• Don't edit the ZOTERO zone of references.bib. It's regenerated on every /sync-bib. Edits are lost.
  • Don't delete the anchor tokens (% <<<SYNC-BIB:...-START>>> / -END>>>). They tell the script which zone is which. If they vanish, the script HALTs and points you at git history.
  • Don't open references.bib in any tool that auto-formats .bib files — JabRef, BibDesk, TeXstudio's .bib mode, VSCode with bibtex-tidy or LaTeX Workshop format-on-save enabled, vim/emacs with auto-format bibtex-mode hooks. They reorder or reformat entries and scramble the zones. Use a plain-text editor or Overleaf's editor.
  • Don't rename citekeys that have appeared in shared drafts. Once a paper has been circulated, its keys are frozen.
  • Don't hand-edit Zotero entries to fix typos in the rendered bib (Path 3 users). Run /fix-bib-in-zotero if you're the bib_keeper, or ask the bib_keeper to run it.

docs.title: Merge conflicts on references.bib
docs.text:
If git flags a conflict in references.bib, look at the markers:

  • Conflict in the ZOTERO zone — accept either side; the bib_keeper will re-run /sync-bib to regenerate. The ZOTERO zone is regenerated from Zotero, so the file content will resolve. If you don't have Claude Code, accept either side and commit.
  • Conflict in the MANUAL zone — both sets of new entries are real work; keep both. Don't blindly pick one side. Merge the entries manually: include all the @article{...} / @techreport{...} / @unpublished{...} blocks from both sides. If the conflict is intricate, /sync-bib --resolve-conflicts parses the markers and offers to merge both sides automatically.

docs.title: What to do when something goes wrong
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause What to do [??] in compiled PDF for a citation Orphan citekey — your .tex cites a key not yet in the bib Wait for next /sync-bib, or add the entry yourself via Path 2 (immediate resolution) Compile fails entirely (won't produce a PDF) BibTeX strict mode rejects undefined citations Path 2: add a real entry to MANUAL right now. Don't wait for the next sync. /sync-bib HALTs: "anchor tokens corrupted" A .bib formatter ate the markers git log -p references.bib → find last good version; revert or restore the markers manually. Then /sync-bib again. /sync-bib fails: "library X not accessible" You haven't been added to a declared Zotero group Ask whoever manages the Zotero group to add you in its group settings /sync-bib fails: "your BBT formula doesn't match the project's" Your Better BibTeX is generating different citekeys than the canonical ones Re-check install/install-better-bibtex.md formula; reinstall BBT with the pinned config Your .tex rename of a citekey doesn't take effect draft_state: shared flipped — keys are now frozen If paper has been shared, citekeys can't be rewritten silently — see "What NOT to do" Same paper appears twice in the rendered bib Two co-authors added it to MANUAL with different citekeys /sync-bib's DOI-collision check should catch this; if it didn't, surface to bib_keeper

docs.title: Per-project quirks
docs.text:
Read each project's CLAUDE.md once when you join. It's just a markdown file in the repo root — open it like any other doc. The zotero: block tells you: - Which Zotero libraries the project uses - Who the bib_keeper is — the one person authorized to run /fix-bib-in-zotero (the command that writes changes back to Zotero). Whoever the team designates. Anyone else can run /sync-bib (read-only) freely. - Whether the project is in drafting or shared state — controls whether /sync-bib rewrites your .tex keys (drafting) or renames Zotero entries (shared) on key mismatch.

If you're not the bib_keeper, don't run /fix-bib-in-zotero against the project — it writes to Zotero, and conflicts arise if two people run it on the same library. The bib_keeper field is also visible as a comment at the top of references.bib once /sync-bib has run.

docs.title: If you have Claude Code but no Zotero
docs.text: You can still run /sync-bib --read-only — it skips Zotero entirely and just runs orphan detection against your local bib, updating project_management/zotero_todo.md. Useful for seeing what's pending without needing Zotero auth. The flag auto-engages when no Zotero MCP is configured on your machine.

docs.title: Want more depth?
docs.text:
• principles/bibliography-and-literature.md — full workflow doc with rationale, all six workflows (A–F; this onboarding page is Workflow C), command list with phases.
  • principles/citation-style.md — what a bib entry should look like (entry types, title capitalization, author format, DOI, special citekey cases).
  • principles/academic-writing.md — broader writing guidance (paragraph structure, prose principles).
  • install/mcp-add-zotero.md — Zotero MCP setup (only if you want Path 3).
  • install/install-better-bibtex.md — Better BibTeX install (only if you want Path 3).

Most co-authors only need this doc. The references above are for the rare day-2 question.

docs.title: Co-author quickstart (start here)
docs.text:
For co-authors and RAs on a team already using this setup. Sizing it up for your own team instead? Start with why collaboration is hard.

This is the fast path: a one-time GitHub setup (~10 min, below), then day-to-day work by asking Claude Code in plain language — no terminal or git commands to memorize. You don't have to learn git to use it; you can pick up as much or as little as you like over time. Prefer to click or type yourself? The same workflow, entirely by hand, is in the handbook and the manual workflow. Everything here is the shortcut.

docs.title: The one idea that makes everything click
docs.text:
There is ONE repository, and it lives on GitHub. Your project folder on your laptop — and every clone_XX/ folder on a multi-author project — is just a local mirror of that one repository. They all sync to the same GitHub.

  • Dropbox keeps your mirror backed up and shares the heavy data files (which never go into git).
  • GitHub is where everyone's work actually meets.
  • Overleaf reads only GitHub's main branch.

Nobody "owns" the project. The top project folder is a shared container — it isn't a git repo at all; it just holds the data everyone shares and one personal clone per person (clone_XX/). You run git only inside your own clone, so two people can never collide on the same git. Everyone can push, and everyone can merge their own work. There is no gatekeeper, and no lead.

Hold onto that picture; every step below is just a consequence of it.

docs.title: What you do ONCE (the only real setup, ~10 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Install Claude Code — the desktop app from claude.com (or the CLI) — and sign in with your Claude subscription.
  2. Get GitHub access, once. Accept the repository invitation (it arrives by email). Then open Claude Code in any folder and say:

    "Help me sign in to GitHub so I can push and pull." Claude walks you through it (usually: install GitHub Desktop, sign in once — that quietly handles authentication forever). You do this one time per computer.

  3. Tell Claude who you are, once — so your name is stamped on your work:

    "Set my git name to 'Your Name' and email to you@university.edu."

That's the entire setup. You never repeat it on this machine.

docs.title: Then: everything is a sentence to Claude Code
docs.text:
Open Claude Code inside your project folder — the one Dropbox already synced to C:\Users\<you>\Dropbox\<project>\. (To do that: in the Claude Code desktop app use Open folder and pick it; or, in the terminal, cd into the folder and run claude. Your project arrived via Dropbox — you do not download it from GitHub.)

Multi-clone projects: if your project folder contains clone_<XX>/ sub-folders (or its CLAUDE.md has a "Multi-clone layout" block), open Claude Code in your own clone_<XX>/ instead of the top folder — everywhere below, "your project folder" means your clone. Not sure which kind you're on? Ask a co-author, or see why. Single-clone projects: the top folder is correct, read on. Claude reads the project's rules on the way in, so it knows the safety conventions. Then just say what you want — in plain words; you don't need the exact phrasing below:

You want to… Say to Claude Code… What actually happens Get set up to work here "Help me set up my own copy to work on this project." Claude walks you through the short one-time setup of your personal copy (or tells you it's already set up). A few steps, once. Save your work "Commit my work." Claude records a snapshot of your changes, with a short note. Share it / back it up "Push my branch to GitHub." Your snapshots go up to GitHub — your off-machine backup, and how the team can get your work. Touches nothing in the shared paper. Propose it for the paper "Open a pull request for my work." Claude opens a pull request on GitHub — a tidy "here's what I changed, please pull it in." Actually put it in the paper (on GitHub, click Merge — or "merge my pull request") Merging the PR into main is the step that reaches the paper. This is a GitHub action, not something Claude does silently — see "two things" below. Get the team's latest "Bring in the latest changes from the team." Claude pulls everyone's merged work into your copy. Check you're working safely "Am I in the right folder to run git here?" Claude runs a quick check and tells you.

Why this path is recommended: when the project is set up for it (its CLAUDE.md carries the team conventions), Claude reads those rules and keeps you on the rails — it won't run git in the shared container folder, won't stage data or secrets, and checks you're in your own copy first. Raw git by hand has none of that. It's not magic, though: if something looks off, Claude tells you and you decide — so the conversational path is easier and safer, not hands-off.

Everything above you can also do by hand — Claude just saves the typing and remembers the rules. Here's the core save-and-share loop both ways:

Ask Claude CodeBy hand

"Commit my work, push my branch, and open a pull request."

Claude stages your changed files (explicit paths, never git add -A), commits with a sensible message, pushes, and opens the PR — pausing for your OK before the push.

git add <file>                 # explicit paths, never `git add -A`
git commit -m "what changed"
git push                       # then open the PR on GitHub

The full by-hand reference is the manual workflow.

docs.title: Two things every co-author gets wrong (now you won't)
docs.text:
1. Pushing is not the same as putting it in the paper. The full chain is:

    your branch → push to GitHub → merge into main → Overleaf "pull from GitHub"

Until the merge into main step, the paper (and Overleaf, if the paper uses it) don't see your work. So "I pushed it" is not "it's in the paper" — the merge is the missing link. (On an Overleaf-mastered project the paper text lives in Overleaf, not the repo, so this chain applies to your code and figures, not the .tex — ask a co-author if unsure.)

  1. You're allowed to merge your own work — but check what your team expects. On a standard private repo GitHub doesn't force a reviewer, so technically you can merge your own pull request. Whether you should is a team norm: a co-author often just merges; a research assistant usually wants the PI to look first. When in doubt, open the PR and say "ask a co-author to review" rather than self-merging. "Allowed" and "expected" are different things — this guide tells you what's allowed; your team tells you what's expected.

docs.title: If you use Codex instead of Claude Code
docs.text: Codex does not automatically read the project's rules, so the safety guardrails don't apply on their own. Two options: prefer Claude Code for anything touching git, or — if you stay in Codex — open the project's CLAUDE.md, read its "Multi-clone layout" section yourself, and be deliberate. The one rule that matters most: never run git in the project root (the top folder); only in your own clone_XX/.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• The daily rhythm, editing the paper text, and the full "when something breaks" playbook → co-author handbook.
  • Confused by a word (clone, branch, push, merge, pull request)? → plain-language primer.
  • Want the AI writing/review tools too (drafting, referee reports, figures)? → what the toolkit is — optional, not needed for the above.

docs.title: Something broke — fixes & recovery
docs.text: Why this page exists. Almost every problem a newcomer hits on this setup is one of a small, known set — and each has a calm, specific fix. This is the page to skim before you panic and the page to search when something looks broken. Most of these are not real damage; they're the structure doing its job in a way that's unfamiliar. Nothing here requires you to be a git expert. When in doubt, the safest move is almost always "stop and ask a co-author" — listed where it applies.

docs.title: Setup and environment
docs.text:
"Rscript / python is not recognized." The program is installed but not on your PATH (the default on Windows). Use the full path from the project's CLAUDE.md instead of the bare name — e.g. "C:\Program Files\R\R-4.4.3\bin\Rscript.exe" code/00_setup.R. If it's genuinely not installed, install R from cran.r-project.org (plain R, you don't need RStudio for setup).

Dropbox folder looks empty or half-there. Wait for the Dropbox tray icon to show a green tick — that means everything has actually downloaded. A folder that's still syncing looks like missing files but isn't. Don't start work (or git operations) until it's green.

"My clone has data/ and literature/ folders too — is that duplication?" No. Inside a clone those folders hold only the tracked skeletons (codebooks, .bib) — a few MB. The heavy raw data and PDFs are gitignored and live once in the shared container. Don't "clean up" the skeletons; they're meant to be there.

Scripts can't find the data. Your clone reaches the shared data through a .data-in-parent marker file at the clone root. If it's missing, create it (touch .data-in-parent) and re-run code/00_setup.*. The setup script's banner should show the data paths pointing at ../data/.

docs.title: "Where did my work go?"
docs.text:
A "conflicted copy" file appeared. Two people (or your own two machines) wrote the same file and Dropbox kept both. Don't delete either blindly — open both, reconcile by hand, keep the right content, then delete the "conflicted copy". Prevent it by the golden rule: one writer per file.

"My file is in Dropbox but a co-author says it's not in git." Both can be true — Dropbox-presence ≠ git-presence. A file is only in the project's real history once you git add + commit + push it. Hand-copying into Dropbox is not enough; commit it too.

"I think I lost work." Usually you didn't. Unpushed commits still live in your clone (and Dropbox backs the clone up). Check git status and git log in your clone first; the work is very often right there. If still stuck, ask a co-author before doing anything destructive.

docs.title: git and clones
docs.text:
Claude opened in the wrong folder / "am I in the right place?" Run the clone-discipline check (or ask Claude "check clone discipline"). It tells you whether you're inside your clone (good) or at the shared container (move into your clone). In the leaderless model there's no "lead" to worry about — the check is purely "are you in a clone?". It now also runs automatically when a session opens, so if you started at the container — or in a clone that's sitting on main, or one missing its .data-in-parent marker — Claude flags it up front instead of waiting for you to ask. It stays silent for a normal, healthy clone.

Claude asked before writing a file and warned about "the SHARED folder." That's the container-escape guard. You (or Claude) were about to write per-clone content — code/, output/, scripts/ — at the shared container root instead of inside your clone. The container is a sync point, not a workspace; a file written there becomes a stale duplicate that Dropbox syncs to everyone. Do the same write inside your clone (clone_<XX>/code/...), commit, and push — it reaches everyone cleanly. If something genuinely belongs at the shared root (a deliberate shared folder), declare it once in the container's CLAUDE.md under housekeeping: forbidden_root_children: (or in .scratch-allow), then confirm to proceed.

/housekeeping says "per-clone content at the container root." The same thing, found by the regular audit rather than at the moment of writing: a code//output//scripts/ folder is sitting at the shared container when its real copy belongs inside each clone (usually a leftover from before the project went multi-clone). Move it into your clone and delete the container copy — or, if it's deliberately shared, declare it as above.

"git push was rejected." Someone else's work landed on the branch first. Pull it in, then push: git fetch origin && git merge origin/main, resolve any conflicts, git push. This is normal, not an error.

"git pull says up to date but main has clearly moved on." Your clone is pinned to your own branch, so a plain pull only fetches your branch. Bring main in explicitly: git fetch origin && git merge origin/main. Do this every few days and always before opening a pull request.

"There's a .git at the shared container root." That's a legacy layout from before the leaderless migration, and it's the one genuinely risky state — a shared root repo whose branch can flip under everyone. Don't run git at the root. Work in your clone, and flag it so the project gets migrated (see the canonical spec, "Multi-clone pattern").

docs.title: Overleaf
docs.text:
A figure I fixed in Overleaf reverted. Figures travel code → git → Overleaf, one way. Editing a figure inside Overleaf gets overwritten on the next regeneration. Fix the script that makes the figure, commit, then bring it into Overleaf. (See the manual workflow.)

"Who can change the Overleaf project?" One person coordinates the Overleaf sync (the Overleaf admin role) so two people don't push conflicting versions through the bridge. That's a one-job designation, not a hierarchy — everyone is still an equal co-author.

docs.title: "We've been copying .tex from Overleaf by hand"
docs.text:
A common habit worth correcting: someone writes in Overleaf, then copies the .tex (or a PDF) into the Dropbox folder by hand. It looks fine — Dropbox and Overleaf match — but git silently falls behind (Dropbox-presence ≠ git-presence), and you end up with two diverging copies of a file that git is supposed to own.

The fix, easiest first:

  • Best — sync through git, don't copy. Use Overleaf's own git access to push/pull between Overleaf and git. Then git is always current and there's nothing to hand-copy; Dropbox updates itself via your clone.
  • If a file did get hand-copied (it happens), the one-line rescue is to also commit and push it to git right after — so the canonical history stops trailing what everyone is reading.
  • Stop hand-copying anything that lives in git. Edit it through git and let it flow; copying tracked files by hand is what creates the diverging copies in the first place.

(The standard flow this replaces is in the manual workflow.)

docs.title: When in doubt
docs.text: Some failure modes — especially multi-clone confusion — are hard to diagnose from a description. Ask a co-author; it's faster and safer than guessing, and it's never the wrong call.

docs.title: Why git, Dropbox, Overleaf & LaTeX
docs.text: Why the toolkit is built the way it is. Nothing here is needed to use it — but understanding the why makes the rules stick, and tells you when a rule does NOT apply. ~5 minutes. For term definitions, see the primer.

docs.title: 1. The two-layer model: Dropbox carries files, GitHub carries meaning
docs.text:
Each layer fails alone. Dropbox can't tell you which version of the code produced the figure in the submitted paper, can't host a review step, and silently lets two editors overwrite each other. Git chokes on gigabytes of data and has no instant sync. Together, each covers the other's gap:

flowchart TB
    subgraph DB["Dropbox — the storage layer"]
        D1["data/ — THE single copy<br/>(gitignored, never duplicated)"]
        D2["instant sync + backup<br/>of everything, incl. unpushed work"]
    end
    subgraph GH["GitHub — the meaning layer"]
        G1["commits: who changed what, when"]
        G2["branches + PRs: review before<br/>anything becomes 'production'"]
        G3["main: always compiles,<br/>always reproducible"]
    end
    DB ---|"same folder,<br/>two record-keepers"| GH

Every hard rule in the handbook is a consequence: data never goes in git (layer 1 owns it), work reaches the team only via push + PR (layer 2 owns meaning), and saving a file shares nothing (saving talks to layer 1 only).

docs.title: 2. One canonical file per artefact
docs.text: No paper_v2.tex, no 02_analysis_final.R. One file; git carries the history. Reasons: (a) filename versions force every reader to guess which is current — git's history doesn't; (b) "v2" conflates document type with revision (a real paper_v1.tex once turned out to be a conference abstract); (c) scripts and tools can rely on stable paths. When you want to experiment freely: that's what a branch is — a whole-project "v2" that can't disturb anyone and gets reviewed before merging.

docs.title: 3. Branch isolation, end to end
docs.text:
The thing that goes wrong in shared folders is uncoordinated parallel work. The system isolates parallel work at three levels:

flowchart LR
    subgraph You["your branch / your clone"]
        A["edit code + paper"] --> B["outputs land in<br/>output/_exploratory/<branch>/"]
        B --> C["copy final exhibit to<br/>output/figures/ (tracked)"]
    end
    C --> D["push + PR"]
    D --> E["review"]
    E --> F["merge to main:<br/>script + exhibit + text<br/>arrive together"]
  • Code and text: your branch — invisible to main until merged.
  • Exhibits: the setup scripts auto-redirect outputs to output/_exploratory/<branch>/ so two people's figures never overwrite. Promotion to the canonical output/figures/ is YOUR explicit copy on the branch — the PR then carries script, exhibit and paper text as one reviewable package. (Nothing moves "automatically on merge"; git merges files, it doesn't run pipelines.)
  • On multi-clone projects, whole working copies: each co-author has their own nested clone (clone_XX/) pinned to their branch, so even Dropbox-level sync can't mix two people's work-in-progress. Only the data stays shared — one copy, reached via a marker file.

docs.title: 4. Replication-first structure
docs.text: The folder layout (data/raw read-only, data/processed regenerable, numbered scripts, flat output/) mirrors what the AEA Data Editor expects in a replication package. The payoff: when the paper is accepted, the replication archive is a packaging step, not a re-engineering project. The same logic drives the data/raw/ read-only hard rule — every result must be reproducible from raw by re-running the pipeline, which is impossible if raw was ever edited in place.

docs.title: 5. Drift resistance: documents lie, generators don't
docs.text: This repo's measured failure mode is documentation going stale (~2-week half-life on inventory docs). The countermeasures are structural, not aspirational: the INDEX is generated from the tools' own metadata and a release check fails if it drifts; the recipes page is grep-checked against the actual command files; canonical specs that ship mirror copies are diff-checked; and the setup templates have a 19-check regression harness. Rule of thumb the team learned the hard way: a claim that something "works" counts only after it has been executed.

docs.title: 6. Why the AI layer is safe to let loose
docs.text: Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md (project rules) plus the user-level rules on every session start. The riskiest operations are gated regardless of what you ask for: pushes need explicit confirmation, data/raw/ writes are refused, broad staging (git add .) is blocked, destructive git operations require approval. That's why the handbook can honestly tell a novice that almost nothing here is unrecoverable if you stop and ask before improvising: the guardrails are in the tool's standing orders, not in the user's discipline.

docs.title: 7. The writing layer: LaTeX and Overleaf
docs.text: The two layers above explain why the project is structured this way; the paper itself rests on one more choice — LaTeX. Plain-text source is what makes the rest work: git can diff it line by line, Claude can edit it directly, and the output is reproducible. Overleaf is an optional add-on for browser compiling and track-changes review of prose (a paid feature the project owner sets up); you can compile LaTeX locally without it. The how-to for both is in LaTeX and Overleaf.

docs.title: Data provenance — raw + cleaning live IN the project
docs.text:
Every replication package must contain the raw data AND the code that cleans it. Importing a cleaned X.dta from another project of yours — even copying its cleaning do-file alongside "for reference" — breaks the chain. A replicator who only has this project must be able to get from the original survey or API export to every analytic file. That is the rule.

This is the AEA Data Editor and Social Science Data Editors line on what a replication package is. It is not a house preference.

docs.title: Where things go (AEA-aligned)
docs.text:
• data/raw/ — raw data files, flat, named clearly so each file is obviously paired with its documentation (MiningSurvey_2024_raw.dta, acled_kenya_2018-2024.csv). The AEA Data Editor's examples are typically flat (data/raw/cps0001.dat). Subfolders by source are also accepted — especially useful when one source ships many files (the AEA template separately notes openICPSR's 1000-file-per-directory cap, an archive limit rather than a structure recommendation).
  • data/documentation/ — codebooks, questionnaires, data-availability statements, dataset-level READMEs. One folder for all per-dataset documentation. Match the filenames so the pairing is obvious: MiningSurvey_2024_codebook.pdf ↔ MiningSurvey_2024_raw.dta.
  • code/01_clean.{R,do,py} — the canonical script that loads raw, applies every transformation, and writes the analytic file(s) to data/processed/. One per language. If a project has multiple data sources, sections inside 01_clean handle each — not a separate cleaning script per source.
  • data/raw/SOURCES.md — one line per raw file: where it came from, when, version/commit if relevant, access terms.

docs.title: "I want to use data from another project"
docs.text:
Common case: project A produced a cleaned dataset; project B wants to use it. The easy-but-wrong move is to copy A's data/processed/X.dta into B and treat A's cleaning code as a reference. That violates the rule — B is no longer self-contained.

The right pattern:

  1. Open a feature branch in B (<initials>/add-survey-data) so the integration is isolated and reviewable before it touches main.
  2. Copy A's raw into B's data/raw/, flat, named consistently with B's other raw. Copy the matching documentation into B's data/documentation/.
  3. Bring the new processing code in as a standalone scratch script on the branch (e.g. code/_exploratory/exp_survey_clean.do), run it, verify it produces the expected data/processed/ output.
  4. Integrate the working logic as a section of B's canonical code/01_clean.{R,do,py} — and delete the standalone scratch script. The merge target is one canonical cleaning file per language; the scratch script is a temporary scaffold, not part of main.
  5. Update data/raw/SOURCES.md with origin project + version/commit + date + access terms.
  6. Run end-to-end, verify, merge.

"Copy the cleaning code as read-only reference" does not satisfy the rule. The cleaning must actually run in this project.

docs.title: Edge cases
docs.text:
• PII / proprietary, but fits on disk. Raw goes in data/raw/ (gitignored where appropriate); provenance in SOURCES.md; the README carries a data-availability statement (how to obtain the data, access terms, ethics approvals). Cleaning code stays in code/.
  • Cannot live locally at all (TB-scale climate reanalysis, restricted-access registry data that the team is licensed to use but not to redistribute in any form). No data/raw/ copy; instead code/00_access.{R,do,py} documents or automates the fetch from the licensed source, and SOURCES.md + the README's data-availability statement carry the access path. The "raw + code in the project" rule applies to whatever portion can move — the access script is the chain's first link.
  • Live-updating sources (an API repulled on a schedule; UCDP / ACLED / WB refreshes). The downloaded snapshot in data/raw/ is dated; the fetch script lives in code/ and is part of the chain; SOURCES.md records the access date and the pinned source version. A re-pull becomes a new data/raw/ file alongside the previous one.
  • Pure theory / simulation. The rule applies trivially: data/raw/ may be empty or absent; processing collapses to the simulation script in code/. The chain "code → outputs" is still self-contained.
  • A published, frozen, citable third-party archive treated as your "raw" (rare but legitimate). The exception applies only if all three are true: (i) the archive has a persistent identifier (DOI, openICPSR study number, Dataverse handle); (ii) the exact version used is immutable and re-fetchable by a third party through that identifier; (iii) the archive is not authored by anyone on the current paper's author list. A sibling project of your own fails (iii); a working-paper replication package on a personal site that you might re-edit fails (ii); an ICPSR study with a fixed version DOI passes all three.

docs.title: In the multi-clone (leaderless) model
docs.text: This rule applies to the container, not each clone. In the multi-clone leaderless layout, data/ lives at the container root and is shared across clones via the .data-in-parent re-anchor — so "into the project's data/raw/" means into the container's single shared data/raw/, not a per-clone copy. The canonical code/01_clean.{R,do,py} lives inside each clone (git-tracked, merges to main like any other code); every co-author runs the same cleaning against the same shared raw.

docs.title: Why this rule exists
docs.text: The AEA Data Editor's policy is short and absolute: every figure, table, and in-text number must reproduce from the deposited package without manual intervention. If your data starts inside another project, you have put a manual intervention at the very first step — "go ask project A's owner for X.dta." A replicator (or a referee, or your future self) cannot do that. The rule rules out the easy version of that defect.

docs.title: How to check
docs.text: /audit-reproducibility and /audit-exhibits walk back from the manuscript's numbers, to outputs, to 02_analysis, to 01_clean, to data/raw/. A data/processed/X.dta with no producing code in code/ is an ORPHAN at the data layer — the same defect class as an orphan exhibit, gated on the same rule.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• AEA Data Editor — Guidance for Authors / Preparing for Data Deposit (aeadataeditor.github.io).
  • Social Science Data Editors — Template README (social-science-data-editors.github.io).
  • Companion: one-click replication on how the chain runs end-to-end across languages.
  • See also: replication packages.

docs.title: Designing experiments
docs.text: Most experiments fail on the whiteboard, not in the data. A control that differs from treatment on more than the one thing you care about, a self-reported outcome where a real-stakes one was possible, a comprehension check that quietly deletes half your treatment group — these are decided in an afternoon and then baked in forever. The experiment-design skill is a thinking partner for that afternoon: it walks your design out of your head one question at a time, pressure-tests each choice against what the literature actually supports, and flags what you forgot.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Run it when you're planning primary-data collection with random assignment — a survey or information experiment, an online study on Prolific/MTurk. It's an interview, not a form: one question at a time, you react, it moves on. It has two modes:

  • design — build a new experiment from scratch (question → arms & cover story → outcomes → integrity checks → randomization → power → a written spec).
  • review — hand it a draft (your own, a co-author's, a student's) and it audits the design against the checklist and returns a graded findings list (HALT / HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW), each with a fix.

It ends by producing a structured design spec that hands off to the pre-registration and irb-application skills (both shipped) — design here, then pre-register, then ethics.

docs.title: How it gives advice
docs.text:
Two rules make the advice trustworthy rather than opinionated:

  1. Every choice is options with pros and cons, each with a citation — you decide. It never quietly picks the "sensible" thing. When a decision has real consequences (an active vs. a passive control, how to power a noisy outcome), it lays out the trade-offs with the source that warrants each, states which way it would lean and why, and waits. There is rarely one right answer; the right answer depends on the experiment.
  2. It reminds you what you forgot. Before it writes the spec, a completeness gate walks sixteen checkpoints — is there one incentivized primary outcome? is the control matched? a pilot plan? — and flags anything missing rather than letting a silent gap through.

docs.title: The load-bearing rules it enforces
docs.text:
A handful of design rules catch most first-draft mistakes, so the skill holds them firm (each is grounded in the literature, and tuned to how careful applied work is actually done):

  • A matched (active) control, differing from treatment only in the payload of interest, so priming and attention difference out rather than confound the effect (Haaland, Roth & Wohlfart 2023).
  • One incentivized, real-stakes primary outcome (a donation, a real choice, an effort task) — self-reported attitudes are secondary.
  • Don't elicit the outcome's prior. Asking people their prior about the outcome primes and anchors it; the randomized control group already is your counterfactual. (Prior elicitation is for information-provision designs whose estimand is belief-updating — a special case, with its own guardrails.)
  • Never exclude on a post-treatment check. Dropping people who fail a comprehension or attention check measured after treatment breaks randomization and biases the effect (Montgomery, Nyhan & Torres 2018). Keep everyone (ITT); use the check as manipulation evidence or a pre-registered subsample/LATE.
  • Always pilot and pre-test before fielding, and calibrate the incentive size from the pilot — even for a design you've run before, if anything changed.
  • Fix the sample size in advance — no peeking-and-stopping (Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn 2011); power for the effect you expect, and for noisy real-stakes outcomes consider pooling several experiments with a pre-specified pooled MDE.

docs.title: What it covers today (and what's on the roadmap)
docs.text:
The deep, validated track is online survey / information experiments — the kind most common in applied micro and political economy. Field RCTs and lab experiments are genuinely different (clustering, take-up/compliance, spillovers; or session effects, repeated games, the strategy method) and are branched but not yet built — the skill will tell you plainly when your study is one of those and offer the shared design spine with that caveat, rather than pretending survey depth transfers. Those two tracks are on the roadmap.

For the figures a design implies: a CONSORT participant-flow diagram and a design-timeline schematic route to the TikZ diagram skill; the balance table and treatment-effect plots route to /descriptives and /coef-plot (in the research house style — no significance stars, no colour-by-significance).

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
The skill's recommendations are grounded in, and cite, a standard toolkit — the full list with links is bundled in the skill's references/background-and-sources.md. The load-bearing ones:

  • Haaland, Roth & Wohlfart (2023), "Designing Information Provision Experiments," JEL 61(1):3–40 — matched controls, obfuscated follow-ups, power floors.
  • Stantcheva (2023), "How to Run Surveys," Annual Review of Economics 15:205–234.
  • Harrison & List (2004), "Field Experiments," JEL 42(4):1009–1055 — the lab/artefactual/framed/natural-field taxonomy.
  • Duflo, Glennerster & Kremer (2007), "Using Randomization… A Toolkit" — power, clustering, stratification.
  • List, Sadoff & Wagner (2011); Bruhn & McKenzie (2009); McKenzie (2012) — allocation, balance, and ANCOVA.
  • Montgomery, Nyhan & Torres (2018) — why post-treatment conditioning ruins an experiment; de Quidt, Haushofer & Roth (2018) — bounding experimenter demand; Lin (2013) — covariate adjustment that cannot hurt precision.

docs.title: Experimental organization
docs.text:
Running an experiment means producing two distinct kinds of artefact, and they belong in two distinct places. The planning lives under project_management/experiments/<NN>/: pre-reg, IRB, randomization script, design memos, pilot notes. The data lives under data/raw/ and data/documentation/ — the actual responses and their codebooks. The split is the load-bearing idea on this page; the rest is just where each thing goes inside it.

Why split this way: planning artefacts are sensitive (IRB applications quote personal information; pre-regs name hypotheses you haven't yet tested) and they belong in the gitignored project_management/ tree. Data artefacts feed the canonical analysis pipeline through 01_clean and 02_analysis, so they belong in data/. Mixing the two (putting the response data inside project_management/experiments/, or the pre-reg inside data/documentation/) breaks both halves: the analysis pipeline cannot find its inputs, and sensitive planning artefacts leak into the git-tracked layer.

docs.title: The two homes
docs.text:
Artefact Where Why Pre-registration project_management/experiments/<NN>/ Planning artefact; sensitive IRB approval (this experiment) project_management/experiments/<NN>/ Specific to this experiment's design IRB approval (project-level / institutional master) project_management/IRB/ Not experiment-specific; lives with other IRB paperwork (folder structure §2a) Randomization script project_management/experiments/<NN>/ Design code; runs once to set up, then frozen Pilot memos ("what we learned") project_management/experiments/<NN>/ Planning artefact Survey instrument drafts project_management/experiments/<NN>/ Planning artefact Pre-analysis plan (PAP) project_management/experiments/<NN>/ Planning artefact Collected response data data/raw/ Canonical data flow Pilot response data data/raw/pilot_<…>.csv (default — cleaned by 01_clean like main data) OR project_management/experiments/<NN>/pilot_data/ if it stays internal only Two valid homes; pick by whether the pilot data feeds the analysis pipeline Randomization assignment file data/documentation/ NOT raw data — it documents the experimental design's realisation (who got which treatment); paired by name with the raw response data Codebook (REQUIRED) data/documentation/ Canonical home for every dataset; codebooks live with the data

A reader who already has the rule can stop here and skip to the worked example. The sections below explain what goes inside each home and the codebook rule that is genuinely load-bearing.

docs.title: What goes in project_management/experiments/<NN>/
docs.text:
Everything you produce while designing the experiment, plus the artefacts that document that design as it ran. The folder is gitignored, so co-author contracts and sensitive planning material are safe to keep here.

project_management/experiments/01_mining_RCT/
  preregistration.md           (or the filed pre-reg PDF — both are fine)
  IRB_approval_2025-09.pdf     (experiment-specific approval)
  design_memo.md               (why this design, which alternatives considered)
  randomization.do             (the script that runs once to set up)
  pap.md                       (pre-analysis plan)
  survey_instrument_draft_v3.docx
  pilot_memo_2025-11.md        (what the pilot taught us)

The randomization script lives here, NOT in code/. The reasoning: code/ is the analysis pipeline you re-run any time the inputs change. The randomization script ran once, produced the assignment file, and is then frozen forever. Re-running it after data collection would invalidate the experiment. Keeping it out of code/ makes the freeze visible.

Project-level institutional paperwork (the institutional master IRB, NDAs, funding paperwork) does NOT live here — that goes to project_management/IRB/ or project_management/admin/ per the folder-structure conventions. Only paperwork specific to this experiment lives in this folder.

docs.title: What goes in data/raw/ and data/documentation/
docs.text:
The collected response data and everything you need to read it correctly. Same rules as any other research dataset (see data-provenance): raw/ is read-only, documentation/ carries the codebook and any data-side metadata.

data/raw/
  MiningRCT_2026_responses.dta
  pilot_2025-11_responses.csv     (if cleaned via 01_clean; otherwise keep it under
                                   project_management/experiments/01_mining_RCT/pilot_data/)

data/documentation/
  MiningRCT_2026_codebook.md
  MiningRCT_2026_randomization_assignment.csv
                                  (who got which treatment — documentation of the
                                   experimental design's realisation, not raw response data)
  pilot_2025-11_codebook.md

The randomization assignment file is the subtlest call: it lives in documentation/, not raw/. It is NOT a raw observation — you constructed it deterministically from the randomization script. It documents the experimental design as it actually ran (which subject IDs ended up in treatment vs. control), and that documentation pairs by name with the raw response data the analysis pipeline reads in.

docs.title: The codebook rule — load-bearing
docs.text:
Every experimental dataset must have a codebook. There are no exceptions, and the timing matters: the codebook is needed FOR the pre-registration, which means it has to exist before data collection starts.

I'd reach for stronger framing than usual on this rule because we've seen the failure mode often enough. The chain is:

  1. The pre-registration specifies which variables you will collect and what each one measures. That commitment is the whole point of pre-registering.
  2. To write that section of the pre-reg honestly, you need to know your variable definitions in advance — which is exactly what a codebook is.
  3. Therefore the codebook is drafted BEFORE the pre-reg is filed and lives in data/documentation/ from that moment, even when data/raw/ is still empty.
  4. The pre-registration in project_management/experiments/<NN>/preregistration.md explicitly links to data/documentation/<experiment_id>_codebook.md. The link in both directions makes the pairing impossible to lose.

The "codebook lives with the data" half of the rule is shared with every other dataset; the "drafted before the pre-reg" half is what makes experimental work special. Together they enforce that you cannot file a pre-registration whose variable definitions you haven't yet written down.

docs.title: Naming convention
docs.text:
Per-experiment subfolder is <NN>_<experiment_id> (e.g. 01_mining_RCT, 02_narrative_priming). The <NN> keeps experiments sortable by order in which they ran; the <experiment_id> keeps them recognisable when you go looking for one.

Data and codebook filenames carry the same <experiment_id> slot:

  • data/raw/<experiment_id>_responses.<ext>
  • data/documentation/<experiment_id>_codebook.md
  • data/documentation/<experiment_id>_randomization_assignment.csv

So 01_mining_RCT gives you MiningRCT_2026_responses.dta paired with MiningRCT_2026_codebook.md. The pairing is by name; tools and humans can both find the codebook for a given dataset without checking a separate registry.

docs.title: What does NOT live here
docs.text:
A few things look like experiments but are not, and putting them under project_management/experiments/ muddles the planning archive:

  • Methodology robustness probes — "what happens if we cluster at the village level instead of the district level?" That is an analytic sensitivity check, not experimental work. It lives in code/02_analysis.<ext> as a section. The clue: the data is already collected; you are only varying the analysis.
  • Grant proposals that fund the experiment — those live in their own folder, outside the research project entirely. See the grants page for the why.
  • A figure showing the experimental design (the treatment-assignment diagram, the timeline) — that is a paper exhibit and lives in output/figures/ if a script produced it, or output/figures_external/ if it is hand-drawn. The fact that the figure ILLUSTRATES the experimental design does not make it experimental work; it makes it a paper exhibit.
  • Day-to-day fieldwork logistics — partner emails, enumerator scheduling, accommodation receipts. Those go in project_management/notes_and_feedback/ with the date prefix, not under experiments/. experiments/ is the design archive, not the operational log.

docs.title: Worked example — a full project shape
docs.text:
A multi-author RCT project, one year in, currently at QJE first-round submission:

mining_RCT_2026/
├── CLAUDE.md
├── README.md
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   │   ├── MiningRCT_2026_responses.dta
│   │   └── pilot_2025-11_responses.csv
│   ├── processed/
│   │   └── MiningRCT_analysis.dta
│   └── documentation/
│       ├── MiningRCT_2026_codebook.md
│       ├── MiningRCT_2026_randomization_assignment.csv
│       └── pilot_2025-11_codebook.md
├── code/
│   ├── 00_setup.do
│   ├── 01_clean.do
│   ├── 02_analysis.do
│   └── 99_run_all.do
├── output/
│   ├── figures/
│   ├── tables/
│   └── figures_external/
│       └── design_timeline_handdrawn.pdf      (paper exhibit, hand-drawn)
├── paper/
│   ├── paper.tex
│   ├── references.bib
│   └── revisions/
│       └── QJE/
├── literature/
│   └── _wiki/
└── project_management/
    ├── TODO.md
    ├── submission_log.md
    ├── submissions/
    │   └── 01_QJE/
    ├── experiments/
    │   └── 01_mining_RCT/
    │       ├── preregistration.md
    │       ├── IRB_approval_2025-09.pdf
    │       ├── design_memo.md
    │       ├── randomization.do
    │       ├── pap.md
    │       ├── survey_instrument_draft_v3.docx
    │       └── pilot_memo_2025-11.md
    ├── notes_and_feedback/
    │   ├── 2026-02-12_meeting_with_partner_NGO.md
    │   └── 2026-03-08_call_with_enumerator_lead.md
    ├── IRB/
    │   └── IRB_institutional_master_2024.pdf
    └── admin/
        └── partner_NGO_data_sharing_agreement.pdf

What is and isn't here is the point of the example. The design timeline figure lives in output/figures_external/, not under experiments/. The institutional master IRB lives in project_management/IRB/, not under experiments/01_mining_RCT/ (the experiment-specific approval does live there). The partner NGO meeting note lives in notes_and_feedback/ with a date prefix, not under experiments/. None of those distinctions matter the day you make them; all of them matter the day a co-author joins and tries to find something.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
• Codebook saved inside project_management/experiments/. Breaks the canonical "codebooks live in data/documentation/" rule and means the analysis pipeline cannot find the variable definitions for the data it is loading.
  • Randomization script in code/. It is not part of the analysis pipeline; it ran once to set up. Putting it in code/ invites someone (or 99_run_all.do) to re-run it, which would invalidate the experiment.
  • Re-running the randomization script after data collection. The randomization assignment is now part of the experimental design's history, not a regenerable artefact. Treat the script as frozen the day data collection starts.
  • Methodology robustness probes labelled as "experiments". A sensitivity check on cluster level is not an experiment; it is an analysis section. Calling it an experiment muddles both folders and the conceptual chain (the pre-reg becomes meaningless if every analysis variant counts as a new experiment).
  • Day-to-day fieldwork logistics in experiments/. Partner emails and enumerator schedules belong in notes_and_feedback/ with date prefixes. experiments/ is the design archive, not the daily operational log.
  • A pre-registration filed before the codebook exists. The pre-reg names the variables; the codebook defines them. Filing in the wrong order means the pre-reg's variable list is provisional — and the whole point of pre-registering is that it isn't.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Short answers to the questions that come up most. Each links to the page with the full story.

Is this the only "right" way to do things? No. It's a working solution. The genuinely required rules are short (never overwrite raw data; commit-to-share; one writer per file; exhibits trace to code); everything else — the exact layout, Dropbox, Overleaf, the tools — is a recommendation you can adapt. → required vs. recommended

Do I need to know git? No — you can pick it up gradually. Claude Code (or GitHub Desktop) handles the mechanics, and the primer defines every term in plain language.

Do I need Claude Code / an AI tool at all? No. Everything works by hand — Claude is a convenience, never a dependency. → the manual workflow, choosing your setup

Do I need Dropbox? Do I need Overleaf? Dropbox is the recommended default (backup + sharing), but a pure-GitHub setup works too. Overleaf is usually not needed — everything compiles locally; its one real draw is track-changes review of prose. → choosing your setup, new to Overleaf?

Who's the lead / who's in charge? Nobody — it's leaderless. Every co-author is equal; main lives on GitHub, owned by no one; anyone can push and merge. → why collaboration is hard

Where's the latest paper? Which clone has it? The canonical version is main on GitHub. On team projects, the shared container also keeps the compiled PDF of the current paper (recompiled automatically whenever anyone merges) so you can grab it for submission without hunting through clones. → what goes where

I have a figure that isn't made by code (a photo, a hand-drawn diagram, a logo) — where does it go? (open question — current answer) In your own clone, under output/figures_external/ — the sibling to output/figures/ that exists specifically for assets no script generates (so the tooling doesn't flag them as "exhibit with no code"). Then commit it, push, open a PR; when co-authors pull main they get it too. There is no output folder at the shared container root — outputs live in each clone and travel via main. (We're still settling the finer points of where working files live; if something feels ambiguous, ask before improvising.) → what goes where

What if I mess up or lose work? Almost nothing here is unrecoverable if you stop and ask before improvising — git history and Dropbox both back you up. → common issues

How do I actually run a skill? Three ways: a slash command (/name), just describe the task in plain language, or let it auto-trigger (a nudge, not a guarantee). → how skills are triggered

How do I set up a new — or existing — project? New: /bootstrap-project. Existing/messy: back up first, then /refactor-structure. → what goes where → "turning a messy project into this"

How do I update the toolkit later? Day-to-day research needs no updating; your installed version keeps working. Only when you want newer features — follow the canonical 4-step ritual in install the toolkit → "Updating later"; that's the full procedure (don't improvise a partial update). → also updates

Is my data safe? data/raw/ is read-only — never overwritten; data/processed/ is rebuildable from raw + code. There's even a guard that asks before any code writes to raw. → working with the shared data

Where do I read these docs / is this online? Yes — the hosted site is at kaligi.github.io/kai-team-claude-docs (search + sidebar; nothing to install, just open the link). The editable source lives in the private GitHub repo under docs/ (ask Kai for an invite). The website is auto-published from there into a separate public repo that contains only the built HTML — so the page is public even though the toolkit's source isn't. You read on the website; you install the toolkit from the private repo (Install).

docs.title: Quick wins to try first
docs.text:
Why start here. The fastest way to trust a new tool is to get one real, useful result out of it in five minutes — before committing to any workflow. Each thing below is self-contained: it works on its own, doesn't touch the collaboration setup, doesn't need you to learn git, and gives you something you'd actually want. Pick one, try it on a real paper of yours, and see whether it earns its place.

A note on honesty: these run on Claude Code with your own Claude subscription, and the data-figure one fetches from public data sources over the internet. They are genuinely useful, not magic — Claude can be wrong, so read its output the way you'd read a sharp RA's first draft.

docs.title: 1. A hostile pre-submission review — adversarial-review
docs.text:
The most valuable thing an AI can do for a paper is attack it. Ask:

"Run an adversarial review of this introduction." (paste it, or give a path)

The reviewer is explicitly tasked to find flaws — weak identification claims, overclaiming, gaps a referee would pounce on — not to reassure you. It's deliberately not balanced unless you ask for balance. Use it on a section you think is finished; it usually isn't.

docs.title: 2. A writing-quality diagnosis — scientific-writing-analysis
docs.text:
For prose rather than argument, this runs a structured analysis based on Lebrun's Scientific Writing — paragraph progression, lead sentences, topic-stress flow. Ask:

"Analyze the writing quality of this section."

You get specific, located feedback ("the lead of paragraph 7 doesn't connect to paragraph 6"), not vague "tighten this up" notes.

docs.title: 3. A publication-quality figure from real data — real-data-figure
docs.text:
Want a clean figure of, say, GDP per capita or battle deaths over time, without hunting down the data yourself? Ask:

"Make a time-series figure of for from World Bank data."

It sources from OWID / World Bank / V-Dem and others, and produces a publication-quality plot. This one needs internet access (it's fetching real data) and an R/Python environment — the most "setup-ish" of the four, but also the most impressive when it lands.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: If one of these earned its keep and you want to use Claude on a shared project with co-authors, that's where the collaboration setup comes in — start with why collaboration is hard, then the quickstart. If you'd rather understand what Claude Code actually is first, read how Claude Code thinks.

docs.title: Folder structure — the full layout
docs.text: Builds on project-structure (the canonical top-level layout) and the where-to-put-things cheat sheet. Where the canonical layout fixes the top-level tree, this page fills in the detail the cheat sheet doesn't have room for: the internal structure of project_management/, multi-paper projects, the grants convention, and the presentations and submissions sub-patterns. Each section states the rule, gives the reason, shows an anchored example, and notes the variant when the default doesn't fit.

docs.title: What this adds (and what is already settled)
docs.text:
The canonical layout in project-structure pins down the top-level tree: data/, code/, output/, paper/, literature/, project_management/, and .claude/tmp/ (session scratch). The cheat sheet pins down most artefact homes inside those. Five things go a level deeper here.

The five gaps:

  1. The internal layout of project_management/ — which subfolders exist, in what order, and when each one is required vs. optional.
  2. project_management/admin/ — what actually lives there. The folder is referenced in the cheat sheet but not described.
  3. Multi-paper projects. What do you do when one research project produces two papers? Per-paper subtrees, shared layout with suffixes, or split into two projects?
  4. Grants — a separate folder convention. Grants behave like a paper project but they are NOT a paper project. Where do they live, and what is the recommended layout for the writeup itself?
  5. Presentations sub-pattern. The cheat sheet says paper/presentations/<venue>_<date>/; the contents and naming inside that folder are not pinned down.

Each section below states the rule, gives the WHY, shows one anchored example, and notes the variant when the default doesn't fit.

docs.title: §1 The internal layout of project_management/
docs.text:
The rule. project_management/ has five canonical subfolders and two top-level files. Create a subfolder only when you have content for it.

project_management/
├── TODO.md                      top-level: live task list
├── submission_log.md            top-level: one line per submission round (see submissions)
├── submissions/                 one folder per round; see submissions.md
├── experiments/                 one folder per experiment; see experimental-organization.md
├── notes_and_feedback/          dated meeting / call / feedback / decision notes
├── IRB/                         IRB approvals + ethics correspondence; see §2a
└── admin/                       other institutional paperwork (NDAs, contracts, funding letters); see §2b

Why this layout. Each subfolder maps to a distinct kind of artefact with its own retention policy. Submissions and experiments are PER-EVENT (numbered, dated, immutable once closed). Notes and feedback ACCUMULATE over the life of the project (dated, queryable, see notes-and-feedback). Admin is one-off paperwork. TODOs and the submission log are the only files small enough and live enough to sit at the top of project_management/ directly.

Skip-the-folder rule. A solo theory project never runs an experiment, so experiments/ should not exist. A project not yet submitted has no submissions/. Create the subfolder the day you have the first file for it. Empty folders are noise.

docs.title: §2a project_management/IRB/
docs.text:
The rule. IRB approvals, ethics committee correspondence, and the institutional paperwork around them. Project-level IRBs live here; experiment-specific IRBs live with the experiment per the experimental-organization page.

Why a dedicated folder. Most projects that touch human subjects collect at least one IRB document, and "where is the IRB letter?" is a real question that comes up two years into a project. A named folder means one answer. IRB-adjacent paperwork (ethics committee questions and answers, amendment filings, expiration extensions) accumulates around the same letters, so co-locating it saves searching.

Skip-the-folder rule. A project with no IRB never creates this folder. Theory papers, descriptive analyses of public data, and similar projects skip it cleanly.

docs.title: §2b project_management/admin/
docs.text:
The rule. Other institutional paperwork that is neither data, nor a submission, nor an experiment, nor IRB, nor a meeting note. Specifically:

  • Funding award letters, grant administrative correspondence, no-cost extension paperwork (the funded paperwork — grant proposals live in their own folder per §4).
  • Co-author contracts, NDAs, data-sharing agreements.
  • Conference / workshop acceptance letters, formal travel reimbursement paperwork relevant to the project.
  • Any other one-off institutional paperwork the project generates.

Why split this from IRB/. Two reasons. Semantically, "an NDA in a folder called IRB" reads oddly to a co-author looking for an NDA. Practically, IRB is the recurring item that deserves its own name; the other admin paperwork is a thin catch-all that benefits from being kept distinct so neither folder becomes a junk drawer.

Skip-the-folder rule. Most projects collect a handful of admin documents at most. If admin/ ends up with one file, that's fine — the folder is a name, not a contract that it must fill up. Most projects without external contracts or grants never create it at all.

docs.title: §3 Multi-paper projects
docs.text:
Those five subfolders cover one paper cleanly. The harder question is what happens when a project grows a second paper — which is where the per-event discipline above starts to strain, and where the next rule earns its keep.

The rule. One project = one paper = one shared pipeline. When a project produces a second paper, GRADUATE the second paper into its own project (the exception — a genuinely shared pipeline — is below). The two then share the data via the standard data/raw/ discipline (whoever owns the raw data keeps it; the second project imports the cleaning code per the data-provenance rule). I default to splitting; the shared-pipeline exception is rarer in practice than it sounds when you first hit it.

Why this default. A two-paper project layout sounds simple in the abstract ("just add paper_B/ next to paper/") and gets confusing fast in practice. code/02_analysis.R belongs to which paper? Are the figures in output/ shared or per-paper? Co-authors who joined for paper B do not need read access to paper A's revisions. The cleanest answer is to take the seam at the project boundary, where the kit's tools (clones, gitignore, submission folders) already work.

The exception — share-the-pipeline split. When the two papers genuinely share the analysis pipeline (same data, same cleaning, same 02_analysis.R, different write-ups), per-paper subtrees inside ONE project are acceptable:

project-root/
├── data/                         shared
├── code/                         shared
├── output/                       shared
├── paper_A/                      first paper: paper_A.tex, references.bib, presentations/, revisions/
├── paper_B/                      second paper: paper_B.tex, ...
├── literature/                   shared (one Zotero project per group of papers)
└── project_management/
    ├── submissions/              flat; per-round folder is NN_<journal>_<paper>/
    └── notes_and_feedback/       shared

The submission folders carry the paper identifier in the name (05_QJE_paperA/, 06_AER_paperB/) so the submission log stays one file. The canonical paper/ becomes paper_A/ + paper_B/ only when both genuinely share the pipeline; otherwise split.

Anti-pattern. Long-lived branches for the second paper. Branches are for in-flight work, not for parallel write-ups; a branch that lives for a year is a sign the split should have happened.

docs.title: §4 Grants — separate folder convention
docs.text:
A grant raises the mirror image of the multi-paper question: it behaves like a paper project but is not one, so it gets the opposite treatment — its own folder, never nested inside the work it funds.

Scope caveat. This page deliberately stays short on grants. The rule for where grants live is firm; the how to structure a grant proposal internally is light-touch.

The rule. A grant proposal lives in its OWN folder, outside any research project. Keep grants out of any single research project so they survive when the project moves on.

Why. A grant is a writing project with its own bibliography, its own panel-interview slides, and its own submission round (the funder is the journal-equivalent). It draws on past research and seeds future research, but its lifecycle does not match any one paper. Mixing it into a paper folder breaks the paper's clean structure; mixing two grants into a single folder loses the per-grant submission history.

Suggested layout (per grant) — the paper layout, scaled down. Not prescriptive; treat it as a starting point.

grant_<funder>_<NN>/
├── proposal.tex                  main writeup
├── references.bib
├── output/                       figures / tables for the proposal
├── presentations/                slides for the panel interview, if any
├── project_management/
│   ├── notes_and_feedback/       feedback from mock review
│   ├── IRB/                      if the grant requires ethics paperwork up front
│   └── admin/                    application paperwork, signed forms, funder correspondence
└── literature/                   reading specific to this proposal

Anti-pattern. Putting a grant folder inside a research project's project_management/. The grant outlives the project; nesting it loses the grant when the project closes.

docs.title: §5 Presentations sub-pattern
docs.text:
Presentations raise a different concern from the boundary questions above: not where the project lives, but whether a folder stays portable when you copy it to a co-author or a conference laptop.

The rule. A talk lives in paper/presentations/<venue>_<YYYY-MM-DD>/, with the deck and all its assets in the same folder so it compiles cleanly.

paper/presentations/
├── NBER_2026-04-12/
│   ├── slides.tex                or slides.qmd
│   ├── figures/                  copies of the figures used in this talk
│   ├── logo_nber.png
│   └── slides.pdf                compiled output (small enough; gitignore the build dir)
├── AEA_2026-01-05/
│   └── ...

Why assets sit next to the deck. A talk deck references figures, logos, a photograph the venue asked for. If those live in a separate assets/ sub-folder, the deck breaks when you copy the folder to share it. Co-located assets keep the talk folder self-contained.

Naming. <venue>_<YYYY-MM-DD>/. Venue is short (NBER, AEA, RESTAT-revise); date is the talk date, not the prep date. Sorting by name then sorts by venue, which is usually what you want when you re-use a talk for a similar audience.

Skip-the-folder rule. Reuse a deck across two venues by COPYING the folder and editing the copy, not by editing the original in place. The previous venue's deck is the historical record; reusing in place erases what you actually presented.

docs.title: Worked example — a complete project tree
docs.text:
Each rule above governs one corner of the tree. Here is how they compose into a single real project, with the skip-the-folder rule visible in what's absent. The default solo-paper project that ran for two years, was presented twice, and is currently at QJE R&R:

gehring2026narrative/
├── CLAUDE.md
├── README.md
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   ├── processed/
│   └── documentation/
├── code/
│   ├── 00_setup.R
│   ├── 01_clean.R
│   ├── 02_analysis.R
│   └── 99_run_all.R
├── output/
│   ├── figures/
│   ├── tables/
│   └── figures_external/
├── paper/
│   ├── paper.tex
│   ├── references.bib
│   ├── revisions/
│   │   └── QJE/
│   │       ├── response_to_referees.tex
│   │       └── referee_reports_formatted.tex
│   ├── presentations/
│   │   ├── NBER_2026-04-12/
│   │   └── AEA_2026-01-05/
│   └── old/
├── literature/
│   └── _wiki/
├── project_management/
│   ├── TODO.md
│   ├── submission_log.md
│   ├── submissions/
│   │   ├── 01_AER/
│   │   ├── 02_QJE/
│   │   └── 03_QJE_revision/
│   ├── notes_and_feedback/
│   │   ├── 2026-03-15_meeting_with_Arne.md
│   │   ├── 2026-04-10_decision_framing_for_intro.md
│   │   └── 2026-05-22_transcript_AEA_session.md
│   ├── experiments/                 (does not exist — no experiment)
│   └── IRB/
│       └── IRB_2024-09.pdf
└── .claude/tmp/

Notice experiments/ is absent — the project has no experiment, so the folder does not exist. output/figures_external/ exists because one figure is a photograph. revisions/QJE/ exists because the paper is currently at R&R.

docs.title: Anti-patterns — the five traps, collected
docs.text:
Each section above flagged its own trap; here they are in one place for a quick pre-flight scan:

  • A project_management/ populated with empty submissions/, experiments/, IRB/, and admin/ folders "in case we need them." Create the folder when you have the first file for it.
  • A second paper started inside the first paper's project as paper2/ without per-paper-subtree (no paper_A/ / paper_B/). Pick the split, don't half-do it.
  • Grant proposals inside a project's project_management/admin/. Grants live in their own folder.
  • Presentation assets in a sibling assets/ folder. Co-locate with the deck.
  • Reusing a talk folder in place for the next venue. Copy the folder; the previous deck is the historical record.
