docs.title: Maintainer notes (for repo owners and people who edit kai-team-claude)
docs.text: This file is for anyone who pushes to the repo — initially Kai, eventually trusted co-authors with PR access. Predocs and read-only collaborators can skip it.

docs.title: Principle: what goes in the repo, what stays in ~/.claude/
docs.text:
A skill / agent / command goes in kai-team-claude if it is:

  • Necessary for team members working on shared papers (would they actually use it?), AND
  • Mature enough to be a stable interface (not a half-finished prototype), OR
  • Pure infrastructure that other items depend on (e.g., agents called by commands).

A skill / agent / command stays in ~/.claude/ only (never in the repo) if it is:

  • A personal experiment or prototype not yet ready for others
  • Specific to a project the rest of the team isn't on (e.g., something for a consulting engagement nobody else is involved in)
  • Project-internal output you don't want others to see (e.g., a skill that contains sensitive review notes)
  • Something whose value is purely speculative — keep it private until proven

When in doubt: err on the side of keeping it local first, share later. It's trivial to add a polished local item to the repo (one cp and a commit). It's much harder to retroactively remove or hide an item that's already public.

docs.title: How personal items are protected
docs.text:
The install scripts (install.ps1, install.sh) use per-item overlay logic:

  • For each item the repo contains (e.g., skills/kai-writing/), the install script replaces just that one in ~/.claude/.
  • Items in ~/.claude/ that are not named in the repo are left alone.

Concretely, if your ~/.claude/skills/ contains:

adversarial-review/         (also in repo)
kai-writing/                (also in repo)
real-data-figure/           (also in repo)
research-presentation/      (also in repo)
tikz-figure/                (also in repo)
_my-private-experiment/     (NOT in repo — local-only)
scientific-writing-analysis-SKILL.md  (NOT in repo — using Anthropic plugin instead)

Running bash install/install.sh after git pull will: - Replace the five items that are in the repo (with backup of previous versions) - Leave _my-private-experiment/ and scientific-writing-analysis-SKILL.md alone

So you can safely accumulate personal items in ~/.claude/ without worrying about the install script wiping them.

docs.title: Naming convention for local-only items
docs.text:
To make local-only items obvious in directory listings (and to avoid future collisions with new repo items), prefix them with _ (underscore):

~/.claude/skills/_my-experiment/
~/.claude/agents/_personal-helper.md
~/.claude/commands/_private-shortcut.md

This isn't enforced anywhere, just a hygiene convention.

docs.title: Auditing what's where
docs.text:
Run the audit script to see, at a glance, what's in your ~/.claude/ vs the repo:

bash install/audit.sh

Output groups items into three buckets: - In both — these will be replaced on the next install - Local-only — these will be left alone (your personal items) - Repo-only — these will be added on the next install

This is the safest way to preview a git pull && install before running it.

docs.title: Adding a new item to the repo
docs.text:
If you've polished a personal skill / agent / command and want to share it:

  1. Decide if it really belongs in the repo. Apply the principle above.
  2. Copy from ~/.claude/ into the repo working copy. 
    cp -r ~/.claude/skills/<name>/ ~/code/kai-team-claude/skills/
    (Or for an agent / command: copy the single .md file.)
  3. Read through the file for personal references that shouldn't be public — project paths, draft notes, references to specific people who aren't on the team.
  4. Sanitize anything inappropriate. If the item references Kai's voice or team conventions, that's fine; if it references a specific manuscript or review note, redact.
  5. Commit and push with a descriptive message: 
    cd ~/code/kai-team-claude
git add skills/<name>          # explicit path — never `git add -A` or `git add .`
git commit -m "skills/<name>: add <one-line description>"
git push                       # ask before pushing (see git-workflow rule)
  6. Tell the team so they git pull && install.

docs.title: Authoring hooks: the payload-source rule (id-mining 001, 2026-07-30)
docs.text:
A hook must match on the specific payload FIELD it means — tool_input.command for "what the session ran", tool_input.file_path/new_string for "what it wrote" — never on the raw stdin payload. The payload spans both halves:

  payload = { tool_input.command , tool_response.output }
                    ^                      ^
            what the hook MEANS      what ALSO gets grepped

The field case: a project-local exhibit-dirty hook grepped the whole payload for fig_*.pdf; a find run to LOCATE a figure to link then tripped it via its OUTPUT, and the Stop gate demanded a visual review in a session that had touched no exhibit. Two of KG's rules (link your artifacts / review changed exhibits) were in mechanical conflict — from one wrong grep.

The asymmetry to check both directions: matching output as well as input fails LOUD AND SAFE (blocks when nothing happened); matching input too narrowly fails SILENT AND UNSAFE (a real graph export inside a subagent or MCP call slips through). Both are payload-source errors.

Shell hooks extract the field first, e.g. CMD=$(python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin).get('tool_input',{}).get('command',''))") — the shipped Python gates all do this; a hand-rolled hook must too. No hook is promoted to the marketplace without passing this check (and its able-to-fail battery must include a probe where the pattern appears ONLY in tool_response and must NOT fire).

docs.title: Removing an item from the repo
docs.text:
Sometimes a shared item turns out to be too project-specific or has been replaced by an Anthropic plugin (e.g., scientific-writing-analysis). To remove:

  1. git rm -r the item in the repo working copy.
  2. Commit and push with a clear message: 
    git rm -r skills/<name>
git commit -m "skills/<name>: remove (now provided by <plugin/replacement>)"
git push
  3. Note: removing from the repo does not delete it from collaborators' ~/.claude/. Their local copies stay until they manually delete them. That's usually what you want (no surprise deletions on git pull).

docs.title: Editing an item that's in the repo
docs.text:
Edit it in the repo working copy at ~/code/kai-team-claude/, then push. Don't edit in ~/.claude/ first — that creates two sources of truth and you'll forget which one is current.

If you want to test a change locally before pushing:

# edit the file in ~/code/kai-team-claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
cp ~/code/kai-team-claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
# test in a Claude Code session
# if good, commit and push
cd ~/code/kai-team-claude && git add skills/<name>/SKILL.md && git commit -m "..." && git push

docs.title: Sanitization checklist before pushing
docs.text:
Before any git push to a public-ish repo (even private with several collaborators):

  • [ ] No absolute paths like C:/Users/<name>/... — use ~/... or relative paths
  • [ ] No hardcoded API keys, tokens, or credentials
  • [ ] No project-internal manuscript IDs (e.g., journal submission numbers)
  • [ ] No personal email addresses other than the maintainer's
  • [ ] No references to specific reviewers, collaborators outside the team, or private project decisions
  • [ ] References to style profiles and team conventions are fine and expected

If unsure: open an Issue rather than push, ask Kai.

docs.title: Cutting a release (versioning)
docs.text:
The kit uses two version levels — see "How versioning works" on the Updates page for the rationale. As a maintainer you touch both:

  1. Per-plugin semver. When you change a plugin's behaviour, bump its plugin.json version (major.minor.patch) in the same commit. Patch = fix, minor = additive feature, major = breaking change.
  2. Add a changelog entry. Put a dated ## YYYY-MM-DD — <headline> block at the top of the root CHANGELOG.md describing what changed and, briefly, why. This is the single source of truth — the site's Updates page pulls it in at build time via a snippet include, so never duplicate it into docs/.
  3. Roll the CalVer cut when the month turns (or when a batch of changes is meaningfully a new vintage): edit the root /VERSION file to the new YYYY.MM. That's the version people quote when they ask "are we on the same conventions?".
  4. Run the gate before pushing: RUN_HARNESS=1 bash scripts/release_check.sh (INDEX freshness, recipe tokens, canonical-mirror sync, the 00_setup harness, and the mkdocs build). Push only when it's green.

docs.title: The manual workflow (by hand, no AI required)
docs.text: Why this page exists. Nothing in this setup requires Claude Code. The folder structure, the git flow, the Overleaf sync — all of it is plain, ordinary tooling you can drive entirely by hand. Claude is a convenience that removes typing and remembers the rules for you; it is not a dependency. If you prefer to work manually, want to save tokens, or are simply more comfortable in your own terminal, this page is the complete by-hand path. The structure is deliberately compatible with manual coding — you can mix: do the prose by hand, let Claude generate a figure, commit yourself.

docs.title: The golden rule: one writer per file at a time
docs.text:
Every other rule is downstream of this one. Two people editing the same file at the same time is the root cause of nearly every collaboration disaster — Dropbox conflicted-copies, git merge conflicts, lost edits. The whole structure exists to make "one writer per file" the natural state:

  • You work in your own clone, so your working copies are yours alone.
  • Shared things that genuinely have one owner (the bibliography, the Overleaf project) have one designated person who writes them; everyone else proposes changes through that person or through a pull request.

If you remember nothing else, remember: before you edit a shared file, make sure you're the only one editing it.

docs.title: Dropbox-presence ≠ git-presence
docs.text:
The single most common confusion. A file being visible in your Dropbox folder does not mean it is in git. They are two independent systems:

Dropbox git What it syncs every file in the folder, instantly only what you git add + commit + push What it's for backup, seeing each other's folders history, merging, the canonical main A new file appears automatically, everywhere only after you commit and push it

So a file can be sitting in Dropbox, synced to everyone, and still be completely absent from git history. That's fine for scratch notes — but for anything that belongs to the project (code, paper text, figures), "it's in Dropbox" is not "it's saved properly". It has to be committed and pushed to be part of the real record.

docs.title: The Overleaf ↔ git ↔ Dropbox triangle
docs.text:
On Overleaf-mastered papers there are three places a file can live, and the sync between Overleaf and git is manual — there is no magic bridge keeping them aligned. This is the part that trips people up, so here it is explicitly:

flowchart LR
    OL["Overleaf<br/>(where prose is written)"]
    DBX["Dropbox folder<br/>(backup + sharing)"]
    GIT[("git / GitHub main<br/>(history + canonical record)")]
    OL -. "manual sync via Overleaf's git: push / pull" .-> GIT
    GIT -. "manual sync via Overleaf's git: push / pull" .-> OL
    GIT -- "auto, via your clone" --> DBX
    DBX -- "auto" --> GIT

The standard: keep git the source of truth. git holds the canonical record, so whatever is authoritative has to reach git. On Overleaf-mastered papers that means syncing Overleaf ↔ git through Overleaf's own git access (push/pull), not by shuffling files around. Dropbox then updates itself, because your clone lives inside it — you don't manage Dropbox by hand at all.

The anti-pattern to avoid: writing in Overleaf and then copying the .tex (or a PDF) into the Dropbox folder by hand. It looks like it works — Dropbox and Overleaf match — but git silently falls behind (Dropbox-presence ≠ git-presence), and you now have two diverging copies of a file that lives in git. If hand-copying has been your team's habit, that's a common mistake with a clean fix — see common issues.

Two corollaries that prevent the nastiest tangles:

  • Figures travel one way: code → git → Overleaf. A figure is generated by a script, committed to git, and then pulled/uploaded into Overleaf. Never "fix" a figure inside Overleaf — the next regeneration overwrites it and the source-of-truth (the script) never learned about your change.
  • Never hand-copy a file that also lives in git. If a file is tracked in git, edit it through git and let it flow — copying it by hand around git creates two diverging versions of the same thing, which is exactly the conflict you're trying to avoid.

docs.title: Doing the core tasks by hand
docs.text:
Each of these is a normal git operation. The full, illustrated runbook is in the setup walkthrough and per-project onboarding; the short version:

Task By hand Set up your clone git clone <repo> clone_<XX> inside the Dropbox folder, then touch .data-in-parent (why) Start work cd clone_<XX>, git checkout -b <XX>/<topic> Save a checkpoint git add <file> (explicit paths — never git add -A), git commit -m "..." Share it git push, then open a pull request on GitHub Get others' merged work git fetch origin && git merge origin/main Merge a PR review on GitHub, then merge (anyone can — there's no lead)

The one habit the structure asks of you is in the first row: work inside your clone_<XX>/, never at the shared container root. Why that matters is the whole of why collaboration is hard.

docs.title: When to let Claude do it instead
docs.text: Everything above, Claude Code can do for you — and it remembers the rules (explicit git add paths, "push asks first", commit-message hygiene) so you don't have to. The trade is tokens and a little trust. A reasonable middle: do the parts you're confident in by hand, and ask Claude for the parts you'd otherwise have to look up. Each task page in this site shows both paths — the manual commands and the one-line Claude request — so you can pick per task, not once-and-for-all.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text: If you've never used Claude Code, start here — it's a five-minute orientation, then pointers to the best existing guides (no need for us to re-write what Anthropic already documents well).

docs.title: What it is, in one line
docs.text: Claude Code is Anthropic's AI assistant that runs in your terminal (or as a desktop app / IDE extension) and can actually read, edit, and run files in your project — not just chat about them. If that distinction is new, read our short How Claude Code thinks — it explains "chat vs. a harness" and, importantly, that you approve every action; it's not autopilot.

docs.title: Get started (external, official)
docs.text:
• Official quickstart — the canonical getting-started guide from Anthropic: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/quickstart. It covers signing in, your first session, and the basic commands. You need a terminal, a project folder, and a Claude subscription (Pro/Max/Team).
  • It also runs on the web, as a desktop app, and inside VS Code / JetBrains — the quickstart lists all of them.

docs.title: Then, for our setup
docs.text:
Once Claude Code itself works, the toolkit (our skills + plugins for economics-paper work) installs on top:

  • What the toolkit is — skills, plugins, the marketplace.
  • Install the Claude Code toolkit — our step-by-step, cross-platform, copy-paste install (this is the one to follow for this kit).
  • First things to try — a useful result in five minutes.

New to terminals too? The terminal in 10 minutes primer removes the nerves first.

docs.title: LaTeX
docs.text: Much of this kit assumes your paper is written in LaTeX, and several pages say "you can just compile it locally." If LaTeX is unfamiliar — or you've always used Word — here's what it is, why it's worth it (especially now, with AI), and how to set it up locally so you can produce a PDF without any online service.

docs.title: What LaTeX is
docs.text: LaTeX is a typesetting system for documents. Instead of formatting by hand as you type (Word), you write plain text with light markup — \section{...}, \cite{...}, an equation between $ … $ — and a compiler turns it into a polished PDF with consistent maths, references, and layout. The source is just text files (paper.tex, references.bib), which is what makes everything else in this kit work.

docs.title: Why LaTeX — especially now, with AI
docs.text:
• Git and an AI assistant both work best on plain text. Because the source is text, git shows you a clean line-by-line history of every change, and Claude Code can read and edit the .tex directly — neither works well on Word's binary files.
  • The old downside is mostly gone. LaTeX's reputation for fiddly syntax was the main reason to avoid it. With an LLM writing and fixing the markup for you, that cost largely disappears — you describe what you want, it produces correct LaTeX.
  • Professional output for free. Maths, cross-references, bibliographies, and tables come out consistent and reproducible, the same every time.
  • Word is still fine if you prefer it — but you give up clean git diffs, smooth AI editing, and the Overleaf track-changes workflow. For a paper that several people and an agent will all edit, LaTeX pays off.

docs.title: Local setup — so you can compile without Overleaf
docs.text:
You don't need Overleaf to use LaTeX; install a TeX distribution once and you can compile on your own machine, offline. Install the distribution for your OS (these are the standard installers — follow their own instructions, nothing to copy from here):

  • Windows: MiKTeX — installs missing packages on demand.
  • macOS: MacTeX.
  • Linux / cross-platform: TeX Live.

An editor helps but isn't required: VS Code with the LaTeX Workshop extension, or TeXstudio — or just compile from the terminal. Once installed, building a PDF is one command in the paper folder:

latexmk -pdf paper.tex

docs.title: LaTeX vs. Overleaf — use either
docs.text: Overleaf compiles in the browser (no local install) and adds track-changes review of prose. Local LaTeX is free, works offline, and integrates directly with git and Claude Code. Many people use both — local for day-to-day editing, Overleaf when a co-author wants to mark up the text. (Overleaf's track changes and git sync are paid-plan features the project owner sets up — see New to Overleaf?.) Which you need is part of choosing your setup.

docs.title: Overleaf
docs.text: Overleaf is a browser-based editor for LaTeX — the typesetting system most economics papers are written in. It's where a lot of co-authors do their actual writing. If you've never used it, this is a short orientation plus the best existing tutorials (Overleaf's own are excellent; no point re-writing them).

docs.title: What it is, in one line
docs.text: Overleaf = write LaTeX in your browser, see the compiled PDF next to it, with several co-authors editing the same document. No local LaTeX install needed to start.

docs.title: Do you even need Overleaf? (often no)
docs.text:
Worth saying up front: Overleaf is optional. Everything in a paper compiles locally — latexmk -pdf paper.tex (or your editor's build button) produces the same PDF on your own machine, with no browser and no account. The git- mastered mode keeps paper.tex in git and never touches Overleaf at all.

The one genuine reason to use Overleaf is track changes — the review/suggesting mode where co-authors mark edits and comments on the prose in the browser and you accept/reject them, the way you would in Word. If your team doesn't need track changes, you can skip Overleaf entirely and compile locally — it's one less moving part. Choose Overleaf for the track-changes review, not out of habit.

docs.title: Learn it (external, from Overleaf)
docs.text:
• Learn LaTeX in 30 minutes — the standard beginner tutorial; assumes zero prior LaTeX and walks you through your first document (titles, math, lists, tables, references): https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Learn_LaTeX_in_30_minutes.
  • More tutorials (figures, bibliographies, tables, beamer slides): https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Tutorials.

docs.title: How Overleaf fits our workflow
docs.text:
This is the part specific to collaborating with this setup:

  • On Overleaf-mastered papers, the prose lives in Overleaf and everything else (code, figures, the bibliography) lives in git. One person is the Overleaf admin (only the Overleaf project owner can set up the Overleaf↔git sync).
  • The bibliography (references.bib) and figures travel code → git → Overleaf, not the other way. Don't hand-copy files that also live in git — keep git the source of truth. The why and the mechanics are in the manual workflow and common issues.

docs.title: Setting it up — the Overleaf owner does this once, first
docs.text:
If a project will use Overleaf, the project owner sets up the Overleaf↔git link, and it's worth doing this first, because it's what connects Overleaf to the GitHub repo — once that link exists, everyone else just clones from GitHub into their folder as usual.

  1. Owner: create (or open) the Overleaf project. In Overleaf, open Menu → Sync → GitHub (or Git) and link it to the project's GitHub repository. (Overleaf's GitHub/Git sync is a paid-plan feature — if Menu → Sync has no Git/GitHub option, the plan doesn't include it; fall back to git-mastered mode and compile locally.)
  2. From then on, syncing Overleaf ↔ git is a manual push/pull through that link — there's no live bridge. The owner (or whoever holds the Overleaf admin role) does the sync so two people don't push conflicting versions.
  3. Everyone else: never set up their own Overleaf↔git link — they clone the GitHub repo into their Dropbox folder (set up your working clone) and edit prose in Overleaf via the browser. Code, figures, and the bibliography still travel code → git → Overleaf.

(Step-by-step for the routine push/pull cycle is on the roadmap; for now the owner uses Overleaf's own Git/GitHub menu to push and pull.)

Not every project uses Overleaf — git-mastered papers keep the .tex in git directly, compiled locally. Which mode a project uses is declared in its CLAUDE.md.

docs.title: Zotero
docs.text: Zotero is a free reference manager — the citation half of writing a paper, and (with one extra plug-in) the thing that feeds Claude's literature workflow without you naming files by hand. This page covers what it is, when it earns its place, what the storage tiers actually limit, and how it plugs into the kit. It is optional throughout; the second section says when you can skip it entirely.

docs.title: What it is, in one line
docs.text: Zotero = a free desktop app where you save every paper you've read, with one click from your browser, and out comes a .bib file your LaTeX paper cites against.

docs.title: Do you even need Zotero? (sometimes no)
docs.text:
Worth saying up front: Zotero is optional. Everything in the kit works without it. You can manage citations entirely by hand — drop a PDF into your project's literature/<citekey>.pdf folder, add a matching entry to references.bib, and \citep{...} it from the paper. That is a valid workflow and some economists run it for years.

What Zotero buys you is the automation around that workflow:

  • One click from a journal page (or Google Scholar) saves both the metadata and the PDF.
  • Browser-side citekey generation (via Better BibTeX) means your authorYEARkeyword citekeys are produced for you, consistently.
  • /sync-pdfs pulls every PDF that's been added to a Zotero collection into your project's literature/ folder, named by citekey — no manual rename step.
  • /sync-bib keeps your project's references.bib in sync with Zotero, so a citation you just added in the browser is available in paper.tex minutes later.

If you read 100+ papers a year and your bibliography spans projects, this saves a lot of friction. If you write one paper at a time and only cite a dozen things, hand-managing the bib is fine and faster to start. I recommend Zotero once your literature collection outgrows your memory of what's in it.

docs.title: Install + Zotero Connector (the browser plug-in)
docs.text:
Install Zotero from https://www.zotero.org/download/; pick your OS, run the installer. Then install the Zotero Connector browser extension (same download page, lower half) — Firefox, Chrome, Safari, and Edge are all supported.

The Connector is the one bit that earns the workflow. With it: open any journal article page, NBER working paper, Google Scholar result, or arXiv preprint, click the Connector button in the browser bar, and Zotero saves the metadata + PDF (where available) to your library in seconds. No manual title/author entry, no PDF download dance.

docs.title: Storage tiers — what your account level changes
docs.text:
Zotero accounts are free, but only the metadata sync is unlimited. PDF / attachment sync is metered, and the storage plans decide how much of your library actually rides along on Zotero's servers:

Plan Annual cost Storage Free $0 300 MB Lab $20 2 GB Professional $60 6 GB Unlimited $120 Unlimited

For context, a typical econ PDF runs 1.5–3 MB, so 300 MB is roughly 100–200 papers depending on figure density, and 2 GB is a few thousand. Above that you're into "I read everything in my field" territory.

What happens when you hit your limit: Zotero stops syncing new PDFs to the cloud. The metadata (title, authors, abstract, citekey) still syncs — so other devices still see the entries — but the PDF lives only on the device where you imported it. For our workflow that means /sync-pdfs running on a different machine won't see the PDF unless you upgrade or fall back to a linked-files setup (you keep the PDFs in a Dropbox/iCloud folder yourself and Zotero just stores the link).

I run Lab tier. Free is fine if you read a modest amount, or if you keep the heavy PDFs in linked-file storage.

docs.title: Notes and annotations inside Zotero
docs.text:
A side benefit worth flagging: Zotero is also a place to read and annotate the papers it stores. The built-in PDF reader lets you highlight, add sticky-note comments, and attach a free-form note to each paper entry. Those notes sync across your devices and stay attached to the paper forever — when you cite it three years later, your highlights are still there.

This is genuinely useful and underused. A two-line note ("this is the paper that shows the IV is invalid when X holds — see footnote 7") on every paper you read pays for itself the first time you go looking for it during a referee response.

docs.title: How Zotero fits our workflow
docs.text:
This is the part specific to the kit. Three skills bridge Zotero into the project:

  • /sync-pdfs copies the PDFs from your local Zotero storage into <project>/literature/<citekey>.pdf for every citekey in the project's .bib. One-way, Zotero → project. After it runs, your literature/ folder mirrors the citations the paper actually uses.
  • /sync-bib refreshes the ZOTERO zone of references.bib from your declared Zotero libraries (group library for shared projects, your personal library for solo work) and detects orphan citations in the .tex. Two-way enough that a citekey added in Zotero in the morning is in paper.tex by lunch.
  • /lit-corpus (independent of Zotero, but pairs with it) converts the PDFs in literature/ into a markdown wiki Claude can scan token-cheaply — see literature for the rest of that pipeline.

The citekey convention the team uses is authorYEARkeyword (acemoglu2001colonial, gehring2025narrative) and Better BibTeX generates it from a template. Install the Better BibTeX plug-in once, configure the citekey template, and every new paper you add to Zotero gets a sensible citekey automatically. Without Better BibTeX, Zotero gives you ugly numeric keys (acemoglu_colonial_2001) that you would not want in a \citep{...} call.

docs.title: When Zotero is the wrong tool
docs.text:
A few uses people try and shouldn't:

  • A general PDF library for slides, course notes, internal reports. Zotero is for citable references — papers, books, working papers, datasets. Put internal reports somewhere else (a Dropbox folder, your project's project_management/).
  • A reading-list manager for "want to read" items separate from the references you actually cite. The collections you build inside Zotero are best aligned with projects/papers, not "to-read" piles. Keep the reading queue elsewhere.
  • A way around paywalls. Zotero respects the publishers' files: if the journal didn't ship the PDF as an open-access file, the Connector saves the metadata but not the PDF. Getting the full text is a separate problem — go through your library's subscriptions or interlibrary loan.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Install the toolkit — Step 3 covers installing the Zotero MCP bridge so Claude can search your library directly.
  • Literature — the markdown-wiki pipeline that turns the PDFs in your literature/ folder into something Claude can scan token-cheaply.
  • New to LaTeX? — the typesetting side; you cite against the .bib Zotero produces.
  • New to Overleaf? — browser LaTeX editor; works fine with a Zotero-managed bibliography.

docs.title: Notes and feedback
docs.text: The team's institutional memory accumulates in project_management/notes_and_feedback/ — a folder that stays local-only and is never committed (see project-structure). Meeting notes, call transcripts, co-author comments, internal discussion transcripts: anywhere a real decision happens without a formal channel. The format is uniform: one file per meeting or topic, prefixed with the date. In eighteen months, when a revision lands or a new co-author joins, this folder lets you answer "what did we actually decide about X?" without re-reading every email thread.

docs.title: What goes here
docs.text:
Inside project_management/notes_and_feedback/:

  • Meeting notes — your notes from any call, your notes from someone else's meeting, voice-memo transcriptions cleaned up to text.
  • Call transcripts — full Teams or Zoom transcripts, optionally with a short summary at the top.
  • Co-author feedback — emailed comments pulled to text, Word track-changes notes flattened to markdown, voice-message transcriptions.
  • Internal discussion transcripts — Slack threads, email threads, anywhere a real decision happens without a formal meeting.
  • Strategic-positioning decisions: "we decided to position this as X because Y". The kind of choice you make once but need to remember.

Reviewer reports do NOT go here. The journal's PDF goes in project_management/submissions/<NN_journal>/ (the submission archive); the agent-formatted TeX version goes in paper/revisions/<JOURNAL>/. See the submissions page for that workflow.

docs.title: Naming convention
docs.text:
YYYY-MM-DD_<kind>_<identifier>.md is the format. The date prefix is the one part I treat as non-negotiable, because the folder accumulates over years; without dates, sorting by date stops working the moment co-authors save files with their own conventions. The <kind> slot tells you the type at a glance: meeting, call, feedback, decision, transcript. The <identifier> slot tells you which one: Arne, Esther, AEA, intro_framing.

Examples:

  • 2026-03-15_meeting_with_Arne.md
  • 2026-03-22_call_AEA_revisions.md
  • 2026-04-01_feedback_from_Esther.md
  • 2026-04-10_decision_framing_for_intro.md

Pick the identifier so a glance tells you what is in the file. meeting_with_Arne beats meeting_3 because the latter forces you to open every file to find the right one. Same logic everywhere else: feedback_from_Esther beats feedback_2, decision_framing_for_intro beats decision_5.

docs.title: Why a fixed structure matters
docs.text:
The case for the convention is simple: a folder with eighty undated free-form notes is unsearchable; eighty files with the same template are scannable. When a revision lands and you need "what did Esther say about the framing?", a structured note answers in five seconds. A free-form one answers in twenty minutes.

The other half of the case is that Claude (and the upcoming meeting-notes assistant; see below) can parse a structured file. A note with Decisions: and Action items: headers is queryable; a stream-of-consciousness file is not. There is also a less obvious benefit: a uniform structure prevents the failure mode where a note records the discussion but not the decision. If the template has a Decisions section, you fill it in even when the meeting felt inconclusive. That habit is how institutional memory survives.

docs.title: File template (recommended)
docs.text:
# 2026-03-15 — Meeting with Arne

**Attendees:** Kai, Arne
**Agenda:** R&R strategy for QJE; division of labour for the response.

## Decisions

- Send the revision to QJE rather than RESTAT (Arne's argument: stronger
  fit with the policy framing).
- Arne drafts the response to Referee 1; Kai drafts response to Referee 2;
  both review each other.

## Action items

- [ ] Kai: draft response to R2 by 2026-03-22
- [ ] Arne: draft response to R1 by 2026-03-22
- [ ] Joint review session 2026-03-25

## Open questions

- Do we need a new robustness check on cluster level? Arne to think about
  it before next call.

## Notes

- Arne mentioned a Blattman paper relevant to the framing — send him the
  citation if I find it.
- Discussion of alternative venues if QJE rejects: RESTAT, JEEA, EJ.

The point is not the exact template (pick the one that fits the team), but that there IS one and the team uses it consistently. Switching template every meeting defeats the searchability the convention was supposed to buy.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
• Free-form notes with no date in the filename. A folder of meeting_notes.md, discussion.md, call_notes_FINAL.md is unsearchable within a month.
  • Notes scattered across multiple folders. A meeting note in working/, a co-author comment in your email folder, a reviewer report in paper/. When you need to reconstruct a decision, you check three places and miss something.
  • Notes that record discussion without recording decisions. "We talked about the framing" is not useful in eighteen months. Force the decision into a heading the template makes you fill in.
  • Voice notes kept as .m4a. Transcribe to text. Audio is not searchable; text is.

docs.title: The meeting-notes assistant
docs.text:
The /meeting-notes skill (project-workflow plugin, shipped 2026-06-23) does this for you: paste a Teams or Zoom transcript (or your raw written notes) and ask, and it produces (i) a date-prefixed note file in this folder using the template above, and (ii) extracted TODOs for project_management/TODO.md, with a confidentiality blocklist applied. The fixed template here is what makes that automation possible: a transcript can be reformatted into a structured note because the structure is known.

Prefer the manual route? Paste the transcript at the bottom of a date-prefixed file, write the Decisions / Action items / Open questions sections at the top by hand, and save it there. Either way, remember: project_management/ is local-only — it is never committed (it is gitignored by the canonical structure, precisely because these notes can contain sensitive discussion).

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• project-structure — where project_management/ fits in the canonical layout.
  • submissions — where reviewer reports actually live (NOT here).
  • data-provenance — the same separation-of-concerns logic applied to data.

docs.title: One-click replication across languages
docs.text:
A replication package is one-click when a third party can clone it, follow the data-availability statement to obtain raw data, and run one command to reproduce every table, figure, and in-text number in the paper — even when the pipeline spans Stata, R, and Python. If a replicator has to alternate between sessions, edit paths mid-run, or remember an undocumented order, the package fails the AEA bar.

The AEA Data Editor's policy is direct:

"The replication package should reproduce the tables and figures, as well as any in-text numbers, by running code without manual intervention. The only exception to this rule is a single change to set a small number of program and data directory paths."

The "single change to set paths" is the only manual edit the replicator is allowed to make. Everything else has to run by itself.

docs.title: The shape
docs.text:
The chain is linear and file-mediated — each step reads what the previous step wrote.

data/raw/  →  code/01_clean.{R,do,py}  →  data/processed/
data/processed/  →  code/02_analysis.{R,do,py}  →  output/tables/, output/figures/
output/  →  paper/paper.tex  →  paper.pdf

Each phase can be in a different language. The handoff is the file system: cleaning writes data/processed/main.dta; analysis reads it. Languages communicate through the data files they share, not through in-memory state. (.dta and .csv are the canonical handoff formats; reach for Feather or Parquet only when the data is large and numeric.)

docs.title: Three valid patterns
docs.text: Pick the one that fits the project's complexity.

docs.title: 1. Single-language pipeline (the simple case)
docs.text: 00_setup → 01_clean → 02_analysis, all in one language. A 99_run_all.{R,do,py} at the top of code/ calls each in order. Most projects start here.

docs.title: 2. Cross-language, file-mediated (the natural extension)
docs.text:
Each phase is in its own language; downstream phases read upstream's output files. The replicator runs each language's main script in order — listed step by step in the README's Instructions to Replicators section, exactly the format the AEA template prescribes:

1. Open Stata, run code/01_clean.do          →  writes data/processed/main.dta
2. Open R,     run code/02_analysis.R        →  reads main.dta, writes outputs

Right pattern when there are 2–3 phases in 2 languages. No top-level orchestrator yet. (When cleaning itself spans languages — e.g. svy weights in Stata then text features from PDFs in Python — name them 01a_clean.do → 01b_clean.py, both writing to data/processed/, and order them in the README.)

docs.title: 3. Cross-language with a master orchestrator (≥5 steps)
docs.text:
The Social Science Data Editors guidance is explicit:

"If more than 4–5 manual steps, please wrap a main program/Makefile around them, in logical sequences."

Default: a shell script (run_all.sh) that calls stata -b do code/01_clean.do, then Rscript code/02_analysis.R, then python code/03_figures.py. Simple, portable across Linux / macOS / WSL, no extra concepts.

Alternatives when they fit:

  • A Makefile with explicit dependencies (02_analysis.R depends on data/processed/main.dta which depends on 01_clean.do). The AEA Data Editor's own template uses this pattern; best when steps can be re-run incrementally. Caveat: Stata .do files don't expose their outputs to make cleanly, so target dependencies in a Stata-heavy project have to be hand-encoded — if most steps are Stata, the shell-script default ages better.
  • A single-language driver (e.g. 99_run_all.do that shells out via shell Rscript code/02_analysis.R). Works when one language dominates.

docs.title: The "single allowed change" — make it mechanical
docs.text:
The AEA's exception ("a single change to set a small number of program and data directory paths") needs an actual mechanism, or replicators will edit 00_setup or _dataroot.do directly — a manual edit of a versioned, distributed file, which defeats the point.

The convention: a gitignored path-roots file that the replicator copies and edits once.

  • The repo ships code/_dataroot.template.do (and its R / Python siblings) — tracked, with placeholder paths and a one-line edit instruction.
  • The replicator copies it to code/_dataroot.do (gitignored) and edits the single line for their machine. The cleaning / analysis scripts do / source / import _dataroot.do — they never see the template.
  • A code/_dataroot.do already on disk is left alone.

That isolates the only manual edit to an untracked file with one line. Everything else runs by itself.

docs.title: Reproducibility across languages (version pinning + random seeds)
docs.text:
The chain above can be file-perfect and still fail at the replicator's machine if software versions or stochastic steps aren't pinned. Both are AEA requirements.

  • Pin the software environment in 00_setup for every language present:
  • Stata: version 17 (or 18, etc.) before the first command — fixes the dialect.
  • R: renv::snapshot() produces renv.lock; renv::restore() is the replicator's first call. Or document the exact R version + a sessionInfo() snapshot.
  • Python: requirements.txt or environment.yml (conda) pinned to exact versions; pip install -r requirements.txt is the replicator's first call.
  • Set seeds immediately before every stochastic step: Stata set seed 20260622, R set.seed(20260622), Python np.random.seed(20260622). A seed at the top of 00_setup is not enough — a bootstrap or simulator that loads a package which itself seeds the RNG will overwrite it. Seed at the point of use.

A "one-click" pipeline without these two pins is silently irreproducible across machines.

docs.title: Tiering: long-runtime projects
docs.text:
Real econometric projects routinely have 6–48h cleaning steps (UCDP geocoding, MCMC, ML auxiliaries). A single "one command" against the full pipeline is correct in principle but operationally hostile — a replicator wants a fast path that rebuilds tables from data/processed/, and a full path that goes from data/raw/.

If any step exceeds ~30 minutes, the master script should expose at least two targets:

  • make all — raw → exhibits, the full pipeline.
  • make analysis — data/processed/ → exhibits, the fast path.

The README must state expected runtime for each. Cached intermediates in data/processed/ are AEA-allowed if produced by code in this project (per data-provenance) and documented in SOURCES.md.

docs.title: What this rules out
docs.text:
• "Run cell 7 of the notebook, then go back and re-run cell 3 with the parameter from cell 7's output." Hidden manual loop — not one-click.
  • "Edit a path constant in 02_analysis.do before running." Beyond the single allowed change (the gitignored _dataroot.do set above), every other manual edit is a defect.
  • "We don't actually have a master script; just run things in whatever order someone remembers." If it isn't written down, it doesn't reproduce.
  • A Jupyter notebook used interactively (run a cell, edit a value, re-run) as the analysis "script." A notebook executed top-to-bottom from the command line (jupyter nbconvert --execute …, quarto render) called by the master script is fine — at that point it is a script.

docs.title: How to set it up
docs.text:
• Day one: 00_setup, 01_clean, 02_analysis in your project's language(s) via /init-replication or /bootstrap-project.
  • Cross the 4–5-step / multi-language threshold: add a master orchestrator. Start with the shell-script default.
  • Pre-submission: /audit-reproducibility walks the chain backwards from manuscript numbers through 02_analysis → 01_clean → data/raw/ and flags any break.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• AEA Data Editor — Guidance for Authors (aeadataeditor.github.io): "The replication package should reproduce the tables and figures, as well as any in-text numbers, by running code without manual intervention."
  • Social Science Data Editors — Template README (social-science-data-editors.github.io): "If more than 4–5 manual steps, please wrap a main program/Makefile around them, in logical sequences."
  • Companion: data-provenance.
  • See also: replication packages.

docs.title: Why structure matters (even solo)
docs.text: This page is tool-agnostic. It's about how to organize an empirical research project so it stays sane over years — no AI, no special software assumed. The toolkit automates a lot of it later, but the principles below stand entirely on their own, and they're worth following even if you work alone in a plain folder.

docs.title: Why structure at all — even working solo
docs.text: The person most likely to need your project organized is future-you, six months from now, reopening it for a revision. A predictable structure means you can answer, instantly: where's the raw data? which script made Figure 3? which file is the current draft? Without that, every reopening starts with archaeology. So the payoff isn't bureaucratic tidiness — it's that the project stays reproducible and resumable by you, and later by anyone else.

docs.title: The principles (the part that doesn't depend on any tool)
docs.text:
1. Separate raw from processed, and never edit raw. The data exactly as you obtained it is the one thing you can't regenerate. Keep it read-only; build everything else from it with code. If a cleaning step was wrong, you fix the code and re-run — the ground truth is untouched. (See data provenance for the AEA-aligned rule that raw + cleaning live IN the project — and why importing already-cleaned data from a sibling project breaks reproducibility.)
  2. Code is the source of every exhibit. Each figure, table, and number in the paper should come from a script you can re-run, not from a one-off you can't reconstruct. "Reproducible" just means: delete output/, run the code, get it back.
  3. One canonical file per artefact. No analysis_v2.do, final_FINAL.tex. One 02_analysis file, one paper.tex — history lives in version control (below) or dated archive copies, not in the filename.
  4. A runnable pipeline. Number your scripts so the project runs top to bottom (00_setup → 01_clean → 02_analysis → 99_run_all), with one setup file owning all paths so nothing is hard-coded to your machine. (See one-click replication for the version of this that works across multiple languages — Stata + R + Python — and the tiered run-all pattern for long-runtime projects.)
  5. Write down what isn't obvious. A short codebook / data dictionary and a README turn "what was this variable again?" into a lookup.

That's the whole core. The concrete folder map that implements it is what goes where; the deeper rationale is the ideas behind it. A standard, reproducible structure is also exactly what a replication package needs — so if you work this way, the package is almost free.

docs.title: Required vs. recommended
docs.text:
Not everything here carries equal weight, and it's worth being honest about which is which — so nobody feels bossed into preferences, and nobody treats a genuinely load-bearing rule as optional.

Required — break these and something real goes wrong:

  • Never overwrite or edit raw data. It's the one thing you can't get back.
  • To share work, commit and push it to git. Saving (Dropbox) is not sharing; the canonical record is git. (Solo with no git, this doesn't apply.)
  • One writer per file at a time (on a team) — two people editing the same file means one silently loses their work.
  • Exhibits trace to code. A number or figure you can't regenerate from a script isn't reproducible — and reproducibility is the credibility floor.

Recommended — sensible defaults you can adapt:

  • The exact folder layout and names (what goes where) — a working solution, not the only one; what matters is everyone uses the same.
  • Keeping clones inside Dropbox, using Overleaf, using Claude Code or the toolkit, the specific multi-clone setup — all genuinely optional choices. Pick what fits; the required rules above hold either way.

When in doubt: the required list is short on purpose. Everything else is a default you're free to change.

docs.title: Working alone vs. with others — and where git comes in
docs.text:
Working solo, the principles above plus a tidy folder are most of what you need. Version control (git) is helpful even then — it gives you a timeline you can roll back and a record of why each change happened — but you can get a long way with disciplined folders and the occasional dated backup.

The calculus changes the moment more than one actor edits the project — and today that's not just co-authors:

  • Co-authors edit in parallel. Without version control, two people changing the same file means one silently overwrites the other (the classic Dropbox "conflicted copy").
  • AI agents — Claude Code, Codex — make many edits quickly. That's a huge speed-up, but it's also a lot of changes to a lot of files. You want each one to be a reviewable diff you can inspect and undo, not a silent mutation. Git is what turns "the AI changed twelve files" into "here's exactly what it changed, keep or revert each."

So the rule of thumb:

You're working… What you need Alone, by hand the folder principles above; git optional but nice Alone, with an AI agent the principles + git — so every agent edit is a reviewable, revertible diff With co-authors (± agents) the principles + git + a collaboration setup so parallel work merges instead of clobbering

The more hands on the project — human or AI — the more git earns its keep. The folder principles are the foundation either way; git is what lets several actors build on that foundation at once without stepping on each other. How that collaboration setup works is Working together; why the AI agents are safe to let loose on a git-backed project is how Claude Code thinks.

docs.title: The anatomy of an empirical paper — the arc and the hidden decisions
docs.text:
This page is tool-agnostic: what an empirical paper is made of, and where one quietly falls apart, no AI and no special software assumed. Why structure matters (even solo) covered where your files go; this covers what the work inside them is.

Carry one paper through the page. Does a new paved road change what farmers grow? 480 villages, 2009–2019, roads finished in different years, so villages connected in 2012 are a comparison for those connected in 2017. Your estimate: a 0.14 rise in the log cash-crop share, standard error 0.05.

Eighteen months after submission Referee 2 asks why the standard errors are clustered at district level when the road was built village by village. You had a reason, worked out over a day last spring, and it is nowhere: not the paper, not a code comment, not your notes. You re-derive it, lose two days, land on a sample rule that is defensible but not quite the one behind the draft's numbers, and every table gets re-run.

Nothing broke. No file was lost, no data corrupted, no step done sloppily. What was lost was a decision, and decisions are the part of a research project with no natural home. The road paper is invented; the failures in it are not.

docs.title: The arc
docs.text:
The arc is the phases every empirical paper goes through: question → data → analysis → exhibits → argument → writing → review → submission. Not a one-way street; you will revisit earlier phases, and that is normal. Naming them lets us point at one precisely, and gives each its own definition of "done" — many stalled projects are stalled because someone is using the definition from a different phase.

flowchart TB
    subgraph F["Establishing what is true"]
        Q["1 · Question"] --> D["2 · Data"] --> A["3 · Analysis"] --> E["4 · Exhibits"]
    end
    subgraph M["Making a reader believe it"]
        G["5 · Argument"] --> W["6 · Writing"] --> R["7 · Review"] --> S["8 · Submission"]
    end
    E --> G
    A -.->|"the data can't answer it"| Q
    G -.->|"the story needs an exhibit<br/>that doesn't exist yet"| E
    R -.->|"a check is missing"| A
    S -.->|"revise and resubmit"| A

Read it top to bottom. Each box is one phase, numbered in the order you first reach it; solid arrows are the forward path. The two boxed groups split the arc in half: the first four establish what is true, judged by whether the finding survives; the last four make a reader believe it, judged by whether an unsympathetic reader is convinced. The one solid arrow crossing between the groups, exhibits to argument, is the handover, where you stop asking what the data say and start asking what a reader will accept.

The four dotted arrows are the returns, each labelled with its trigger: analysis back to the question when the data can't answer it, argument back to exhibits when the story needs one that doesn't exist, review back to analysis when a check is missing, submission back there when the revise-and-resubmit lands eighteen months later. All four land on a phase you thought was finished, which is the most useful thing the picture says. No dotted arrow marks a failure; they are the normal shape of the work.

What "done" means, phase by phase, on the road paper. I'd defend the first four hard; treat the rest as the defaults I use.

  • Question — one sentence naming the outcome, the comparison that identifies the effect, and why the answer isn't known: does road access shift crop mix toward cash crops, villages connected early against those connected later?
  • Data — every variable in a file your code built from raw data, every source nameable, down to the merge key you check by hand on 20 villages before trusting it on 480 (the standard data provenance sets).
  • Analysis — specification fixed and the choices behind it written down: clustering level, sample window, which years drop. Then name the result that would make you drop the claim and check you ran that test. If you can't name one, the analysis isn't finished, it's just extensive.
  • Exhibits — an exhibit is any figure or table that carries evidence in the paper, the umbrella word so we don't say "figures and tables" forty times. Done when each shows one thing you can state in a sentence.
  • Argument — claims and exhibits map both ways: every claim points to evidence, every exhibit supports a claim. An exhibit supporting nothing is a missing paragraph or a table to cut, and you have to say which.
  • Writing — each paragraph delivers one takeaway you could state without rereading it. Hold on to this one; it gets a name below.
  • Review — someone whose job was to find problems has tried, and you answered each objection in writing. Your own reread counts for little: you know what you meant, so you read what you meant.
  • Submission — a stranger rebuilds every number from your raw data and code without asking you, the standard a replication package is held to and the argument for one-click replication from day one.

docs.title: The hidden decisions
docs.text:
Each phase produces two things: the work, and the decisions about the work. A research decision is a choice you make once and then rely on many times: what to call a concept, which exhibits exist and what each shows, what a given paragraph should say, where a piece of evidence gets cited. Not the work itself, the standing choice the work then follows, which is why losing one hurts more than losing an afternoon of code.

Hidden decisions are the research decisions everyone makes but rarely writes down. Four kinds show up in every empirical paper:

  • What each concept is called — one name per idea, plus the alternatives ruled out. That agreed name has a standard label, the canonical term, and its own page: consistent terminology.
  • Which exhibits exist and what each is named — not the numbers printed in the draft, an actual list: this figure exists, it shows this, its identifier is this.
  • What each paragraph should say — the takeaway from the writing phase above has a name: the lead, the one-sentence takeaway a paragraph is written to deliver. Decide the lead before you draft; the paragraph then earns it.
  • Where each exhibit gets cited — which section, which paragraph, in what role. An exhibit cited nowhere is invisible; one cited in four places is usually doing four jobs badly.

They stay hidden for an honest reason, not a lazy one. Each felt obvious the moment you made it, so writing it down felt like recording that water is wet. The cost lands later, once the obviousness has evaporated.

Before. In March you call the treatment "the road" everywhere. In July a co-author points out that "market access" is the accurate concept, since a road ending 30 km short of a market does little. You fix the abstract and the introduction, the files open that afternoon; the data section still says "road", Figure 2's axis reads "road completion year", the appendix says "connection". In September a balance table becomes Table 2, so heterogeneity slides from 3 to 4: your text names it three times, you fix two, miss the one in the conclusion, and your script still writes tab3_het.tex.

After. Both decisions were written down as they were made. One line fixes the name to road access and bans "the road", "market access" and "connection", so a single plain-text search returns 31 hits in six files and you fix 31, prose and axis labels and captions together. A second line records that the heterogeneity table shows effects by distance to market, comes from 04_het.R, and is called tab_het in every note, so inserting a table changes one line and no cross-references. Same research, both times.

docs.title: Why writing them down pays even alone
docs.text:
The rule: the person who most needs your decisions written down is a version of you who has forgotten them. The objection runs the other way, that this is overhead for teams and you are one person who remembers your own project. I made it for years, and it is wrong for exactly that reason.

Future-you at the revise-and-resubmit. Remember the headline from the top of the page: 0.14, standard error 0.05. Work those two numbers through. A 95% confidence interval is roughly the coefficient plus or minus two standard errors, so 0.14 − 0.10 = 0.04 at the bottom and 0.14 + 0.10 = 0.24 at the top. The t-statistic is the coefficient over its standard error, 0.14 / 0.05 = 2.8, past the 1.96 that convention treats as the 5% threshold. You know the effect is positive; you don't know how close to zero it sits.

That 0.05 is the district-clustered standard error, and why it was chosen is what Referee 2 asked: roads were approved district by district, so villages inside a district aren't independent draws. Cluster at village level and it falls to 0.032, lifting the t-statistic to 0.14 / 0.032 = 4.4. Both clear 1.96, so the finding survives either way. The word "precisely" doesn't: the honest interval still runs 0.04 to 0.24, a factor of six end to end.

Economists differ on how conservative to be about clustering, and my point isn't which camp wins. It's that you had the reason in the spring and lost it. One line then answers Referee 2 in ten minutes; two days of re-derivation buys a reason you can defend, which is not the reason you actually had.

A referee asking why. "Why drop 2015?" has a good answer: the census changed its crop categories, so the outcome isn't comparable across the break. It also has a bad answer, which is any answer composed after the question arrives, because by then you can't tell yourself apart from someone rationalising. That is the analysis phase's own test from the arc, arriving eighteen months late.

Write the reason down the day you make the choice, not the day you're asked for it. Where it goes matters less than that it goes somewhere; the three we keep are a terminology file, a list of exhibits, and a short plan per section carrying each paragraph's lead. Two of those I'd argue for hard, terminology and the exhibit list, because I've watched both go wrong on every multi-author paper I've been part of. Leads I hold loosely: on a short paper you can carry them in your head, and some people genuinely draft better without them.

docs.title: When this stops being optional
docs.text: Everything above holds with no AI near the project; it held for the generation who wrote their papers on a typewriter. What an AI collaborator changes is the price of leaving a decision unwritten. A co-author who doesn't know you renamed the treatment will probably ask. An assistant that cannot see the decision will not ask: it writes "market access" into your data section, fast and confidently, across eight files while you make coffee. So the decisions have to live somewhere an assistant reads before it writes. Which document holds each, and what stops it drifting, is Where AI fits the paper — loops, gates, and the store; terminology already has its own page.

docs.title: Consistent terminology — the per-paper glossary
docs.text: Halfway through a paper, the same idea is "the documentary" in the intro, "the film" in the data section, and "the narrative treatment" in a figure caption. A reader can't tell whether those are one thing or three. AI agents make this worse, not better: ask one to rewrite a paragraph and it cheerfully swaps in a synonym it likes. This page is about pinning your vocabulary once, in one place, so it stays consistent everywhere — and making sure an agent can suggest a name but never impose one on you.

docs.title: One file per paper
docs.text:
A paper carries a single file, paper/CONCEPTS.md. Its core is a small table: each recurring concept, the canonical term you've chosen for it, the banned alternatives that should never appear, and a short label for figures.

The payoff is propagation from one source. When you decide "drop 'documentary', call it the narrative treatment," you change one row, then sweep every figure and prose mention in a single pass — zero drift. The file also records what each concept means and how they relate, so a label means the same thing on page 3 and page 30.

docs.title: The agent proposes; you decide
docs.text:
This is the part that matters. An AI agent may propose a term — it adds a row marked proposed — but it can never make that term official. Only you approve one, and approving is a deliberate act: you mark the row approved and add a dated line to the file's approval log. The toolkit enforces only the terms you approved. A name an agent invented has no power over your draft until you've signed it.

Two consequences worth knowing:

  • The glossary never overrides your writing voice. It governs which word you use for a concept — nothing about sentence style, your phrasing, or the AI-tell words the writing tools already screen out. If an approved term ever clashes with your style guide, the style guide wins and the term goes back to you for a rethink.
  • If a term isn't pinned, an agent asks rather than guessing. When you write with kai-writing, it loads the glossary first, and if a needed term is missing or used two ways, it raises the question instead of quietly picking one.

docs.title: The check that catches drift
docs.text:
check_glossary.py is a small gate that greps a draft against the banned terms of your approved rows before it ships. It's a hard check — an exit code, not a polite reminder — so it doesn't get skipped:

  • clean — no banned terms; good to go.
  • a banned term slipped in — it names the line and the approved replacement; fix and re-run.
  • gate inactive — no glossary yet, or nothing approved. This is not a pass: it's a nudge to pin your core terms first.

An --audit mode confirms every enforced term has a logged approval, so a term can't quietly become official without your sign-off on record.

docs.title: Getting one
docs.text:
• New paper — /bootstrap-paper scaffolds an empty CONCEPTS.md alongside the LaTeX. It ships inert: nothing is enforced until you approve your first term, so it can't impose anything out of the box.
  • Existing paper — /bootstrap-paper --seed-glossary paper.tex drafts the glossary from your prose. It counts what actually recurs, then walks you through the concepts one at a time, proposing a canonical term for each so the common case is a one-word "yes." It writes an enforced term only when you confirm it in that moment.
