• What it does: publication-quality choropleth & country-level maps from real data in R (sf + ggplot2), with the map-specific traps handled -- name/ISO reconciliation + a loud anti-join, equal-area projection, skew-aware binning, rates-not-counts, and an explicit no-data key.
  • When to use: a research / working-paper / policy-brief map where the geography IS the unit -- "make a map", "choropleth", "map X by country", "shade countries by X".
  • Example: "choropleth of battle deaths per capita by country, 2018-2024"
  • Not for: lecture / slide maps (the lecture-pipeline data-visualizer owns those); non-map charts like time series or scatter (use real-data-figure).

docs.title: qualitative-survey-coding
docs.text:
• What it does: turns open-ended survey responses into validated, paper-ready quantitative variables using an LLM as the coder with human validation. Handles codebook design, hard-code vs free-code decisions, inter-coder agreement, and the audit trail.
  • When to use: "code these open-ended answers", "classify free-text survey responses", "turn this text into a measure", "design a codebook for open-ended", any qualitative-to-quantitative conversion of survey text.
  • Example: "code these 800 free-text answers about trust in government into a 3-level scale"
  • Not for: quantitative survey processing (use /descriptives or /regression); a literature corpus (use /lit-corpus).

docs.title: real-data-figure
docs.text:
• What it does: publication-quality figures from REAL data -- time series, scatter, coefficient, lollipop -- sourced from OWID, World Bank, V-Dem, UCDP, ACLED and others, cleaned and plotted in the research house style with honest self-scoring.
  • When to use: any figure whose value depends on real numbers being correct, or when you name a source (OWID / World Bank / V-Dem / UCDP / ACLED) -- "plot GDP for these countries", "chart the democracy index over time".
  • Example: "plot GDP per capita for England vs France, 1600-1800, from Maddison"
  • Not for: maps shaded by country (use map-figure); coefficient plots from a SAVED model fit .rds (use /coef-plot); schematic / conceptual diagrams (use tikz-figure); pure data download with no plot (use data-catalog).

docs.title: review-figure
docs.text:
• What it does: a cold-eyes, data-grounded correctness gate for a finished figure. A
  • When to use: right before a data figure is shown / put in a paper / dropped in a deck,
  • Example: "review-figure output/figures/fig3_typology.pdf with the script's"
  • Not for: producing figures (real-data-figure / coef-plot); general hostile

docs.title: scientific-writing-analysis
docs.text:
• What it does: analyses scientific manuscripts for writing quality using Jean-Luc Lebrun's "Scientific Writing" (2007) framework augmented with econ-specific conventions (Cochrane, McCloskey, Nikolov). Diagnoses paragraph progression, lead sentences, flow, structure -- HOW the prose works, not what it claims.
  • When to use: "analyze the writing quality", "Lebrun review", "diagnose this draft's structure", "what's wrong with the flow".
  • Example: "scientific-writing-analysis of the intro and the contribution section"
  • Not for: actually rewriting (use kai-writing); checking factual / argumentative content (use /review-paper or adversarial-review); AI-voice tells specifically (use humanize).

docs.title: simulation-figure
docs.text:
• What it does: builds Monte Carlo simulations + interactive parameter explorations that show how econometric methods break under assumption violations -- weak IV, parallel-trends, staggered DID, TWFE bias, exclusion-restriction failure. Produces BOTH a static multi-panel PDF (for Beamer/print) AND an interactive Plotly HTML with animation slider (for RevealJS/browser).
  • When to use: "simulate", "Monte Carlo", "show what happens when the instrument is weak", "demonstrate IV bias", "stress test the identification", "when does this method fail" for a talk, lecture, or appendix.
  • Example: "simulate weak-IV bias as the first stage F drops from 30 to 5"
  • Not for: real-data plots (use real-data-figure); a single conceptual diagram (use tikz-figure); a lecture map (lecture-pipeline data-visualizer).

docs.title: tikz-figure
docs.text:
• What it does: builds, tests, and debugs publication-quality TikZ figures -- mechanism diagrams, DAGs for causal identification, game trees, decision trees, flowcharts, schematic maps, schematic time series. Uses the Cunningham "standalone-test" pattern so compile errors are crystal-clear.
  • When to use: "make a DAG", "mechanism diagram", "causal diagram", "game tree", "decision tree", "flow chart" in LaTeX/Beamer/Quarto; also when diagnosing a failed TikZ compile ("undefined key", "missing $", "you need \usetikzlibrary{...}").
  • Example: "build a DAG for the IV identification of X -> Y with Z"
  • Not for: real-data figures (use real-data-figure); choropleths (use map-figure); Monte Carlo simulations (use simulation-figure).

docs.title: work
docs.text:
• What it does: "Lead orchestrator for Kai Gehring's research tasks (/work). Plans a multi-step task as a PLAN FILE (the single source of truth), executes ONE unit at a time through the existing skills (kai-writing, real-data-figure, r/stata research workflows), gates every unit (deterministi...
  • When-to-use card not yet written (add a <!--card ... --> block to the SKILL.md).

docs.title: The skills, by family
docs.text:
This is the by-purpose view of the toolkit: skills grouped by what you'd reach for them to do, each one expandable for when and how to use it. It's the counterpart to the full list of commands & skills (the exhaustive flat catalogue with exact invocation) — start here to find the right tool, go there for the complete reference.

How to read this: each entry is collapsed — click it to see when to use it and how to fire it. Most skills auto-trigger on matching language; anything with a /name you can also type explicitly (see Triggering skills). Install is per plugin — see Install the toolkit.

docs.title: Writing & editing
docs.text:
kai-writing — drafts and revises academic prose in your voice

For writing or polishing any paper prose — contribution paragraphs, intros, abstracts, referee responses. Runs two drafters → critic → rewriter internally, so you see a revised draft, not a first pass. Fire it: ask "write/revise this in my style," or it auto-triggers on prose tasks.

kai-pedagogical-writing — teaching & explanatory prose in the same voice

The teaching-register sibling of kai-writing: lecture notes, intuitive explanations, student-facing material. Same drafters → critic → rewriter architecture, pedagogical register. (Journal prose stays with kai-writing.) Fire it: "explain this for students" / "write the teaching version."

scientific-writing-analysis — diagnoses writing quality (Lebrun framework)

For a structured critique of how a section is written (paragraph progression, lead sentences, flow) rather than what it claims. Fire it: "analyze the writing quality of this section."

/academic — heavyweight orchestrator across several dimensions at once

When a task spans review + polish + figures + bibliography together. Reach for the individual skills when it doesn't; reach for this when it does. Fire it: /academic (or it engages when you're working across a paper).

docs.title: Review & critique
docs.text:
adversarial-review — hostile pre-ship review of any artefact

The default before shipping anything (figure, plan, code, draft). Independent agents tasked to find flaws, graded HALT/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW/NIT — not reassurance. See Reviewing with adversarial agents. Fire it: "run an adversarial review of this."

/review-paper — full 6-agent pre-submission referee report

A journal-grade referee panel (contribution, identification, consistency, maths, tables, claims) for a finished paper targeting a named journal. Fire it: /review-paper.

/review-paper-light — ~1-minute pre-screen

A fast 2-agent check (contribution + identification) to decide whether a paper is ready for the full report. Run it first. Fire it: /review-paper-light.

/review-grant — 6-agent funder-panel review

A pre-submission panel review of a grant proposal for a specified funder. Fire it: /review-grant.

/review-r — reviews existing R scripts

Checks R code already on disk for quality, reproducibility, and correctness. Does not write new scripts. Fire it: /review-r.

/review-stata — reviews existing Stata .do files

The Stata counterpart to /review-r: 12-category review of existing do-files. Fire it: /review-stata.

bib-audit — catches hallucinated and broken references

Dual-Claude audit of a .bib file for fabricated, chimeric, or malformed entries before you submit. Fire it: auto-triggers on .bib work, or ask to "audit the bibliography."

docs.title: Figures & diagrams
docs.text:
real-data-figure — publication figures from real data

Time series, scatter, coefficient, lollipop — sourced from OWID, World Bank, V-Dem, UCDP, ACLED, and others, with research-house design. (For maps shaded by country, use map-figure below.) Fire it: "plot for from data." map-figure — publication-quality choropleth & country maps

Country/region polygons shaded by a value (GDP, conflict deaths, refugee stock) in R (sf + ggplot2). Handles the map-specific traps that quietly break a choropleth: country-name/ISO reconciliation with a loud anti-join, equal-area projection, skew-aware binning, rates-not-counts, and an explicit "no data" key. Research/paper maps only — lecture maps go through the lecture pipeline. Fire it: "make a map / choropleth of by country." tikz-figure — TikZ diagrams

DAGs, mechanism diagrams, game trees, decision trees, flowcharts — built and compile-tested. Also debugs failed TikZ compiles. Fire it: "make a DAG / mechanism diagram of …"

simulation-figure — Monte Carlo & parameter explorations

Shows how an estimator breaks under assumption violations (weak IV, parallel- trends, staggered DID). Produces a static PDF + an interactive HTML. Fire it: "simulate what happens when …" / "show when this method fails."

/coef-plot — one coefficient/event-study plot from a saved fit

Atomic plot from a saved regression (.rds) or fresh estimation. (For a plot hand-entered from a paper's table, use real-data-figure.) Fire it: /coef-plot.

review-figure — cold-eyes correctness gate on a finished figure

Independent check of a produced figure AGAINST its underlying numbers — labels, units, magnitudes, source lines — before it reaches the paper. Offer it after any real-data-figure / map-figure / coef-plot output. Fire it: "review this figure" (with the data at hand).

docs.title: Data, tables & analysis
docs.text:
data-catalog — find and retrieve empirical data sources

Catalogue + search + download for economics / political-economy / conflict data, outside a lecture context. Fire it: "find data on …" / "download ." /descriptives — publication-ready descriptive & balance tables

Summary stats, treatment-vs-control balance, distribution/missingness diagnostics. Fire it: /descriptives.

/regression — estimate one specification

A single regression (or a small column-stack of related specs) for analysis. Fire it: /regression.

/data-analysis — full R analysis pipeline (umbrella)

Spans exploration → cleaning → regression → publication-ready tables and figures. The umbrella skill; the atomic skills above are its parts. Fire it: /data-analysis.

build-fragment-table — paper-ready regression tables

Both halves of Kai's outline-in-paper + fragment-from-code pattern (no stars; coef / [SE] / {p}; Mean-Control + N rows). Pairs with the exhibits workflow. Fire it: "build the table for this regression."

/build-data-source-table — data-sources appendix table

Generates the LaTeX data-sources table from the datasets: block of your replication metadata (the YAML is the source of truth). Fire it: /build-data-source-table.

sync-codebook — keep survey + derived codebooks in sync

Two-codebook (survey-frozen + derived-live) synchronization for survey + analysis projects. Fire it: /sync-codebook.

stata-replication — end-to-end Stata replication pipeline

Scaffolds the canonical 00_setup / 01_cleaning / 02_analysis triad per the one-canonical-script rule. Fire it: auto-triggers on Stata replication work.

docs.title: Experiments & research design
docs.text:
/experiment-design — design a survey/information experiment through conversation

Interviews you one question at a time to design — or review — an experiment: a matched control, an incentivized primary outcome, integrity checks (no post-treatment exclusion), randomization, and power, then emits a spec that hands off to pre-registration and ethics. Deep for online survey/information experiments; field-RCT and lab tracks are on the roadmap. See Designing experiments. Fire it: /experiment-design, or "help me design a survey experiment" / "critique my experimental design."

pre-registration — registry-ready pre-registration + pre-analysis plan

Picks the right registry with you (AEA RCT for field RCTs; AsPredicted or OSF for survey/lab; OSF for observational DiD/RD/IV), fills its exact fields from the design spec or an interview, and writes the PAP content: directional hypotheses, ONE primary outcome, the estimator, a multiple-testing pre-commitment, power/MDE, ex-ante exclusions. Refuses retrospective "preregistration" of results already seen. You upload the document yourself. Fire it: "preregister this study" / "draft the PAP" / "AsPredicted".

irb-application — the ethics application + consent text

Triages the review route (European university committee vs US IRB exempt/expedited/full, incl. the Swiss non-medical carve-out — always the committee's call, never asserted), drafts the committee-agnostic protocol substance (procedures, consent text for online studies, risks, the deception-vs-obfuscation line with a mandatory debriefing plan, payments, GDPR data protection), and checks consistency against the design spec and pre-registration. Offers the Asiedu et al. journal ethics appendix. Fire it: "draft the ethics application" / "IRB" / "consent form".

docs.title: Bibliography & citations
docs.text:
/sync-bib — refresh references.bib from Zotero

Rebuilds the ZOTERO zone of your .bib and flags orphan citations in the .tex. Read-only against Zotero — safe for anyone to run. Fire it: /sync-bib.

/add-cite-from-zotero — add one reference

Pulls a single BibTeX entry from Zotero into the manual zone of references.bib without changing your global setup. Fire it: /add-cite-from-zotero <query-or-citekey>.

/suggest-jel — JEL classification codes

3-5 suggested JEL codes (primary first) for a paper or proposal. Fire it: /suggest-jel (paste the abstract).

lit-review — structured literature search + synthesis

Search, thematic clustering, citation extraction, and gap identification. Fire it: "do a literature review on …"

lit-corpus — turn a folder of PDFs into a markdown corpus

Converts academic PDFs into a token-efficient corpus for literature work. Fire it: "build a corpus from these PDFs."

/sync-pdfs — pull cited PDFs from Zotero

Copies PDFs from local Zotero storage into literature/ for every citekey in the project's bib. Fire it: /sync-pdfs.

docs.title: Project setup & hygiene
docs.text:
/bootstrap-project — day-1 setup for a new or messy project

Scaffolds the canonical folders + CLAUDE.md + .gitignore; asks project mode, collaborators, code stack. Fire it: /bootstrap-project in the project folder.

bootstrap-paper — scaffold a new paper in house style

A LaTeX paper skeleton in Kai's conventions (preamble, sections, bib zones). Fire it: "scaffold the paper skeleton."

/refactor-structure — reorganize the folder/file layout

Surveys the layout against the canonical structure and proposes a safe, confirm-each-step refactor (never deletes). Back up first. Fire it: /refactor-structure (read-only plan; --apply to act).

/restructure-project — reorganize CLAUDE.md content

The content counterpart to /refactor-structure (which does the folders). Fire it: /restructure-project.

/housekeeping — read-only project audit

Flags drift, stragglers, and hygiene issues without changing anything. Fire it: /housekeeping.

/git — conversational git for non-experts

Plain-language git help — describe what you want, no commands to memorise. Fire it: /git (or just describe the git situation).

check-clone-discipline — confirm you're in your own clone

On multi-clone projects, checks you're standing in your clone_<XX>/ before any git write. Cheap insurance against the shared-root hazard. Fire it: auto, at session start on multi-clone projects.

/overleaf-sync — resolve Overleaf↔GitHub conflicts

Diagnoses and recommends fixes for sync conflicts (often post-restructure). Fire it: /overleaf-sync.

meeting-notes — transcript to structured note + TODOs

Turns a Teams/Zoom transcript (or raw written notes) into a date-prefixed note in project_management/notes_and_feedback/ plus extracted TODOs, with a confidentiality blocklist. See Notes and feedback. Fire it: paste the transcript and ask for meeting notes.

Workflow helpers — /check-rules · /new-sprint · /plan-status · /learn

Small hygiene commands: re-read the active rules; start a fresh sprint plan; report sprint status; append a one-line memory correction. Fire them: type the /name.

docs.title: Replication & reproducibility
docs.text:
init-replication — scaffold the replication package

Adds replication_metadata.yaml + 00_setup scripts + a paper/README placeholder to an existing project. Fire it: "set up the replication package."

audit-reproducibility — check the paper's numbers against the code

Cross-checks numeric claims in the manuscript against actual R/Stata/Python outputs. A pre-submission gate. Fire it: "audit reproducibility of this paper."

/audit-exhibits — provenance manifest for every exhibit

Classifies each file in output/ as CODE-REPRODUCED / EXTERNAL / MANUAL / ORPHAN; --strict fails on any orphan. Fire it: /audit-exhibits.

docs.title: Talks
docs.text:
research-presentation — design academic talks

Conference, seminar, job-market, brown-bag talks — architecture by length, intro design, identification defense, slide rhetoric. Fire it: "design my seminar / JMP / conference talk."

docs.title: Cross-session coordination
docs.text:
/coord — a message channel between your own sessions

Lets your Claude Code sessions in different project folders leave each other messages (single user, many projects — not team chat). Fire it: /coord <verb> or "check coord."

docs.title: For toolkit builders (maintainer note)
docs.text:
spec-gate — anti-drift gate for long agentic builds

A builder's primitive, not a research-workflow tool: turns a build spec into a fail-closed checklist (spec-gate/conditions.yaml) that re-verifies on a cadence, so long multi-session builds stop silently drifting from settled decisions. Co-authors doing paper work will not need it; reach for it when building pipelines or skills of your own. Fire it: /spec-gate-init in the project being built.

docs.title: Submissions
docs.text: A submission round produces two distinct kinds of artefact, and they belong in two distinct places. The journal-facing record (what you sent, what you received) lives in project_management/submissions/<NN_journal_round>/, gitignored and version-frozen. The collaborative working area (the response-to-referees TeX you and your co-authors edit together) lives in paper/revisions/<JOURNAL>/, git-tracked and Overleaf-synced. Mixing the two breaks the workflow: the journal record stops being immutable, or the response stops reaching your co-authors through Overleaf.

docs.title: The two homes — and the split
docs.text:
Artefact Where Why Submitted paper PDF (version-frozen) project_management/submissions/<NN_journal_round>/ Immutable archive of what you sent Cover letter PDF (version-frozen) project_management/submissions/<NN_journal_round>/ Immutable archive Response-to-referees PDF (R&R+) project_management/submissions/<NN_journal_round>/ Immutable archive Referee reports as received (journal PDFs / txts) project_management/submissions/<NN_journal_round>/ Original journal correspondence Editor letter as received project_management/submissions/<NN_journal_round>/ Original journal correspondence Cover letter TeX source (editable, per round) project_management/submissions/<NN_journal_round>/overleaf/ Submission-specific; usually drafted by the author of record Response-to-referees TeX source paper/revisions/<JOURNAL>/ Collaborative — co-authors edit it together in Overleaf Agent-formatted referee reports (one TeX per referee) paper/revisions/<JOURNAL>/ Lives next to the response so the response can \input it Editor letter formatted TeX (optional) paper/revisions/<JOURNAL>/ Same workflow as the referee reports Submission log (one line per round) project_management/submission_log.md Navigation index across rounds

A reader who already knows the rule can stop here and skip to the worked example. The sections below explain why the split exists, what goes inside each home, and what does NOT go in either.

docs.title: Why the split
docs.text:
The submission round's working files split because paper/ is the co-author-shared surface and project_management/ is the author-of-record-private surface. paper/ is what gets pushed to GitHub and synced into Overleaf, so anything that lives there reaches every co-author the moment you push — and they can mark it up in Overleaf's track-changes view, the standard collaboration workflow for a response. project_management/ is gitignored: it lives on your laptop and never reaches anyone else.

The response-to-referees is the central collaborative artefact of a revision — each co-author owns parts of it, marks up parts of others' drafts, and the team negotiates the final framing in track-changes. That work belongs in paper/revisions/<JOURNAL>/ so Overleaf can pick it up. The cover letter is shorter, editor-facing, and usually drafted by the author of record alone; it belongs with the submission packet for that round.

The originals (the submitted PDF, the referee PDFs as the journal sent them, the editor letter) stay in project_management/submissions/ because they are frozen documentary record. You may read the referee PDF a hundred times during a revision; you should never edit it. I never touch a submitted PDF after it goes in, even to fix an error I spot later: it is the record of exactly what the referees and editor saw, and the corrected version belongs in the next round's folder.

docs.title: Where the response-to-referees TeX lives — and why per-journal
docs.text:
paper/revisions/<JOURNAL>/ mirrors the paper/presentations/<venue>_<date>/ convention from the folder structure: per-venue subfolder by short name, not by round number. If the paper goes through three rounds at QJE, all three rounds' working response files live in paper/revisions/QJE/ and git history carries the per-round versions. If the paper is then rejected at QJE and resubmitted to RESTAT, a fresh paper/revisions/RESTAT/ workspace is created — the QJE folder stays as the historical record of what happened there.

The per-journal grouping matches how co-authors think about the revision: "we're working on the QJE response," not "we're working on round 2." It also makes the response TeX easy to find in a year-old project where you've forgotten the round numbering.

docs.title: Worked example — a paper at QJE R&R after one initial submission
docs.text:
The shape after one R&R round:

project_management/submissions/
├── 01_QJE_initial/              (initial submission to QJE)
│   ├── paper_v_submitted.pdf
│   ├── cover_letter.pdf
│   └── overleaf/
│       └── cover_letter.tex
└── 02_QJE_R&R/                  (R&R round at QJE)
    ├── paper_v_resubmitted.pdf
    ├── cover_letter.pdf
    ├── response_to_referees.pdf   (the frozen PDF)
    ├── referee_1.pdf              (as received from journal)
    ├── referee_2.pdf              (as received from journal)
    ├── editor_letter.pdf          (as received)
    └── overleaf/
        └── cover_letter.tex       (R&R cover letter — short, editor-facing)

paper/
└── revisions/
    └── QJE/                       (Overleaf-synced revision workspace)
        ├── response_to_referees.tex
        ├── referee_1_formatted.tex   (agent-generated from referee_1.pdf)
        ├── referee_2_formatted.tex   (agent-generated from referee_2.pdf)
        └── editor_letter_formatted.tex

Notice the split: the response TeX is in paper/revisions/QJE/, the response PDF is frozen in project_management/submissions/02_QJE_R&R/. The referee PDFs (as received) are in submissions; the formatted referee TeX (with structured comment numbers for the response to address) is in paper/revisions/QJE/. The cover letter PDF + its Overleaf TeX source stay together in submissions because the cover letter is per-round and author-of-record-private.

If the QJE rejects and you resubmit to RESTAT, the next state adds:

project_management/submissions/
└── 03_RESTAT_initial/
    └── ...

paper/revisions/
├── QJE/                          (historical — stays as the QJE record)
└── RESTAT/                       (fresh workspace)
    └── ...

The QJE workspace is not deleted; it documents what the QJE round looked like in case you need to retrace the framing decisions when responding to RESTAT.

docs.title: Naming convention
docs.text:
Per-round subfolder is <NN>_<journal>_<round>. The <NN> keeps rounds sortable in disk order; <journal> keeps them recognisable; <round> distinguishes initial from revision rounds (and helps when the same journal sees two rounds).

Examples:

  • 01_QJE_initial — first submission, QJE
  • 02_QJE_R&R — R&R round at QJE
  • 03_QJE_R&R2 — second R&R at QJE (rare but happens)
  • 04_AER_initial — paper rejected at QJE, resubmitted to AER

The & in R&R is a real character in the folder name; on Windows that is fine, on filesystems that complain you can use R-and-R. Match what your filesystem accepts and apply it consistently across rounds.

docs.title: Why gitignored
docs.text:
project_management/submissions/ is gitignored for three reasons:

  • Strategic framing. Cover letters and response-to-referees often contain reviewer-anticipation reasoning, competitor-paper comparisons, and framing decisions that the author of record drafts before sharing with co-authors. Until that draft is ready to share, it should not auto-propagate via git.
  • Confidential journal correspondence. Some editor letters explicitly request confidentiality. The referee PDFs are usually marked confidential by the journal regardless. Keeping them out of git means they do not accidentally end up on a public GitHub fork.
  • The journal portal is the official record. This folder is the working copy of the submission packet, not the canonical one. The journal's portal is where the official version lives; this folder is for you to read and re-read during the revision.

The collaborative half — paper/revisions/<JOURNAL>/ — is tracked in git, because the whole point of putting the response there is to share it with co-authors via Overleaf. The split is what lets both rules hold at once.

docs.title: The submission log
docs.text:
project_management/submission_log.md is the one-line-per-round navigation index across the whole project's submission history. One line per round: date, journal, round type, outcome. Live, hand-maintained, short.

Example:

# Submission log

| Date submitted | Journal | Round | Outcome | Folder |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-01-10 | QJE | initial | R&R (2026-04-22) | 01_QJE_initial/ |
| 2026-06-15 | QJE | R&R     | ... pending     | 02_QJE_R&R/      |

The log answers "what's the current status of this paper?" at a glance. The detailed materials live in the per-round subfolders; the log is the table of contents.

docs.title: What does NOT live in either home
docs.text:
A few things look like submission materials but are not:

  • Internal pre-submission feedback (mock referee from a colleague, talks-feedback that fed into the framing) — those are research-process notes and go in project_management/notes_and_feedback/ with date prefixes per the notes-and-feedback page. The boundary: anything you wrote or received as part of your own collaboration process, not the journal's response.
  • Drafts of the manuscript between rounds. The manuscript is in paper/paper.tex with git history carrying the rounds. There is no separate "draft of round 2" file; round 2 is the state of paper/paper.tex when you submitted it. The frozen PDF in submissions/02_QJE_R&R/ is the snapshot.
  • Grant proposals that fund the work. Grants live in their own folder outside the project per the grants page.
  • Talks built from the paper (seminar slides, conference decks). Those go in paper/presentations/<venue>_<date>/, not in a submissions or revisions folder.

docs.title: Disclosure statements the journal will require (added 2026-07)
docs.text:
Two compliance items are now standard at submission time and belong in every pre-submission checklist:

  • AI-use disclosure. Elsevier journals (JDE, JPubE, EJPE, Journal of Econometrics, and the rest of the family) require authors who used generative AI in the writing process to insert a "Declaration of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the writing process" section immediately above the references, using the publisher's template sentence; AI may be used "to improve the language and readability" and cannot be listed as an author (Elsevier generative-AI policy). Springer Nature, Wiley, Taylor and Francis, and SAGE have similar disclosure requirements. The AEA journal-policies page carries no generative-AI policy as of 2026-07 (AEA policies), so AEA submissions currently need no AI statement -- re-check at submission time.
  • Conflict-of-interest / funding statements. The AEA Disclosure Policy is mandatory for every author: each author submits a disclosure statement identifying potential conflicts of interest, and authors with nothing to disclose must say so explicitly (AEA Disclosure Policy). Most other publishers require an equivalent declaration plus a funding acknowledgement.

Practical rule: when assembling a submission packet, look up the target journal's publisher, apply its AI-disclosure template if one exists, and verify a COI/funding statement exists for every author before the packet freezes. Both are cheap to include and expensive to be caught missing.

docs.title: Cross-cutting with the toolkit
docs.text:
The submission workflow integrates with several existing skills:

  • /review-paper — 6-agent pre-submission referee panel before sending. Run it on the manuscript before the submitted PDF is frozen.
  • /review-paper-light — the fast pre-screen variant when you want a quick sanity check rather than the full panel.
  • bib-audit — catches hallucinated, chimeric, or otherwise broken references in references.bib before the journal does. Run it as a pre-submission gate.
  • audit-reproducibility — confirms the paper's numeric claims match the actual code outputs before the submitted version freezes. Run it on every round; the cost of a mismatch grows after a referee notices it.
  • /respond-to-referees (queued, not yet shipped) — agent-formatting of referee PDFs into the structured TeX that goes in paper/revisions/<JOURNAL>/. Until it ships, the formatting is manual.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
• Submitted PDFs in paper/old/. Loses the per-round bundling with the cover letter and the response. The submitted PDF, cover letter, response, and journal correspondence all belong together as one round's bundle.
  • Cover letters in random root-level files. Every submission's cover letter is per-round and lives in that round's submissions/<NN_journal_round>/ folder, with its editable TeX in the overleaf/ subfolder.
  • Editing a submitted PDF after submission. Version freeze means freeze. The PDF you sent is what the referees and editor saw; if it contained an error, it is part of the historical record. The next round's PDF (in the next submissions/<NN>/ folder) is where the corrected version lives.
  • Response-to-referees TeX in project_management/. Defeats the Overleaf-collaborative workflow; co-authors never see your draft until you email them the file. Put it in paper/revisions/<JOURNAL>/ so the Overleaf sync makes it available the moment you push.
  • Referee reports filed under notes_and_feedback/. Referee reports are journal correspondence, not internal discussion notes. They go in project_management/submissions/<NN_journal_round>/ (the as-received PDFs) and, in formatted form, in paper/revisions/<JOURNAL>/.
  • Numbering rounds without <journal> in the name. 01/, 02/, 03/ makes a one-paper project briefly tidy and a three-paper, two-rejections-and-an-R&R history impossible to navigate. Keep <NN>_<journal>_<round> everywhere.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• folder structure — the project_management/ subfolder list this page assumes, including the paper/revisions/<JOURNAL>/ convention's analogy to paper/presentations/<venue>_<date>/.
  • notes-and-feedback — internal pre-submission feedback (NOT here).
  • where-to-put-things — the cheat-sheet hub.
  • project-structure — the canonical project layout.

docs.title: How Kai's team is set up
docs.text:
These are sensible defaults for a team adopting this workflow — the choices that, in practice, prevent the collaboration problems described in why collaboration is hard. They're recommendations, not requirements: the rest of the workflow works whatever you pick. The how for each lives on the linked page, so there are no step-by-step commands here (nothing written twice).

  • Keep everything in Dropbox. Put each clone_<XX>/ inside the shared Dropbox project folder rather than in a separate folder outside it. Why: you get git history and Dropbox backup of work you haven't pushed yet — an unpushed afternoon survives a laptop dying. → Set up your working clone.
  • One canonical data copy. Don't duplicate data/ into each clone; reach the single shared copy through the .data-in-parent marker. Why: N copies drift; one copy can't. Reads are free; only writes need coordinating. → Set up your working clone · Working with the shared data.
  • Turn on publish-on-merge. Install the post-merge hook so the current paper and exhibits always appear at the container. Why: one obvious place to grab the latest paper at submission time — no "which clone has it?". → Set up your working clone.
  • One Overleaf admin on Overleaf-mastered papers. Prose lives in Overleaf, everything else in git; one person sets up the Overleaf↔git sync (only the Overleaf project owner can). Why: it avoids two people pushing conflicting versions through the bridge. → Why collaboration is hard · Daily workflow & recovery.
  • Announce before rebuilding the analysis dataset. Adding a variable is fine to just merge; a change that moves everyone's results gets a heads-up first and a line in the data changelog. Why: data has no automatic merge, so a silent rebuild changes everyone's numbers under them. → Working with the shared data.

Adopt the ones that fit your project. None of it is enforced — these are simply the defaults that keep a multi-author paper out of trouble.

docs.title: Terminal
docs.text:
Why this page. A terminal is the one small prerequisite under everything else here — installs, git, and running a script all happen there. Ten minutes now removes the panic from every later step, so it's worth doing first if the terminal is unfamiliar.

If you have never opened a terminal in your life, this page walks you through the absolute basics. After 10 minutes of reading and trying the commands, you'll be able to follow the main README.md install instructions without panic.

If you've used cd and ls before, skip this page.

docs.title: What is a terminal?
docs.text:
A terminal (also called "command line", "shell", "console") is a window where you type a command and press Enter, and the computer does it. Most modern apps hide the terminal behind buttons, but everything underneath is just commands. Researchers use terminals because some tools — like git, Claude Code, Stata's batch mode — are easier to drive by typing than by clicking.

You'll only need a small handful of commands for the kai-team-claude install:

  • cd <folder> — change directory (move into a folder)
  • pwd — print working directory (where am I right now?)
  • ls (macOS/Linux) or dir (Windows) — list files in this folder
  • mkdir <name> — make a new folder
  • git clone <url> — download a GitHub repository
  • node --version, claude --version — check that something is installed

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
1. Press the Windows key (or click the Start button), type "Terminal", press Enter.
  2. The app you want is called "Terminal" or "Windows Terminal".
  3. Don't open "Command Prompt" (cmd.exe) — it's older and some commands won't work the same.
  4. The window opens with a PowerShell prompt by default. That's what we'll use. You'll see something like: 
    PS C:\Users\YourName>
    The PS means PowerShell. The path after it is your current location.

If "Terminal" doesn't exist on your Start menu, install it from the Microsoft Store (search "Windows Terminal") — it's free.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
1. Press Cmd+Space to open Spotlight search.
  2. Type "Terminal", press Enter.
  3. A window opens with a prompt like: 
    yourname@mac ~ %
    The ~ means your home folder. The % is where you type.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text: You already know.

docs.title: Where am I?
docs.text:
pwd
Prints your current folder, e.g., C:\Users\YourName or /Users/yourname.

docs.title: List what's in this folder
docs.text:
macOS/Linux: 

ls

Windows PowerShell: 

ls
(Yes, ls works on PowerShell too — it's an alias for dir. Either works.)

docs.title: Move into a folder
docs.text:
cd Documents
Moves you into the Documents folder (must exist in your current location).

cd ..
Moves you up one level (out of the current folder).

cd ~
Moves you to your home folder. (~ is shorthand for the home folder on every OS.)

cd ~/code
Moves to the code folder inside your home folder. The slash direction (/ vs \) doesn't matter on PowerShell — both work.

docs.title: Make a new folder
docs.text:
mkdir code
Creates a folder called code inside the current folder.

docs.title: Run a command
docs.text: Just type the command and press Enter. Examples: - node --version — prints the installed Node.js version, or "command not found" if not installed - git --version — same for git - claude --version — same for Claude Code

docs.title: Copy-pasting commands safely
docs.text: Some commands in our install instructions are long (e.g., the claude mcp add zotero … line). Always paste them as a single line. Line breaks in the middle of a command break it.

docs.title: How to paste
docs.text: OS Shortcut Notes Windows PowerShell Right-click in the window, OR Ctrl+V Right-click pastes whatever is on your clipboard Windows Terminal Ctrl+Shift+V Standard paste shortcut macOS Terminal Cmd+V Standard paste Linux Terminal Ctrl+Shift+V (Plain Ctrl+V doesn't work in most terminals)

docs.title: Replacing placeholders
docs.text:
When you see something like: 

claude mcp add zotero -e ZOTERO_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY_HERE -e ZOTERO_LIBRARY_ID=YOUR_USER_ID …

Don't paste it as-is. Replace YOUR_KEY_HERE with your actual API key, and YOUR_USER_ID with your actual numeric user ID. Then paste the whole line.

docs.title: If a command runs off the screen
docs.text: Long commands wrap to a new visual line in the terminal — that's just display, the command is still one line internally. Press Enter only at the very end.

docs.title: Reading errors
docs.text:
Most errors look scary but are actually short. Read the last few lines — the rest is usually just a stack trace.

Common errors and what they mean:

Message Likely cause command not found: <name> The program isn't installed, OR it's installed but not on your PATH (close and reopen the terminal). permission denied / EACCES You need elevated privileges. On macOS/Linux, try the same command with sudo in front (it'll ask for your password). repository not found (during git clone) The URL is wrong, OR the repo is private and you don't have access. cannot find path / no such file or directory You're in the wrong folder. Run pwd to see where you are, then cd to where you should be.

docs.title: When you get stuck
docs.text:
1. Read the error — usually it tells you exactly what's wrong.
  2. Copy the exact error text (highlight, right-click → copy).
  3. Email Kai the error text plus the README step number you were on. Don't try to fix it by clicking around — most stalls are 30-second fixes once we see the message.

docs.title: A quick sanity check
docs.text:
Before starting the kai-team-claude install, try these in your terminal:

pwd
cd ~
pwd
ls

If those four commands work without error, you're ready. If any fails, ping Kai before going further.

docs.title: What the toolkit is
docs.text:
Why the toolkit exists. Out of the box, Claude Code is a capable generalist that doesn't know how an empirical economist works — left alone it'll happily git add ., state a citation it isn't sure of, or produce a serviceable-but-ugly figure. The toolkit is the accumulated set of guardrails and capabilities that make it good at this job specifically: drafting and reviewing papers in a real voice, building figures from real data, sourcing datasets, referee reports, citation hygiene, replication packages. That's the problem it solves — turning a generalist into a research assistant that already knows your conventions.

Why this page. Before the full list of every command, here's the two-minute picture: what these tools are, how you get them, where they live, and when to update. Once you have that, What's inside is the complete catalogue. (This page is the what; The ideas behind it is the why it's built this way.)

docs.title: Skills, commands, plugins — the words
docs.text:
• A skill is a packaged capability Claude Code can use — e.g. "review this paper like a referee," or "build a figure from World Bank data." You trigger it by asking in plain language (or with a /name); Claude loads the skill's instructions and does the task that way.
  • A command is a skill you invoke by name with a leading slash, like /suggest-jel.
  • A plugin bundles related skills, commands, and agents — e.g. academic-workflow (paper work), project-workflow (repo + bibliography hygiene), talks (presentations).
  • The marketplace is just the catalogue Claude Code installs plugins from. Here, that catalogue is this repository.

docs.title: What a skill actually is — it iterates, it doesn't answer once
docs.text:
This is the part that's easy to miss. A skill is not a single prompt that spits out one answer. It's a packaged procedure — often a build → check → refine loop, sometimes several sub-agents working in turn — that runs before you see anything. The point of bundling it as a skill is exactly to encode "do it properly," not "take one shot."

A few concrete shapes this takes:

  • Self-critique loops. kai-writing runs two drafters → a critic → a rewriter internally, so what reaches you is already a revised draft, not a first pass. Review skills (/review-paper, adversarial-review) run several independent agents tasked to find flaws.
  • Build → render → check → fix. A figure skill should build the figure, render it, look for the obvious problems — a legend overlapping a bar, unreadable axis labels, a wrong unit — fix them, and repeat once or twice before showing you. You should be seeing a checked, refined proposal, not the raw first attempt. (Where a skill doesn't yet iterate enough, you can just say "check it and fix any obvious issues, iterate up to three times" — and that instruction can also live permanently in your personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so it applies everywhere.)

The build → check → refine loop, for a figure:

flowchart LR
    A["you ask"] --> B["build the figure"]
    B --> C{"self-check:<br/>legend overlap? axis labels?<br/>units? obvious errors?"}
    C -->|"issues found"| D["fix"]
    D --> B
    C -->|"clean (or after 1-3 rounds)"| E["show you the<br/>refined result"]

Where adversarial review fits. That "find the flaws" pass is itself a skill you can run on demand (adversarial-review, /review-paper). It can also be wired to fire automatically — the same hook mechanism that already guards raw data could, for example, run a quick figure-review after a figure is written or nudge an adversarial pass after a draft changes. (That auto-wiring is a roadmap item, not on by default yet — today you invoke it.)

docs.title: How you get it
docs.text:
The toolkit lives in one GitHub repository — github.com/KaliGi/kai-team-claude (private; ask Kai for an invite) — and installs into Claude Code:

  • The easy way: add the marketplace, then install the plugins you want — a few lines, walked through in Install the Claude Code toolkit.
  • Where it lands — two tiers on your machine (~ is your home folder):
  • The ~/.claude/ tier (copied by the install script): skills, agents, writing principles, templates, and these docs — loaded automatically in every Claude Code session. This is your copy; updating the shared repo replaces only the items that come from it, leaving your own private experiments in ~/.claude/ untouched.
  • The plugin tier (added via /plugin install …): the slash-commands, managed by Claude Code's own registry.

docs.title: When (and how) to update
docs.text: When a teammate says "pull the latest," or you want a newly added skill, re-run the marketplace update — it's a ~30-second step, not a reinstall. The Updates page shows the version you're on and what changed in each release.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
→ Install the Claude Code toolkit, then browse What's inside and How to do a task — or jump to First things to try for a quick win.

New to git or terminals? The 10-minute primer defines clone, repo, and commit in plain language first.

docs.title: Triggering skills
docs.text: There are three ways to put a skill to work. They all run the same skill — pick whichever is easiest in the moment.

docs.title: 1. A slash command — /name (most explicit)
docs.text: Type the command, e.g. /suggest-jel or /review-paper. This is the surest way: you're naming exactly what you want, so there's no guessing. Use it when you know the command's name. The full list is in what's inside (every command and skill, one line each).

docs.title: 2. Just ask in plain language
docs.text: Describe the task and Claude picks the matching skill — "review this paper like a referee," "build a figure of GDP per capita from World Bank data," "suggest JEL codes for this abstract." Best when you don't remember (or never knew) the exact name. You don't need the magic words; a clear description of the goal is enough.

docs.title: 3. Auto-trigger (a nudge, not a guarantee)
docs.text: Some skills are written to fire on their own when the context matches — e.g. when you're editing a .tex file, or ask for a real-data figure, the relevant skill may kick in without you naming it. This is convenient, but treat it as a nudge, not a promise: auto-triggering depends on the model recognizing the situation, and it won't always fire.

docs.title: If a skill doesn't fire when you expected
docs.text:
Just name it explicitly — that's what options 1 and 2 are for: use the /command, or say "use the X skill to do this." Being explicit always wins over hoping it auto-triggers. If you're not sure a capability exists at all, scan what's inside or how to do a task first.

Rule of thumb: know the name → slash command; know the task but not the name → just ask; neither → check the index. Don't rely on auto-trigger for anything important — name it.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text: Why this page exists. You're working with a toolkit that changes — conventions get sharpened, skills get added, occasionally something is renamed. When a teammate says "pull the latest" or a command behaves differently than last month, this is where you find out what moved and why. Read the top entry after any update; that's usually all you need.

docs.title: What version am I on?
docs.text: The kit as a whole is versioned CalVer — YYYY.MM, the month of the cut. The current version is in /VERSION. Individual plugins also carry their own major.minor.patch semver in their plugin.json, so you can pin one plugin without tracking the whole kit. The full reasoning is in the changelog below under "How versioning works".

docs.title: To update
docs.text:
You rarely need this; consumers update opt-in (your installed version keeps working). Only whoever maintains the toolkit updates after every change.

When you do update, follow the canonical 4-step ritual — it's the single source of truth, and a partial (plugin-only) update leaves you half-updated: install the toolkit → "Updating later".

docs.title: 2026-08-12 — spec-gate 0.18.0: the stale-set resolver — incremental recomputation lands (KG-ruled)
docs.text:
• stale_set.py — “only the affected parts get redone”, mechanized. KG named the gap reviewing the pipeline map ("we have not thought about this carefully enough yet"); the stage-spec had admitted it since day one ("'depended on' is undefined — no dependency graph in any file"; the dry run: 3 sentences of feedback → 46 edit sites → 6 silent inconsistencies, found by hand). The insight that made it cheap: the EDGES ALREADY EXIST in the store's schema — cites, verbatim-inherited shows, placement→section ids, hash-keyed receipts. The resolver is a READER over them: give it what changed (E-ids, section ids, exhibit files, plan files, numbers.json) and it prints the precise redo list — each item with WHY and the gate that verifies its redo — plus what stays green. Coarse cases stay honest and loud (numbers.json has no per-key trace map yet; deck papertags noted, not parsed). Battery 13 probes with SELECTIVITY as the property under test: an E01 edit implicates E01's receipt and citers and must NOT touch E02's. Wired into kai-writing's reopen doctrine: compute the stale set FIRST.
  • validate_manifests false-RED fixed (taskboard session's report): the hook-path regex ran over json.dumps output where quotes arrive escaped, so every quoted path captured a trailing backslash and read as missing — ALL hooks reported absent while every file existed. Capture class now excludes the backslash; proven able-to-fail on a genuinely missing ref. Repo spec-gate: all four conditions GREEN (docs re-read + receipted, authoring probe re-judged by a fresh-context agent, 0.85).

Notable changes to the kai-team-claude marketplace. Maintained chronologically (newest first). Format loosely follows Keep a Changelog.

To install or update plugins, restart Claude Code and run:

/plugin marketplace update kai-team-claude
/plugin install <plugin-name>@kai-team-claude

docs.title: How versioning works
docs.text:
Two levels, on purpose:

  • The kit as a whole uses CalVer — YYYY.MM, the month of the cut. The current version lives in /VERSION (now 2026.07). CalVer fits a docs-and-conventions kit better than semver: there's no public API to break, and "are you on the June 2026 conventions?" is the question people actually ask.
  • Each plugin carries its own semver in its plugin.json (major.minor.patch) so an install can pin a specific plugin without tracking the whole kit. Bump the plugin's semver in the same commit that changes its behaviour.

Entries below are chronological (newest first). Dates are the change date; they roll up into the monthly CalVer cut.

docs.title: 2026-07-31 — project-workflow 1.61.1: the question gate names the LIVE ask (id-mining refinement)
docs.text: • gate_question_discipline now skips ANSWERED popups (their tool_result is in the transcript): id-mining's field case had the gate name a popup that was already answered and acted on, sending the session to re-litigate a resolved question while the actual live defect — a bare dangling "A or B?" closer — went unnamed. The gate judges the turn's LIVE state; battery +2 probes (answered popup passes / same popup unanswered still blocks). The bare-"A or B?" tell itself stays deliberately UNARMED: it is mechanically indistinguishable from a legitimate INTERVIEW-mode question, which by KG's own ruling carries no forced options — arming it would punish the ruled mode. Documented in the gate header with the rest of the not-armed set.

docs.title: 2026-07-31 — project-workflow 1.61.0: the write-time colour gate (pn's escaped pink, mechanized)
docs.text: • gate_theme_colors.py (universal PreToolUse): a Write/Edit that introduces an off-catalog hex into a colour-bearing file (.tex/.qmd/.sty/.scss/.R/.py/.yaml) is DENIED with the nearest catalog colour named — the swap KG asked for, computed. The field case (pn 002): a ported Beamer preamble's #994C9E pink survived three review rounds until KG caught it by eye; ports bypass every "don't hand-type hexes" rule because the hex isn't typed, it rides in. Design carries the day's audit lessons: catalog regexed from kai_theme.yaml (yaml-parse in a hook path silently disarms on yaml-less machines — audit M4), scans NEW content only (payload-source rule), neutral greys pass, auditable inline waiver % theme: allow #HEX (<reason>), fail-open, silent where no theme is installed. Battery 9 probes; probe 1 IS the pn case.

docs.title: 2026-07-31 — The portability audit: two adversarial sweeps, 9 shell + 16 python findings, all HIGH/MED fixed (KG-mandated)
docs.text:
• KG's instinct was right ("whether there might not be even more that we have overlooked"): two independent audit agents, seeded with the five already-caught bugs, swept every shell script (both repos) and all 150 Python files. Confirmed defects fixed in one batch:
  • Shell (coord 0.6.1 + repo tooling): find -printf in newest_mtime silently returned 0 forever on macOS — the "STATE.md older than inbox" rebuild trigger NEVER fired (the sibling of the already-fixed stat bug); acceptance.sh had CRLF endings (unparseable on Mac), MSYS-only default paths that made the PRIVACY gates pass vacuously (G16 grepped a nonexistent tree), and GNU touch -d; pwd -W in a smoke test; a GNU stat one-liner in the git-workflow principle backing the 5MB guard; release_check remediation strings said bare python. Plus a bug in MY OWN bash-3.2 rewrite: BSD awk does not interpret -F'\x1f', so every STATE section printed EMPTY — caught by the repaired acceptance suite (G27), which now runs green on macOS for the FIRST time: 32 PASS / 0 FAIL, exec bits restored, 22 message-schema warnings repaired (headers only, bodies untouched). G16 then fired for real: mac-day-one.md leaked the private coord path into the team-visible repo — redacted.
  • Python (aw 1.46.1, spec-gate 0.17.1, talks 1.9.1, pw 1.60.1): the skill-description lint exited 0 with pyyaml missing (PASS with the lint never run — now exit 2); validate_fragment crashed at import on 3.9 with an exit code aliasing "fragment failed validation" (future-import added, and the py-compat guard that would have caught it was widened from talks-only to ALL 87 shipped scripts); release_check callers re-misreported generator refusals as staleness one level up (exit codes now checked, stderr shown); sglib's bare import yaml made every spec-gate entry point die with exit 1 = "conditions RED" (now exit 2); the reground nudge silently disarmed on yaml-less machines (now stdlib-only — verified firing under system 3.9); gen_bindings wrote platform-dependent line endings its own --check could not see (newline pinned + .gitattributes covers .sty/.scss/.do); lockdown_grep passed on ZERO extracted numbers (now INACTIVE exit 2); a ≤ glyph crashed cp1252-piped PASS output; render_slide's dead /c/ Windows fallback + exit-0 selftest skip. Documented-not-changed: the early-draft vacuous-pass trio (exhibit-refs/label-refs/number-trace), manifest timestamps, spec_gate shell=True (per-audit reasoning in the reports).

docs.title: 2026-07-31 — KG RULES the paper-exhibit font set: 10 / 9 / 8, one register for tables AND figures (theme 0.3.0)
docs.text:
• The ruling (live interview; pn's exhibit-font-discipline thread was the seed): ONE register for all exhibit text — 10pt tables-standard + in-figure titles/direct labels (\small), 9pt dense tables + axis titles + tick text (\footnotesize), 8pt notes of tables and figures + source lines + map legends (\scriptsize). Body prose stays 11; page footnotes stay LaTeX-automatic ("I would not change that"). HARD FLOOR 8pt — a 13" laptop at fit-page renders ~60–75% linear, so smaller is unreadable without zoom. Evidence: measured across KG's own working papers, Insuring Peace 2024 runs exactly this shape; the drift papers ran 6pt tables.
  • Wired through every surface that decides a font size: kai_theme.yaml 0.3.0 paper block (ruling + quotes + rationale) → regenerated R/py bindings (theme_paper(): title 11→10, axis text 8→9, caption 7.5→8); theme_conformance.py now measures RENDERED spans in figure PDFs — off-set or sub-8pt = RED, photos pass vacuously, and because it reads the export it catches Rule 2b downstream rescales too (battery +4, able to fail); check_table_format (aw 1.46.0) gains the carve-out the set implies — \scriptsize legal inside tablenotes (it IS the ruled note size), still banned in the tabular body, \tiny banned everywhere (probe 5 deliberately INVERTED, +2 probes); tikz-figure trap 0 = the size discipline; review-figure checks the register and keeps the human-judgment slot for baked-in text (photos/maps). Reviewer agents are now aware by construction.
  • Still open with KG: figure display-WIDTH classes — a visual artifact session with examples (2x1/2x2 panels are the complication).

docs.title: 2026-07-30 — coord 0.6.0 + hook doctrine: two Mac-killers out of housekeeping.sh; the payload-source rule written down (id-mining field fixes)
docs.text:
• housekeeping.sh ran ZERO successful STATE rebuilds on the Mac since the migration — two stacked bash portability bugs (id-mining 001 found the first; fixing it exposed the second): GNU-only stat -c (BSD needs -f; portable fallback applied here + three more sites in the coord repo's acceptance.sh) and then declare -A at the addressee grouping (bash-4+; macOS ships 3.2 — same class as the template-harness false-green). Grouping is now a temp-file group-by. First successful Mac rebuild 2026-07-30; note the first fixed run saw real mtimes at last, so the 14-day closure legitimately archived 16 long-quiet threads in one sweep.
  • The payload-source rule is doctrine (docs/maintainer-notes.md, "Authoring hooks"): a hook matches the payload FIELD it means (tool_input.command), never raw stdin — which also carries tool_response, so a find that merely LISTS a figure tripped a project-local exhibit gate and blocked a session that had touched no exhibit. With the loud-safe/silent-unsafe asymmetry and a promotion bar: no marketplace hook without an output-only must-NOT-fire probe.

docs.title: 2026-07-30 — project-workflow 1.60.0: file-link gate resolves from the LAUNCH DIR (uam field fix)
docs.text: • The dead-link problem's real defect was in the GATE, not the model (uam trace, 2026-07-23): gate_file_links.py resolved hrefs from the payload's shell cwd — which DRIFTS with persistent-shell cd — while the client resolves from the immutable session launch dir. A cd'd shell made the gate reject CORRECT links and dictate DEAD ones; the model was right and the blocking hook overrode it, so no model-side rule could ever stick. Base is now $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR (payload cwd only as a named fallback), the deny message STATES the base ("Bash cd drift never changes the link base"), separators normalize cross-OS, case-only misses suggest the exact-case href. Battery +5: the uam inversion pair (correct-href-under-drift passes; drifted-bare-href blocks with the launch-relative fix), fallback naming, backslash normalization, case recovery — plus the runner now strips its own real CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR, which would have silently overridden every temp-dir probe.

docs.title: 2026-07-30 — project-workflow 1.59.0: the 4c post-paper lifecycle (mandate item e)
docs.text:
• /promote-canonical — the once-per-paper canonical handover (pn 019; KG: "what we now build is the new canonical file... did we specify how this is resolved?"). Four steps, two HUMAN gates: rename the blessed built file to the PAPER's name (fixing every reference in the same commit); retire the old canonical ONLY after Kai confirms the Overleaf main-document repoint (retiring first breaks the compile exactly when co-authors are looking); rewrite the CLAUDE.md source-of-truth line (the stale line is how the corpse gets re-forked); record the handoff. Then the R8 checklist + the Publish flow. Refuses to run "while at it" — the command IS the blessing ceremony.
  • git-assistant gains the Publish intent (merge-safe + grab-point): fetch first; if origin/main moved, MERGE — never rebase/force a shared branch (the RA's Overleaf-bridge figure commit near-miss is the cited case); re-verify; push with KG's per-push approval; then recompile and drop <paper>_YYYY-MM-DD.pdf into the container's paper/ grab-point — part of publish, not a favour (it held a month-old PDF when nobody owned the step).

docs.title: 2026-07-30 — Prewriting build §5.6: the ruled stage flow reaches the skills
docs.text:
• kai-writing — the stage-gate ladder is now the RULED flow: A → A' (interpretation receipts, check_interp --record after the cold-eyes pass — leads may only assert receipted interpretations) → B → B' (fact-verification SCRIPT over the full design matrix, output stored beside the section plan — never a spot-check) → C. Sign-offs run sign_stage.py (immutable snapshot + mirror refresh — a hand-signed stage is what G-mirror refuses). The two R1 INTERVIEW MOMENTS are scripted in: moment 1 at exhibit planning (two input styles, KG picks; AI-introduced interpretations enter as status: PROPOSED), moment 2 user-activated at skeleton checkpoints (bring the open PROPOSED queue — never make KG ask). Delivery refuses while undrained PROPOSED remain (check_drain --strict-status) and promotion runs check_promote.
  • academic-workflow 1.45.0 — bootstrap-paper asks the R8 preamble question UP FRONT: canonical template preamble, or lifted verbatim from a KG-named reference paper — asked before scaffolding, because the R8 failure was front matter improvised mid-session after the skeleton had already become the conference draft. Skipped on --update or when the invocation names a source.

docs.title: 2026-07-30 — spec-gate 0.17.0: the R5 sign step ships — promote-on-sign made mechanical (G-mirror)
docs.text: • sign_stage.py, two verbs, one owner of the mirror format. sign: immutable stage snapshot (<stem>_s<N>_signed.md — a re-sign of an existing stage refuses; a reopened stage is a NEW number, not an overwrite), then the mechanical R5 mirror refresh: every canonical paper/plan/ file copied to project_management/plan_mirror/ (clone or container level, resolved loudly; multi-clone layouts land the mirror at the CONTAINER, the shared co-author surface) with its authority line rewritten to reference (mirror; canon = paper/plan/) and the copy made read-only; a sign-time receipt records every mirrored hash. check (G-mirror): refuses signed-without-mirror, a tampered or missing mirror copy (the receipt is the guarantee — read-only is best-effort), and a hand-signed snapshot absent from the last receipt ("stale mirror at sign"). Canon running ahead of the mirror BETWEEN signs is legal by design — mid-stage thinking stays clone-local (KG's ruling, verbatim). Battery 15 probes; mirror joins the registry opt-in (S9 now proves 16 gates able-to-fail). Build order §5.4 done; §5.6 (skill wiring) is next.

docs.title: 2026-07-30 — spec-gate 0.16.1: G-authority reaches the case that motivated it
docs.text: • {legacy_flags} emit-time sweep: plan_to_conditions now passes old STANDALONE drafts (\documentclass files that are not the resolved master, in paper/ and at root) to check_authority as --legacy. The R2 ruling was triggered by exactly this shape — a stale full draft OUTSIDE paper/plan/ treated as binding — which the 0.16.0 wiring (plan-dir only) could not see. Section/fragment files (no \documentclass) are never swept: a live section is not a legacy document. Non-breaking: unmarked legacy defaults to reference (a printed note); the dead-cite scan gains reach when KG marks a draft superseded. Battery +S10 (draft in, master + sections out).

docs.title: 2026-07-26 — Template harness: macOS bash 3.2 false-green fixed
docs.text: • templates/tests/test_setup_templates.sh — two mechanisms against one false-green: on macOS's stock bash 3.2 the harness aborted mid-run (declare -A is bash-4+; the subsequent assoc-array assignment becomes an expansion error under set -u) — and bash 3.2 exits 0 on that abort, so RUN_HARNESS=1 release_check.sh printed "PASS — template harness green" after only 2 of 15 checks had executed. Fix 1: C2 agreement bookkeeping rewritten without associative arrays (newline-separated LANG=path records + scalar count) — the harness is bash-3.2-clean end to end; R + Python batteries verified executing on macOS (15 PASS; missing Stata stays an honest SKIP → exit 2). Fix 2: a verdict-flag EXIT trap — every legitimate ending records a verdict first; any exit without one (machinery breakage, whatever exit status bash claims) forces a loud exit 3 and cleans the sandbox. set -e / trap ERR were not options: the C4/C5 runners are expected to hard-error. Battery falsified in all directions: sabotaged template → exit 1; skipped language → exit 2; injected mid-run abort → exit 3; KT_HARNESS_ALLOW_SKIP=1 → genuine exit 0.

docs.title: 2026-07-26 — Prewriting build 2/7: the five ruled gates join the emission registry (opt-in)
docs.text:
• spec-gate 0.16.0 — plan_to_conditions registers all five R1–R8 gates: authority, placement, interp, drain, promote are now scriptable registry entries, each with a known-bad fixture proving it can go RED. New emit-time resolutions (never walk-up discovery — pn's RED-as-noise defect): {plan_dir}, {project_flag}, {drain_plan_flags}, {promote_tex_flag}. Verified end-to-end on a scratch project: all five emit as deterministic checks with substituted paths and execute correctly (drain goes RED under --strict-status on a status-less ledger, as designed).
  • OPT-IN by name — the default gate-sets are UNCHANGED. Registering a gate makes it runnable, not attached. Attaching any of these today would paint every live field ledger RED for R1–R8 fields nobody asked them for, and build order §5.7 records KG's promise that uam + id-mining comment on artifact shapes BEFORE gates harden.
  • Registry meta-probe (S9): the battery now runs EVERY registered gate's selftest and asserts it exits with its pinned code — 15 gates, all RED on their fixtures. S4 only ever exercised the two gates its fixture plan declared, so a gate could previously join the shelf with a selftest that silently passed (broken fixture path → exit 2).
  • Checking gates no longer create state: check_interp and check_promote read receipts without state_dir()'s mkdir — a gate that writes while reading littered every project (and every fixture run) with empty state dirs.

docs.title: 2026-07-25 — Prewriting build 3/7 (third tranche): G-promote ships — the R8 promotion checklist
docs.text: • spec-gate 0.15.0 — check_promote.py (R8): the skeleton→paper gate, run on what the READER sees (extracted PDF text, --text pages or --pdf via PyMuPDF — extraction exits 2 rather than silently degrading) plus what only the source shows (--tex). Print side: Abstract + Conclusion headings, JEL with a real code, the bracket-placeholder denylist in print, the acknowledgments joke class (aperitivo / lorem ipsum / save the world), the p ¡ OT1 mojibake, and page numbers on 3+-page documents (KG reviews by scrolling). Source side: the empirical/identification span must carry a numbered equation env (KG: "I never want to see it missing"; per-REGRESSION granularity waits on the fragment manifest and says so on every run — no silent caps), and an appendix with floats needs at least one body reference (a dangling promise otherwise). With --ledger: the abstract-rewrite receipt, keyed to the results-ledger hash (--record-abstract), goes STALE when the ledger moves. Battery 19 probes, able to fail, CI-safe text fixtures. Still open from items 2–3: the plan_to_conditions G-* emission wiring (next unit) and G-floats (waits on pn's four scripts).

docs.title: 2026-07-25 — Prewriting build 3/7 (second tranche): G-interp ships — the A' verification receipt
docs.text: • spec-gate 0.14.0 — check_interp.py (R3.1, stage A'): every RULED shows line requires a verification RECEIPT proving someone held it against the rendered exhibit — not just copied it consistently (consistency is not truth: the last paper's leads matched the brief perfectly and the figures not at all). Receipts reuse the probe semantics (interp_<EID>.json in the spec-gate state dir): keyed to the exhibit file hash (re-render → STALE) AND the shows text (edit → STALE), must name the verifier, and a recorded does-not-hold FAILS LOUDLY — a known refutation is fixed and re-verified, never ridden along. --record mode is the single owner of the receipt format. Battery 13 probes, able to fail.

docs.title: 2026-07-25 — Prewriting build 3/7 (first tranche): G-authority, G-placement, G-drain ship with batteries
docs.text:
• spec-gate 0.13.0 — three of the five ruled check scripts: check_authority.py (R2: every paper/plan/*.md declares binding | reference | superseded near the top; closed vocabulary; a binding file naming a superseded one is a DEAD CITE; unmarked legacy inputs default to reference; the constraint-vs-source judgment is honestly out of scope — it routes through the R2 challenge flag). check_placement.py (R6: placements speak the closed vocabulary — id first, criterion after; appendix requires a named criterion; redundant-with-E# must name a real block; demotion requires title provenance; (distrust) on an appendix move fails — distrust is a cut). check_drain.py (R1 pre-final gate: refuses while status: PROPOSED interpretations remain; waivers must be RECORDED in the ledger with date
  • quote; --strict-status for final-paper runs where untracked = not drained). Batteries 10+11+10 probes, all able to fail; self-review caught and killed one false-pass route pre-battery (appendix argument mentioning "main 4.2" would have been classified as main placement). Still open in this tranche: check_interp (R3.1) + check_promote (R8) + plan_to_conditions emission — G-interp needs its A' verification-record design settled first.

docs.title: 2026-07-25 — Prewriting build 1/7: the ruled schema lands in templates (+ field-scoped gate vocabulary)
docs.text:
• project-workflow 1.58.0 — templates carry the R1–R8 schema: EXHIBIT-DECISIONS.md gains producer: (R4, fact field — script path + line range, manual (<reason>) for hand-made), the CLOSED R6 placement vocabulary (id first, criterion after: appendix A.2 (redundant-with-E02) / (reference-only) / (demoted-from-main); distrust = cut, never an appendix move), conditions: (R5b, provisional), notes: decided at planning (R7), and the block-level status: PROPOSED | CONFIRMED drain marker (R1); order is REMOVED (stage-spec v2 — placement already determines order, the two contradicted twice in the dry run). All paper/plan/ templates + the new BLOCKERS.md template (R5a, home project_management/) carry R2 authority headers. section_plan.md's how: now demands the printed panel/column + autoref landing spot, with how: standard as the explicit shorthand (R7).
  • spec-gate 0.12.0 — field-scoped vocabulary: CONFIRMED is legal on the status field ONLY; on any other field it stays an unknown-status FAIL (a global addition would let title CONFIRMED slip the must-rule check — the v1 false-PASS class). R6 criterion suffixes parse without breaking section-id resolution. Batteries +7 probes (47/47 + 30/30), each able to fail.
  • R5c verified already-closed: live probes show sec3_data_plan.md under paper/plan/ and project_management/BLOCKERS.md both ALLOW in the shipped structure gate — uam's denial was against an older manifest; no gate change needed.

docs.title: 2026-07-24 — Rulings day: pre-writing stage fully ruled (R1–R8); question discipline gets two modes and a gate; field fixes built shell-blind
docs.text:
• KG ruled ALL EIGHT pre-writing decisions in one arc (rulings agenda = the record; working/prewriting-build-spec.md = the binding build translation): R1 interview mode with a single pre-final PROPOSED-drain gate + self-initiated questions; R2 authority markers with a mandated CHALLENGE process (dispute → flag to KG; silent deviation AND silent compliance both violations; rulings versioned, never overwritten); R3 BOTH verification layers (exhibit-interpretation ledger before leads + full-matrix fact script before prose); R4 required producer: pinning; R5 git paper/plan/ canon + read-only mirror on signed stages (BLOCKERS.md derived to project_management/); R6 closed placement vocabulary; R7 how: names the printed panel + autoref spot; R8 the full promotion package — bidirectional completeness + a deterministic printed-output component checklist on EXTRACTED PDF text + float placement (G-floats) + per-regression estimating equations + the post-paper lifecycle (promote-to-canonical with human-gated Overleaf repoint, grab-point PDF refresh, merge-safe publish).
  • Question discipline, mechanized after KG's "I must make decisions that lack sufficient context": the principle gains Step 0 (a fact a read-only check settles is NEVER a question — the uam 20-second case), two modes (decision = options+pros/cons; interpretation = multi-round interview, no forced options), the context-sufficiency test, the popup channel rule (never when deciding requires looking at artifacts), and sentence-asks-carry-the-paragraph. project-workflow 1.57.0 ships gate_question_discipline — a Stop hook blocking the two near-zero-false-positive tells (artifact-referencing popup; resolvable fact dressed as a decision), 8-probe battery.
  • academic-workflow 1.44.0 — both confirmed-live uam gaps closed: F1 non-prose group strip (multi-group \graphicspath residue no longer a "sentence"; brace-wrapping prose is NOT an evasion) + F2 origin-ref port pass (landed-on-main prose recognized lazily via git show, fail-closed, memoized). Battery +4 probes incl. a real bare-origin fixture. kai-writing adds port-verbatim-first and sentence-asks-carry-the-paragraph.
  • talks 1.9.0 — three KG standing rules from live deck reviews: estimating equation mandatory per regression shown; papertags from the .aux; the closer is CONCLUSION (question restated, contribution dominant). Lint code follows.
  • Allowlist resilience (KG-mandated): coding-workflow.md gains the emit-BARE-commands doctrine (full paths only for tools not on PATH; never widen patterns — chaining hole); read-only allowlist additions proposed to KG (sessions cannot edit their own permission config — the classifier enforcing that is working as intended).
  • Built SHELL-BLIND: the Bash-wrapper outage (two-machine evidence pack in coord) blocked all execution; every change above was written file-only with batteries prepared — the first working shell runs batteries → release_check → ship.
  • Mac first-shell run (the ship): batteries caught two real defects, both fixed before commit. (1) F2 never worked as written — git ls-tree ignores a *.tex pathspec (unlike ls-files) and, run from the paper/ subdir, emits cwd-relative names git show <ref>:<path> can't resolve; fixed with ls-tree --full-tree + Python .tex filter (verified git 2.50). (2) gate_file_links _ABS_PAT only caught Windows drives + git-bash /c/ mounts, so on macOS a POSIX-absolute href (/Users/…) slipped through as "relative", resolved, and was not blocked — the gate silently failing at its one job; fixed to treat any leading / as absolute. Both batteries green; principles/ coding-workflow.md mirror re-synced to satisfy release_check.

docs.title: 2026-07-23 — Field day 3: version-floor gate born, ports unblocked, drafter discipline binding
docs.text:
• spec-gate 0.11.0 — the deployment gap gets a GATE (pn's F7). Three stale-cache incidents in one week (a fixed root-.bib denial re-reported as fresh by another project; aw stuck at 1.41.0 in pn's field run; the check's FIRST live run catching a stale cache on KG's own machine) earned the class a mechanical answer: check_plugin_floor.py compares the installed plugin cache against a declared floor, and plan_to_conditions.py now emits a plugin-version-floor check into EVERY conditions.yaml, pinning the repo's plugin versions at emit time. Stale cache → RED with the exact update command, instead of a confident, obsolete refusal the project then has to report as a bug. Plan-level waiver version_floor: waived (<reason>) keeps test fixtures machine-independent. 6/6 battery on a synthetic cache (numeric version compare, not lexicographic); full emit suite green.
  • academic-workflow 1.43.0 — co-author ports pass ALL lints (narrow form). uam's verbatim port of a co-author's formal model was impossible through the pipeline (voice + para-length lints fired on prose that is not ours to restyle) and landed via the raw-Python bypass — exactly the evasion the gates must not train. Now: when EVERY produced sentence already exists verbatim in a git-tracked repo .tex, all lints skip; ANY new sentence → full lints, so produced prose cannot ride in on a port's coattails. Plus: build_agent_prompt.py embeds intro-architecture.md as a MANDATED file whenever the task mentions intro/introduction/contribution (pn 015: three sessions made the P2 mistake with the doc on disk; "a rule out of attention is absent" — the fourth cannot dispatch without it in context), and writing_style_kai.md states the generated band is DESCRIPTIVE, never a target (KG ruling — padding a sentence to reach the mean is a defect). SKILL.md makes pn's drafter discipline binding: findings applied as MINIMAL EDITS; unavoidable rebuilds use the reviewer's verbatim sentence.
  • project-workflow 1.56.3 — *.ps1 joins the code/ allow list. The canon itself ships code/run_all.ps1 as the AEA Windows replication entry point; per the yaml's own header the prose doc wins, so the omission was the bug (uam field report).

docs.title: 2026-07-21 (evening) — Rule 2b: figure fonts pinned at export; hygiene batch; planning-evidence net widened
docs.text:
• Theme: PINNED EXPORTS (exhibit-font Rule 2b, un-deferred by KG). The figure-side of the table discipline: fonts are only TRUE at the export size, so rescaling a themed figure re-sizes every font in it. The yaml gains the export doctrine; the GENERATED R + Python bindings gain kai_save() with REQUIRED width_mm/height_mm (placement width is a conscious choice — measure \the\textwidth, never guess) and no bbox_inches='tight' (a crop changes the placed size); theme_conformance.py now REDs unpinned ggsave() (missing dims or scale=) and tight-bbox savefig() in .R/.py scripts, docs files exempt. Suite 15/15.
  • Working-notes hygiene batch: the ~20 older working/ files landed in three explicit commits (session-note updates; untracked audits/protos/ plans; the collaborator-roster template with example rows only); a nested duplicate directory (working/working/, proven a stale subset) removed.
  • Planning evidence: the pre-writing ask extended to uam (an oversight — 001 went only to pn and id-mining; uam has the longest planning-doc history) + a scoped reminder to pn naming exactly what remains open (Q6: which file went stale first, one document or several).
