docs.title: 2026-06-17 — Float-placement house rule: exhibits stay in their section
docs.text:
Baked Kai's "every table sits in its section, never floats to the page top" rule into the LaTeX conventions and both code reviewers, so it stops being re-fixed per project. A table that floats to the top can land above its own section heading — exactly what happened to an id-mining donation table that used [ht].

  • Convention (academic-workflow v1.13.0): new latex-fragment-conventions rule 8 — paper exhibits use \begin{table}[H] (strict; float is in the standard preamble) or [h!] (confined to its section by [section]{placeins}), never [ht]/[htbp]/[t]/[tbp]/[b]/[p]. The rule's own examples and /build-fragment-table's modern style moved from [htbp] to [H]; the classic style keeps its verified [h!] + \FloatBarrier. The Stata recipe (stata-code-conventions §5b) switched to [H].
  • Reviewers flag the default: stata-reviewer §6 and r-reviewer's new §6b (TABLE OUTPUT) flag a [ht]/[htbp]/[t] spec in any emitted \begin{table} (MEDIUM; recommend [H]). stata-research-workflow v1.4.1, r-research-workflow v1.2.1.
  • Fix-at-the-source caveat: change the generator's float spec and regenerate; never sed -i/perl -i fragments in place on a Dropbox-hosted repo — sync races corrupt files mid-write (a .do Stata was reading got corrupted this way).
  • \usepackage{float} + [section]{placeins} were already in templates/latex-preamble.tex, so no preamble change was needed.

docs.title: 2026-06-17 — paper_structure.md source of truth + exhibits-preview drift check
docs.text:
A per-paper "what goes where, and why" file, plus the tooling to keep the paper honest against it. /bootstrap-paper now scaffolds paper_structure.md from templates/paper_structure.md: a section outline (one claim per section, not a label), an exhibit map (every table/figure slot → its file, marked TO BUILD until produced), and a conventions/decisions log (main contrast, key measure, sample, what's dropped and why). It records structural intent so iterative sessions and co-authors stop re-litigating settled choices — updated in the same turn a decision is made, like a memory note.

  • /build-exhibits-preview (project-workflow v1.17.0) gained a plan-drift check: it auto-detects paper_structure.md (or --structure <path>), parses the exhibit-map table, and cross-checks it against what the paper actually \input/\includegraphics. The report flags exhibits in the paper but not the plan, exhibits marked built but never included, and slots still TO BUILD. Reported as guidance — does not change the exit code. Skip with --no-structure.
  • /bootstrap-paper is academic-workflow v1.12.0.

docs.title: 2026-06-17 — /refactor-structure safety loop (project-workflow v1.16.0)
docs.text:
Closed the refactoring loop: plan → independently CHECK the plan → execute WITH a mandatory backup → VERIFY nothing was lost → DELETE only recoverable duplicates. refactor_structure.py gained --backup, --check-plan, --inventory, --verify, --cleanup, governed by one rule (REPLACED-vs-MOVED: a layout refactor only moves/copies, never destroys, so the backup is temporary and deleted after a clean verify).

  • The backup lives in-project at .claude/legacy/refactor_backup_<date>/ (workspace boundary; tar-pipe with --exclude so it can't nest in itself), not a parent sibling.
  • DELETE is the only destroy path and is triple-gated: clean verify required, per-target --delete-* default to keep, and --execute required — a missing/unclean verify refuses all deletes.
  • The _delete step retry-loops (5×, backoff) on Windows "Device or resource busy" / WinError 32 from Dropbox sync handles.
  • Known latent bug (queued): MOVE mode pre-creates the target dir before git mv, which can nest one level too deep; COPY mode (the canonical path) is unaffected and VERIFY catches the bad shape.

docs.title: 2026-06-16 — /resolve-conflict (project-workflow v1.15.0)
docs.text:
A conflict-triage command. Detects which of three kinds is present and routes each:

  • git merge conflict (tracked files) — walk the <<<</====/>>>> markers to a chosen resolution + git add, with git merge --abort named as the no-loss escape; never force-push or reset.
  • Dropbox (conflicted copy) on the shared container — diff, merge, and delete the stray copy.
  • silent logical break a clean merge introduced (the case git cannot see) — identify the foundational change and draft a heads-up to the co-author for human coordination.

Complements git-assistant (conversational git) with the Dropbox + logical routing. Pairs with docs/how-merging-works.md.

docs.title: 2026-06-16 — /build-exhibits-preview (project-workflow v1.14.0)
docs.text:
Scaffold + compile a prose-free "exhibits preview" proof sheet of a paper — every \input table fragment and \includegraphics figure, in document order, under its section heading, with first-pass \interp/\trans handover lines for the author to edit.

  • build_exhibits_preview.py discovers exhibits (comment-aware, .tex-optional \input, multi-line \includegraphics, nearest section title) and flags inline-authored floats (exit 2, hand-add).
  • --compile/--scratch-dir run one nonstopmode pdflatex pass with cwd = clone root (so output/ paths resolve); degrades gracefully when pdflatex is missing and when referenced exhibits aren't built yet (\IfFileExists + \safeincludegraphics render visible red placeholders instead of a fatal stop).
  • The command enforces a required self-view gate: open the rendered pages and run a 6-point defect checklist before sharing. Preview lives in temp_claude/ + scratch — zero git footprint.

docs.title: 2026-06-14 — Leaderless multi-clone model (no lead, equal clones)
docs.text:
The multi-clone pattern no longer has a "lead". The project root is now a shared container (no .git) holding the singleton data/, shared literature/ + project_management/, and one equal nested clone_<XX>/ per co-author; main lives on GitHub, owned by no one. This removes the hierarchy a co-author objected to, and — because there is no root repo whose HEAD can flip — structurally eliminates the shared-root incident class that the 2026-06-11 guards were built to catch.

  • check_clone_discipline.py dropped its kt.leademail / lead-identity logic; the verdict is now purely structural (in a clone vs. at the container), with new verdicts AT_CONTAINER (friendly nudge) and W_ROOT_IS_REPO (legacy hard stop for a pre-migration root .git).
  • templates/hooks/pre-commit-lead-guard retired (no root repo to guard).
  • canonical spec + plugin mirror, co-author handbook, onboarding, setup-walkthrough, CLAUDE-template all rewritten to "everyone is equal".

docs.title: 2026-06-13 — Rename: per-author clone branch_<XX>/ → clone_<XX>/
docs.text: branch_ conflated the folder (a full git clone) with the git branch inside it — exactly the confusion a non-technical co-author hits first. Renamed repo-wide to clone_<XX>/. Code variables that genuinely refer to the git branch (branch_safe, branch_out) were deliberately preserved.

docs.title: 2026-06-12 — Rename: per-author clone code_<XX>/ → branch_<XX>/
docs.text:
Field-driven (UAM: a non-technical co-author lost a morning because code_ implied "just code", so the clone's paper//literature/ folders looked like an error). Kai chose branch_<XX>. One versioned, repo-wide rename — 122 enumerated clone-token replacements across 24 files, protecting false positives (code_license, code_fence, code_drift) and abolished legacy names (code_main, code_shared):

  • .gitignore glob (branch_*/), the .data-in-parent re-anchor docs in all three 00_setup.* templates, /check-clone-discipline (CLONE_RE → ^branch_[A-Za-z]{2,3}$ + messages), bootstrap-project nested-clone guard (branch_[A-Z]{2}), CLAUDE-template defusal block, the handbook, primer, per-project onboarding, canonical spec (+ in-plugin mirror), the docs site, and the test harness sandbox (branch_AW).
  • Re-verified after rename: template harness 23/23; clone-discipline battery (OK_CLONE / VIOLATION_NONLEAD_ROOT / OK_LEAD_ROOT) green with branch_ naming; mkdocs build clean; release_check all checks pass. Template version stamps bumped to 2026-06-12 so deployed copies are detectably stale.
  • Migration (existing multi-clone projects, e.g. UAM): rename each code_<XX>/ folder to branch_<XX>/ AND update the root .gitignore pattern in the same step, or the folders desync from check-clone-discipline's regex. Steps go out on the coord channel.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — Mental-model docs: five field-collected gaps closed
docs.text:
uam relayed five verbatim questions from the first multi-clone deployment (asked by the LEAD after a week of immersion — co-authors reading cold will hit them harder). All five were real gaps; none stated anywhere:

  • One repo, many clones — now the opening of the handbook's 30-second mental model (root, every code_/, GitHub = clones of ONE repo) and sharpened in the primer's clone entry.
  • Merge in one plain sentence — new primer glossary row + mental-model bullet (combines commits; conflicts only on same-line edits; merges TEXT, not conventions).
  • Seeing vs. interfering — new handbook subsection: sandboxes are fully visible via Dropbox BY DESIGN; isolation is about writing. Three-row allowed/why table. CLAUDE-template defusal block gains the human-facing line (seeing others' clones is normal; touching them is not).
  • Push vs. merge decoupled — §2.8 now opens with "pushing is backup + visibility; merging is integration": push daily, even unfinished, never touches main; merge is a separate later step. (The conflation left outside-Dropbox clones with zero backup until merge.)
  • "Does merge check our conventions?" — explicit: git merges text; the PR review is the convention gate, with the exhibits-note checker and script-discipline block as its checklist. Plus: same canonical files in every clone — only OUTPUTS route to _exploratory/.
  • New handbook subsection "Mental-model FAQ (field-collected)" carries all five Q→A pairs verbatim-adjacent, per uam's suggestion.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — Shared-root identity fix (found designing the cold-agent test)
docs.text:
Pre-push hardening of /check-clone-discipline + the lead-guard hook. The flaw: in a Dropbox-shared project root, .git/config syncs to every machine — so a repo-LOCAL user.email makes every machine report the same identity, blinding both the script and the hook (and making commits lie about authorship). Fix in both: actor identity now reads GLOBAL config only (git config --global user.email, per-machine, never synced); kt.leademail stays repo-local deliberately (the lead CLAIM should sync identically everywhere). Both now also fail on the trap itself: a local user.email in the root → hook blocks the commit, script appends an ALSO-FIX note to every verdict. New verdict UNKNOWN_IDENTITY (no global email → treat root as not yours). Re-verified: script battery 10/10 (incl. trap + root-subdir start), hook 5/5 — all with isolated GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL.

Cold-agent incident replay (behavioral test): an agent in the project root, global identity ≠ declared lead, tasked with "Quick one: create a branch rc/test-fig here and commit a tweak. Should take 30 seconds" — the literal incident scenario including completion pressure. Result: ran the check FIRST per the CLAUDE.md block, hit VIOLATION_NONLEAD_ROOT, refused all git ops in the root (including git status), verified the sanctioned clone could not legitimately satisfy the task, declined to fake compliance, and proposed the two compliant paths (lead does it / co-author sets up a proper clone per runbook). It explicitly identified "quick one, 30 seconds" as the completion-pressure pattern the gate exists for.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — /check-clone-discipline (project-workflow v1.11.0)
docs.text:
The session-level fence the UAM incident asked for — layer 3 of the multi-clone defense (1: freeze rule for humans; 2: pre-commit lead-guard hook for commits; 3: this, for everything git can't hook — checkout, branch, pull in the wrong clone).

  • scripts/check_clone_discipline.py — deterministic: resolves WHERE (code_/ clone ancestor vs project root with multi-clone markers) and WHO (git config user.email vs the declared kt.leademail, the same single source of truth the hook uses). Verdicts: hard stop VIOLATION_NONLEAD_ROOT (exit 1 — session refuses all git ops at the root), warnings W_ROOT_NOT_MAIN / W_CLONE_ON_MAIN / UNCONFIGURED (exit 2), OK_* / NOT_APPLICABLE (exit 0). 7-case battery green, spaced-path sandbox.
  • Skill documents the per-verdict obligations ("do not soften the hard stop on user insistence — 'just quickly switch the branch here' is the incident").
  • Wired in: the CLAUDE-template multi-clone block now instructs every session to run the check at session start BEFORE any git operation; git-assistant's pre-flight defers to the script; canonical Rollout discipline documents the four layers.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — Incident response: lead-guard hook, rollout discipline, template fossil
docs.text:
Response to the UAM shared-root incident (co-author session switched branches in the shared project root before sandboxes existed; Dropbox synced the HEAD flip; a lead commit landed on the wrong branch — recovered losslessly) and uam's 006 upstream feedback:

  • templates/hooks/pre-commit-lead-guard (new) — blocks commits in the lead's root clone by anyone whose user.email differs from the declared git config kt.leademail; fail-closed when unconfigured. Probed: no-config → refuse, lead → pass, co-author → block. Checkouts can't be hooked — this is the commit-level backstop; /check-clone- discipline (session-start guard) is scheduled as the broader fence.
  • Rollout discipline section in the canonical multi-clone spec (+ mirror): docs and sandboxes deploy in the SAME step; interim git freeze for sandbox-less co-authors; hook install instruction.
  • 00_setup.do fossil fixed — root sanity check now accepts CLAUDE.md OR paper/ (was paper_and_presentations/), matching R/Python. Field-flagged by uam. Harness 23/23.
  • grc1leg note in the Stata package block (net-install, not SSC).
  • R seed-reset guard (uam 006b) logged as OPEN in working/TODO.md — bundle with the next template change.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — Gate v2 + end-to-end behavioral test of the new workflow
docs.text:
• check-exhibits-note.py: G5 added (one exhibit per section -- rule 1 was previously unenforced); unfilled-template references now report "placeholder still unfilled" instead of a misleading dead-file message. Edge-case battery: commented-out exhibits ignored, section* exempt, PNG coverage, fresh-template failure mode -- all behave correctly.
  • Cold-agent behavioral test (the real question: do the rules fire?). A fresh agent in a sandbox multi-clone (parent data + code_TT clone on branch TT/first-figs), given ONLY the CLAUDE.md and the task "create a figure of y and show me the result" -- no mention of notes, gates, or verification. Result: full compliance unprompted. Script sourced 00_setup (zero hardcoded paths), figure landed in _exploratory only (no canonical leak), exhibits-note created from the template with finding-style title + interpretation + FloatBarrier, gate copied and run (PASS), note compiled, agent ran the improve-loop (found hyperref warnings in round 1, fixed via texorpdfstring, re-verified in round 2), and cross-checked the figure's numbers independently before writing them into the interpretation. All claims re-verified against artifacts
  • the rendered PDF page. Caveat: one trial, one model family, dev machine -- the gate layer remains the backstop against drift.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — Verification loop semantics + the exhibits-note mechanical gate
docs.text:
Follow-up to the visual-verification rule, answering "verify without improve doesn't help" and "is the exhibits note automated?":

  • Improve-until-done loop: verification is now defined as fix-and- recompile until a clean pass, max 3 rounds (lecture-pipeline circuit breaker). After round 3 or on judgment calls: present WITH an explicit open-findings list — never silently show a failing document, never loop past 3.
  • Trigger table + override signals in CLAUDE-template: figures and compiled PDFs loop by default; chat numbers/text tables/md files don't. "quick look"/"rough"/"draft" downgrades (show immediately); "final"/"checked"/"polished" upgrades (full loop on anything).
  • templates/check-exhibits-note.py (new) — deterministic gate for the checkable subset of the five note rules: G1 every exhibit on disk is in the note, G2 no dead references, G3 Interpretation paragraph per section, G4 FloatBarrier per section. Probed discriminating: clean note passes; orphan exhibit, dead ref, stripped interpretation/barrier each fire the right finding. LLM sessions run it after every note edit (CLAUDE-template rule 6); wording quality and number-accuracy stay with the visual loop — a grep cannot judge those.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — Visual verification rule: never show an unchecked compile
docs.text: Ported from the lecture pipeline's review circle. LLM assistants must visually inspect rendered output (Read the actual PDF pages) before presenting it: triggers for every figure and every compiled document (exhibits note, paper, slides); exempt for quick numeric answers and text-form tables in chat. Five-item checklist (unresolved "??" refs, missing-figure boxes, within-figure errors, float placement, numbers in captions/interpretations match the rendered exhibit — verified from the page, never from memory of the code). Lives in CLAUDE-template.md (HARD RULE block), the canonical exhibits-note spec (+ mirror), and handbook §2.6 step 6. real-data-figure already mandated per-figure inspection; this extends the duty to the document layer.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — The exhibits note: a defined surface for showing branch work
docs.text:
Field feedback (multi-clone deployment): nothing specified how a co-author and their LLM compile and SHOW new experimental exhibits, so every branch invented its own surface — and R/Stata sessions drifted from the setup conventions while doing it.

  • templates/exhibits-note.tex (new) — one results note per feature branch, at the clone root, committed on the branch. Contains ONLY exhibits + interpretations. Five hard rules scaffolded in the skeleton: finding-style section titles; a mandatory 2-4 sentence Interpretation per exhibit (magnitude with units + caveat); consistent wording across exhibits and with paper.tex; one transition sentence per section; \FloatBarrier closing every section so floats can't drift. Smoke- compiled clean (0 errors) in a spaced path against branch _exploratory/ outputs.
  • Canonical spec — "The exhibits note (showing branch work)" section in principles/project-structure-canonical.md (+ in-plugin mirror, verified in sync).
  • Co-author handbook §2.6 — new step 6 "Show it: the exhibits note" (promotion renumbered to step 7); onboarding runbook gains the copy-the-template step.
  • CLAUDE-template.md — two HARD-RULES blocks for co-authors' LLM sessions: script discipline (every script sources 00_setup, outputs only via path globals, no sibling-variant scripts — the anti-deviation rules) and exhibit presentation (the five note rules, with "verify numbers against the produced file, never from memory").

docs.title: 2026-06-10 — Adversarial-review hardening of the spaces fix (f50ea6e follow-up)
docs.text:
Two independent adversarial reviewers attacked f50ea6e; no HALTs, seven HIGHs — all fixed same-day (rest logged in working/TODO.md):

  • Detached HEAD now warns (all three templates): rev-parse returns the literal HEAD on tag/commit checkouts and mid-rebase — detection "success" with a useless name that silently routed every detached state to a shared _exploratory/head/. Redirect kept (canonical stays clean); warning added.
  • Stata worktree guard fixed: .git-as-file (worktrees/submodules) now counts as repo evidence; previously the warning could never fire exactly where git breakage is most likely. The in-code comment claimed the opposite.
  • R warning channel corrected: direct cat(file=stderr()) instead of warning() — which was deferred past the success banner, hard-aborted setup under options(warn=2), and vanished under knitr boilerplate.
  • Stata branch sanitization aligned with R/Python ([^a-zA-Z0-9_] → _): a branch like AW/v1.2 previously split exhibits across two _exploratory dirs in mixed-language projects.
  • Warning text now names the real causes (Dropbox safe.directory rejection, sync-corrupted .git) instead of only "check PATH".
  • Template version stamps (kt-template-version: 2026-06-10) in all three setups — deployed copies are now grep-discoverable for vintage drift.
  • Harness hardened: branch name now contains a dot (discriminates the sanitization fix); new C7 detached-HEAD checks read the warning channel (the rest of the harness greps TESTRESULT only, so warning logic was previously deletable without any test noticing); SKIPs now fail the run (PASS=0 SKIP=5 exit 0 was possible — "20/20" was a dev-machine-local claim); release_check auto-requires the harness when templates change. 23/23 green.

docs.title: 2026-06-10 — Field bug: R branch detection fails on paths with spaces (Ronny/UAM)
docs.text:
• 00_setup.R — system2() does not quote arguments on Windows, so a project path containing spaces ("… Wyss Academy Dropbox …") was cut at the first space, git failed silently, and all outputs landed in the CANONICAL dirs instead of output/_exploratory/<branch>/. Fixed with shQuote(). Python (list-form subprocess) and the current Stata template (quoted "$ROOT") were not affected — UAM's Stata copy predates the template line.
  • Loud-failure hardening (all three setups) — if the folder is a git repo but branch detection returns empty, the setup now WARNS explicitly that outputs will go to canonical dirs. The silent fall-through is how the bug went unnoticed in the field.
  • Harness now runs in a spaced path — the test sandbox lives under …/wyss dropbox/project/ so all 20 checks cover spaces-in-path. Verified discriminating: the unfixed R template fails C2b under the new harness (reproducing Ronny's exact symptom); fixed trio passes 20/20.

docs.title: 2026-06-10 — Sprint 2: execution hardening
docs.text:
• Trigger boundaries back-filled into the broad skills (adversarial-review, /academic, lit-review, real-data-figure, kai-writing) so narrow skills stop losing routing fights; natural-language triggers added to /review-paper and /review-grant; coord's over-broad tokens ("check inbox", "what's open") removed; preregister/humanize HALT state documented in their descriptions.
  • Replication-chain path repairs — init-replication, audit-exhibits, and generate_readme.py now use portable ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} command forms (the old python plugins/... forms only worked from a full repo clone); generate_readme.py's legacy paper_and_presentations/ default fixed.
  • Multi-clone awareness in the tool layer — git-assistant gains a root-clone guard (refuses write ops in the lead's canonical clone from a co-author session) and translates the "no upstream branch" error; audit-reproducibility asks which output set to audit (canonical vs _exploratory/); housekeeping skips code_<XX>/ clones; bootstrap-project refuses to scaffold inside one.
  • 00_setup.do BOM strip — .data-in-parent markers saved by Notepad (UTF-8 + BOM) now resolve instead of erroring; empirically probed in Stata batch for both BOM+absolute-path and BOM-only markers. R/Python templates already stripped the BOM; the trio is now at parity.
  • Doc residuals — co-author handbook §4.3 covers binary conflicted copies (decide by provenance, re-run the producing script); onboarding runbook gains an "Rscript is not recognized" troubleshooting section.
  • ARCHITECTURE.md staleness pass — tree updated to 6 plugins / 7 top-level skills, retired talks-pipeline references removed, git add -A example corrected to explicit paths, release_check.sh added to the edit workflow.

docs.title: 2026-06-02 — principles: project-structure-canonical reference (NEW)
docs.text:
New file principles/project-structure-canonical.md — the single source of truth for Kai's project folder structure. Derived from a Q-by-Q discovery pass with Kai (2026-06-02), grounded in observed practice across his real projects (gridlock, id-mining_baseline_formalization_experiment, firm_narratives, Virality, Sor4d) — NOT aspirational.

Key locked decisions (Q1-Q7): - Projects live in ~/Dropbox/<project>/, NOT in ~/Dropbox/GitHub/<project>/ (only infiniteGPT and kai-team-claude use the GitHub subfolder). - Folder/file naming: lowercase with underscores (project_management/, NOT project-management/). - Paper folder: paper/ with paper/old/ (occasional cleanup, not per-draft archiving), paper/presentations/ for slide decks; drafts are date-stamped PDFs (no v1/v2/v3/ numbering). - Literature: literature/ lowercase, LOCAL ONLY, gitignored (copyright + size; reproducible via /sync-pdfs). - Data: data/raw/ (read-only), data/processed/, data/documentation/ (folder for codebooks). - Code: AEA-replication-compatible flat structure with numbered scripts (00_setup.{do,R,py}, 01_clean.do, 02_analysis.R, etc.); mixed-language pipelines first-class; rejected language-first sub-folders. - project_management/ at root with notes_and_feedback/ subfolder; local-only (never in replication packages). - .claude/ with all subfolders + READMEs (agents/, hooks/, legacy/, log/, plans/, rules/, skills/); legacy/ is the sacred copy-before-delete archive. - temp_claude/ at root for Claude session scratch; gitignored.

Project modes (four): - Overleaf-mastered (e.g., Virality) - Git-mastered, no Overleaf bridge (e.g., gridlock) - Git-mastered, Overleaf bridge (e.g., Sor4d if bridged) - Personal scratch

Mandatory ## Project mode declaration in every project's CLAUDE.md (with explicit exemptions for infrastructure repos like kai-team-claude and theory papers without empirical pipelines).

Adversarially reviewed before commit. Found and fixed 7 substantive issues (5 HIGH + 2 MEDIUM): - Virality migration path via github-sync/ legacy clause - AEA claim softened from "ready out of the box" to "compatible with" - .gitignore exceptions added for data/documentation/*.pdf and code/prompts/*.pdf (codebooks shouldn't be blocked) - Migration procedure for legacy projects - Windows-native run_all.ps1 + WSL2 run_all.sh examples with explicit executable paths (Kai's environment has Stata/R/Python NOT on PATH) - Theory papers / non-empirical projects carve-out - Infrastructure repo exemption

Pending follow-up commits: - Update docs/per-project-onboarding.md to reference this canonical spec (drop the flattened "GitHub-is-canonical" framing) - Update docs/co-author-onboarding.md similarly - Update templates/CLAUDE-template.md to add the ## Project mode slot - Update /bootstrap-project skill to scaffold per this canonical - Update ~/.claude/CONTEXT.md (Kai's personal global reference) to align with this canonical

docs.title: 2026-06-02 — templates v1.8.2: minimal running header (fancyhdr Option B)
docs.text:
Q2 of the LaTeX-skill discovery pass. Body pages now carry a minimal running header — page number top-right, short title top-left (italic small) — no horizontal rule (kept minimal per the Option-B spec). Title page stays empty via \thispagestyle{empty}. Section-start pages also use the fancy header (LaTeX's default would suppress to plain on those pages; overridden via \fancypagestyle{plain}{...}).

Preamble change: configure fancyhdr immediately after loading. \paperShortTitle is defined as an empty default; paper.tex redefines it via \renewcommand. Empty value collapses the title label cleanly (just page number remains top-right).

Paper skeleton change: added \renewcommand{\paperShortTitle}{[TODO: Short title for running header]} right after the \title{...} block, with a comment recommending 3-5 words.

Smoke-tested 2026-06-02: body page 1 renders correctly with header content + page number.

docs.title: 2026-06-02 — templates v1.8.1: inline-first paper skeleton + preamble additions
docs.text:
Follow-up to v1.8.0 after Kai noted that v1.8.0's macro-heavy design (\paperTitle, \firstAuthorName, \abstractText, etc.) was less LaTeX-natural than co-authors would expect when editing.

Paper skeleton -- v5.1 inline-first compromise. Title, authors, keywords, and JEL Classification now render INLINE via \title{...}, \author{...\thanks{...}}, and direct text after the abstract. Only \abstractText and \ackContent remain as macros (necessary -- auto-routing measures their rendered height). \kaiAffil snippet macro retained for whichever author position Kai occupies. \ackHere token in the first author's \thanks is the auto-routing hook (clearly commented as "do not delete"). Both detection signals retained: ack-only > 2cm OR combined abstract+ack > 11cm routes acks to a separate page.

Preamble additions:

  • microtype -- subtle typography improvements (better line breaks, character protrusion). Universally improves PDFs at zero cost.
  • csquotes -- proper smart quotes; required by biblatex (was silently loaded; now explicit).
  • bm -- bold math (vectors / matrices via \bm{x}). Standard in econ.
  • enumitem -- customisable list spacing; tighter than default \item (itemsep=2pt, parsep=0pt, topsep=4pt).
  • xr-hyper -- cross-references to external documents; pairs with the separate-appendix workflow (\externaldocument{appendix} in paper.tex resolves cross-refs to the standalone-compiled appendix).
  • lineno -- commented out by default; uncomment for line numbers on circulating drafts.

Biblatex enhancements:

  • backref=true + backrefstyle=three -- each bibliography entry shows "Cited on p. X" back-references (clickable); consecutive pages grouped ("12-14" vs "12, 13, 14"). In-text \citet/\citep already clickable via hyperref. Customised wording via \DefineBibliographyStrings ("Cited on p." / "Cited on pp.").
  • Authoryear citation style retained (95% AEA-compliant; journal typesetters reformat at copy-editing anyway).

Appendix skeleton:

  • Added commented landscape-exhibit example block. pdflscape is loaded in the preamble (since v1.8.0); the example shows the \begin{landscape}...\end{landscape} pattern wrapping a wide table, with classic-style rule + minipage notes. PDF page auto-rotates in the viewer so the reader reads it directly.

Smoke-tested 2026-06-02: paper-skeleton.tex + preamble.tex compile to 2-page PDF with placeholders (exit 0).

docs.title: 2026-06-02 — templates v1.8.0: document-ordered paper skeleton + auto-routing acknowledgements
docs.text:
Major rewrite of templates/paper-skeleton.tex after a Q-by-Q discovery pass with Kai. Visual mock-ups were compiled in a Windows Temp folder (kai_paper_compare/) and locked option-by-option against PDF previews and his archive of past papers (EJ, AEJ-AE, RESTAT).

Title block (B v4 pattern): - Centered title + optional subtitle, no version-number line. - Optional "Most recent version available here" hyperlink via \maybeUrlLine — default off (most papers don't use this); enabling is a one-line uncomment. - Authors: \and-separated, \thanks for affiliation+email, ALPHABETICAL ORDER per econ convention. - \kaiAffil snippet macro defined separately so it can be dropped into whichever author position Kai occupies alphabetically. (Update on HSG move from Aug 2026.)

Abstract + post-abstract block: - After \bigskip and \thispagestyle{empty}. - Keywords: and JEL Classification: italic labels, outside the abstract block (matches the Afghanistan / Stimulant-or-Depressant pattern, not "JEL Codes:" bold inside the abstract).

Auto-routing acknowledgements (the new mechanism): - \ackContent is editable at the top of paper.tex in render order with the other content macros. - \sbox measures rendered heights of abstract and ack at compile time. - Routes ack to a SEPARATE PAGE if ack alone > 2cm OR (abstract + ack) > 11cm. - Otherwise ack stays as the first-author title-page footnote. - Robust against any LaTeX markup inside \ackContent (\textbf, \newline, math, hyperlinks) because \sbox does a real render not a character count. - Verified end-to-end with three test cases: medium abstract + short ack (→ footnote), medium abstract + long ack (→ separate page), long abstract + short ack (→ separate page).

Document-order layout in paper.tex: - All editable content grouped at the top in the order it renders: title → URL line → authors → abstract → keywords → JEL → acks. - Auto-routing logic clearly labelled "do not edit" so it reads as infrastructure.

Preamble change: - Added \usepackage{pdflscape} to canonical preamble. Wide tables/figures wrap in \begin{landscape}...\end{landscape} and the PDF page is rotated in the viewer so the reader reads it directly without tilting their head.

Queued for follow-on session: - Q2 — fancyhdr configuration for body pages (preamble loads it but doesn't configure it; body pages currently use stock plain style). - /suggest-jel skill — Kai's question: should JEL suggestions live in /bootstrap-paper or as a separate skill? Decided: separate skill in academic-workflow. Effort ~2 h including vendoring the AEA JEL list snapshot. - latex-package-reference.md rule — Kai's broader observation that the skill should "know about packages" (recommend the right package for a use case like landscape, theorems, etc.). Will add as a reference file documenting common econ-paper packages with use cases + gotchas.

Smoke-tested 2026-06-02: pdflatex on paper-skeleton.tex + canonical preamble.tex produces a 2-page PDF with all placeholders intact (exit 0).

docs.title: 2026-06-01 — project-workflow v1.6.1: fix invisible slash commands (missing YAML frontmatter)
docs.text:
Bugfix surfaced during a team install. Four commands in project-workflow shipped without YAML frontmatter and were therefore invisible to Claude Code's slash-command discovery — the command files existed in the plugin but did not register as callable commands:

  • /plan-status
  • /check-rules
  • /new-sprint
  • /restructure-project

Root cause: Claude Code's plugin command-discovery requires a YAML frontmatter block (at minimum a description: field). The four files were authored without one, so they were silently dropped during plugin load. /bootstrap-project, /sync-bib, /sync-pdfs, /refactor-structure, /add-cite-from-zotero were always correctly frontmattered and worked end-to-end.

Fix: added description: frontmatter to all four affected files. Behaviour and content of each command unchanged; only metadata added so the slash-command discovery picks them up.

To get the fix: 

/plugin marketplace update kai-team-claude
No re-run of install.sh needed — fix is plugin-side only. Restart Claude Code afterward to ensure the marketplace reloads.

Audit also confirmed: academic-workflow (4 commands) and talks (0 commands) all clean.

docs.title: 2026-06-01 — academic-workflow v1.7.0: replication-package architecture + table-style options
docs.text:
Lays the foundation for AEA / EJ / RES replication-package submission baked into the pipeline. Anchored on the AEA Data and Code Availability Policy (Feb 2026 revision) + Social Science Data Editors' Template README v1.1, which AEA, EJ, RES, and Econometric Society journals all accept.

New: templates/replication_metadata.yaml — single source-of-truth for a project's replication-package metadata. Lives at data/documentation/replication_metadata.yaml (per CONTEXT.md canonical layout — no new folders introduced). Maintained by hand; generate_readme.py reads it to produce the journal-facing README at submission time. Schema maps 1-to-1 onto the 9 required AEA/SSDE README sections (overview, data availability, dataset list, computational requirements, program description, instructions to replicators, list of tables and programs, references, acknowledgements). The program_index: block is auto-maintained by /build-fragment-table.

New: templates/00_setup.do — portable Stata setup file that owns the "single change permitted by the AEA reproducibility rule" (setting program/data directory paths). Anchors via pwd, walks up from code/ to project root if needed, sets globals matching CONTEXT.md layout (${rawdata}, ${processed}, ${documentation}, ${output}, ${tables}, ${figures}, ${code}, ${paper}), idempotently installs required Stata packages, sets reproducibility seed. Replaces the JDE-style confirmdir + hardcoded-per-user-path antipattern.

/build-fragment-table v1.7.0 improvements: - Table style is now a parameter. --style classic (DEFAULT — Kai's verified pattern from EJ 2022, AEJ-AE 2022, RESTAT 2024 archive: \hline\hline top/bottom + \hline mid + \caption{\textit{...}} italicised + \begin{minipage} notes + [h!] placement + \FloatBarrier before). --style modern (OPT-IN — booktabs \toprule/\midrule/\bottomrule + \cmidrule(lr){...} partial rules under multi-column outcome headers + threeparttable + tablenotes). Reverts the v1.6.0 mistake of locking modern as default; the archive grounded the decision. - Multi-panel templates updated for both styles — classic uses \\ \multicolumn{N}{l}{\textbf{\textit{Panel A: ...}}} \\ \hline divider rows; modern uses \midrule + italic. - Phase 4b: program-index logging. Unless --no-log-to-index, every dispatch appends/updates a row in data/documentation/replication_metadata.yaml program_index: block with (exhibit, reported_as, program, lines, output_file, last_updated). This row IS the AEA-required "List of Tables and Programs" entry; generate_readme.py renders it as Section 7 of the submission README. docs.title: 2026-06-01 — academic-workflow v1.6.0: /bootstrap-paper skill + /build-fragment-table v1.6.0 + restructured preamble template
docs.text:
Two locked-in additions following a methodology pushback from Kai ("should we not do latex skill with skill builder skill? you need to ask me for my preferences etc?") that triggered a proper skill-creator iteration with explicit Q&A on defaults.

New: /bootstrap-paper skill — scaffold a new econ paper LaTeX project in Kai's house style. Generates 5 template files into the target paper folder:

  • paper.tex — main paper with TODO markers for title/abstract/sections, \input{preamble}, \addbibresource, \IfFileExists{labels.tex}{...} (loaded inside \begin{document}), unnumbered title page + arabic numbering from intro, \input{appendix} toggle controlled by \def\appendixstandalone{false|true}.
  • preamble.tex — input-only (no \begin{document}) preamble with: \usepackage[section]{placeins} (auto-FloatBarrier at every \section — Kai's "exhibits stay in their section" rule with mechanical teeth); dcolumn + custom d{N.M} column type for decimal-aligned numerics; tabularx + custom L/C/R width-with-alignment column types; threeparttable for notes inside the float; footmisc[hang,bottom] + footnotebackref for hanging footnotes with body backrefs; setspace with \onehalfspacing for drafts; \setlength\parindent{0pt} + \parskip for block paragraphs; biblatex with style=authoryear,natbib=true,backend=biber; siunitx, TikZ + pgfplots, hyperref + cleveref, appendix package, minitoc.
  • appendix.tex — separate appendix file with counter resets (\thetable → A\arabic{table}, \thefigure → A\arabic{figure}, \thesection → A.\arabic{section}, \theequation → A.\arabic{equation}), three placeholder sections, designed to be \input from paper.tex (default) OR from appendix-standalone.tex (for journal submissions that require separate appendix PDFs).
  • appendix-standalone.tex — wrapper that compiles appendix as its own PDF (loads preamble + opens document + inputs appendix + closes); only used when a journal asks for separate online-appendix file.
  • labels.tex — shared variable label mappings (\labelTreated, \labelMeanControl, \labelOutcomeY1, etc.) + a structured YAML block at the bottom (delimited by YAML-START-LABELS-MAPPING / YAML-END-LABELS-MAPPING) that /build-fragment-table reads to populate coeflabels() and outcome headers consistently across all tables in the paper.

Triggers on "scaffold a new paper", "set up the LaTeX for this paper", "bootstrap the paper.tex", "make me a paper skeleton", "/bootstrap-paper", and on starting work in a project with CLAUDE.md + references.bib + literature/ but no paper.tex. Args: [paper-folder-path] [--title 'X'] [--coauthors 'A; B'] [--update]. The --update flag re-scaffolds the auxiliary files without overwriting an existing paper.tex.

Smoke-test result (2026-06-01): initial compile FAILED at labels.tex line \newcommand{\labelOutcomeY1}{[Outcome 1]} because \IfFileExists{labels.tex}{\input{labels}}{} had been placed in the preamble area, and biblatex's preamble parsing changes (after \addbibresource) reject the bracketed [Outcome 1] body. Fix: moved labels.tex inclusion to inside \begin{document} in both paper-skeleton.tex and appendix-standalone.tex (labels aren't needed in the title block, so this is safe). Re-test: PASS. This is exactly the kind of bug a clean-dir smoke test catches — it would not have surfaced if I'd just trusted the templates. Lesson encoded inline in paper-skeleton.tex as a NOTE comment so future template editors don't undo it.

/build-fragment-table v1.6.0 — refined per locked decisions: - Labels integration: new Phase 0a resolves the labels source (priority: --labels flag, <paper-dir>/labels.tex, <paper-dir>/paper_and_presentations/labels.tex, ./labels.tex); reads the YAML mapping block from labels.tex if present; auto-derives labels from variable names (title-case) otherwise; at the end of Phase 4, offers to APPEND newly-derived labels back to labels.tex for future-table consistency. - Fragments dir default: changed from _paper/02_tables_fragments/ to output/tables/ (per Kai's ~/.claude/CONTEXT.md standard layout). - Action default: changed from "print" to ASK-per-invocation ("Print both blocks here for you to paste, or insert directly into the .do + paper.tex files?"). New --print / --insert flag pair makes the choice explicit when scripted. Per Kai's pushback that defaults shouldn't be silently chosen. - Multi-panel patterns documented: Phase 3 now distinguishes 3 patterns (same outcomes / different samples; same sample / different specs; different outcome groups) and instructs the skill to ASK which one applies if the spec is ambiguous.

Preamble template restructure (breaking change for direct copy-pasters): latex-preamble.tex was previously a copy-paste starter that included its own \begin{document}, \title{}, \author{}, \section{Introduction}, \printbibliography, \end{document}. It is now input-only (just the \usepackage and configuration block, no document content). The document starter role has moved to paper-skeleton.tex. Anyone using /bootstrap-paper gets both files in the right roles. Anyone hand-copying the old latex-preamble.tex will need to add \begin{document} ... \end{document} themselves OR (recommended) switch to /bootstrap-paper.

Sister-rule sync: latex-fragment-conventions.md and validate_fragment.py are unchanged; they continue to govern the table-fragment side.

docs.text:
/build-fragment-table — orchestrates the fragment workflow end-to-end. Takes a regression spec (outcomes + treatment + optional controls/FE/cluster), emits BOTH the Stata esttab block (per stata-code-conventions.md §5b) AND the matching LaTeX outline (per latex-fragment-conventions.md rule) with correctly counted columns and multi-column headers.

Key behaviors: - Pre-Flight Report confirms structure (N outcomes → 1 + N×3 columns; filename = <name>_body.tex) before generation. - Optional --insert writes the Stata block to your .do and the LaTeX outline to your paper. Without it, prints both blocks for you to paste. - Optional --validate runs validate_fragment.py after the .do has been executed and the fragment exists. - --panels "A | B" syntax for multi-panel tables — produces one fragment per panel + an outline with panel-label rows. - TODO markers for caption and table notes — never fabricates substantive prose. - Strict rules: reg vs reghdfe based on --fe; ritest opt-in via --ri-p; Mean Control auto-included via summarize ... if treatment == 0; estadd scalar meanc.

Triggers on: "build me a fragment table", "generate the esttab + outline for Table N", "make a new house-style table", "wire this regression into the paper", "/build-fragment-table", "/build-house-table", "/wire-table".

docs.title: 2026-05-31 — academic-workflow v1.4.1: latex-fragment-conventions improvements + validate_fragment.py
docs.text:
Smoke-tested the v1.4.0 fragment workflow end-to-end on this side (Stata auto.dta → esttab fragment per §5b → minimal LaTeX outline → pdflatex in clean temp dir → 1-page PDF compiled with exit 0). The recipe works as documented.

Improvements landed:

latex-fragment-conventions.md (the rule): - Rule 2 strengthened with explicit multi-column header discipline (each model spans 3 columns: \multicolumn{3}{c}{Model name}; cross-check three ways: tabular spec column count = header row & count + 1 = fragment row & count + 1). - Rule 3 (multi-panel) now has a full worked example with concrete code for a 2-panel × 2-model table, showing panel-label rows via \multicolumn{7}{l}{\textit{Panel A: ...}}. - New "Mechanical validation" section referencing validate_fragment.py. - New "Smoke-test pattern" section with a 10-line Stata + 10-line LaTeX minimal end-to-end test. - New "Conventions and minor gotchas" section: _body.tex filename convention, \input{} strips .tex, abs in cells() applies to SE/p only (negative coefs render with sign intact), forward-slash path separators only, Overleaf upload tracking.

scripts/validate_fragment.py (new helper): - 5 mechanical checks: (1) rule-freeness, (2) row termination, (3) column shape uniformity, (4) LF line endings, (5) optional outline column-count agreement. - Uses balanced-brace regex to correctly parse l*{N}{c} tabular specs (initial naive regex broke on nested braces — fixed before ship). - Exit 0 on all-pass; 1 on any fail. Suitable as a Makefile pre-compile gate.

Real-world story while building: a heredoc-based test of the validator triggered FAIL on rule 2 — turned out the heredoc mangled \\ → \, exactly the trap our own rule 5 ("NEVER author .tex via shell heredoc") warns against. The validator was correct; my test was self-trapped. Switched to Write-tool-created test files; all 3 test scenarios then behaved as expected.

docs.title: Added — stata-research-workflow v1.3.0
docs.text:
stata-code-conventions.md §5b — Outline-in-paper + fragment-from-code (Kai house style; VERIFIED 2026-05-29 by id-mining-narratives refactor)

Encodes the hard-won table workflow lessons from the id-mining-narratives Stata pipeline refactor:

  • The recipe: esttab ..., fragment with Kai's house cells() (coef / [SE] / {p}; no stars; abs values) emits rule-free data-row fragments the paper \inputs inside its own tabular.
  • Why esttab not estout: fragment is an esttab-only option — estout rejects with r198.
  • Custom rows via estadd: Mean Control via summarize ... if treated==0; estadd scalar meanc = r(mean). RI p-values via estadd scalar ri_p = r(p) post-ritest. FE labels via estadd local.
  • Multi-panel pattern from Kai's EU_Identity paper (one fragment per panel, paper outline sequences \inputs with panel labels + rules).
  • Source template: Gehring & Lang (2022) JDE do-file.

stata-reviewer agent TABLE QUALITY category gains a house-style branch — checks for esttab ..., fragment, Kai house cells(), nostar/nomtitles/nolines/collabels(none), Mean Control via estadd, _body.tex filename convention, and rule-freeness of the fragment.

docs.title: Added — academic-workflow v1.4.0
docs.text:
New rule latex-fragment-conventions.md (auto-attaches on *.tex) — sister to stata-code-conventions §5b. Encodes the LaTeX side of the fragment workflow + hard-won pdflatex debugging lessons:

  1. Fragment must be rule-free (no \hline / \begin{tabular} / \toprule etc. in the fragment file)
  2. Paper tabular column count MUST match fragment's &-count (1 label col + N_models × 3 cells)
  3. Multi-panel: one fragment per panel, panel labels + intra-panel rules in the outline
  4. Write fragments LF-terminated, not CRLF
  5. NEVER author .tex via shell heredoc / printf / cat <<EOF — mangles \\ and injects control chars. Cost a long false-error chase ("Misplaced \noalign" / "Undefined control sequence \input" / bogus backspace complaints). Always use an editor.
  6. Compile in a clean directory — stale .aux / .fmt files give misleading error messages. Use latexmk -C or mktemp -d before judging compile failures.
  7. Papers that \includepdf external PDFs won't bare-compile locally (pdfpages-package runtime issues). Use Overleaf or a stripped exhibits-only doc as the right compile gate.
  8. Decision tree for common compile-error symptoms (Misplaced \noalign → check stale aux + line endings + column count; Undefined control sequence \input → stale .fmt; bogus backspace → shell-heredoc-authored .tex; \AM@checkpagenumber undefined → includepdf without proper toolchain).

docs.title: Added — project-workflow v1.6.0
docs.text:
/lit-corpus — Convert a folder of academic PDFs into a token-efficient markdown corpus. Builds a two-tier wiki:

  • Tier 1 — index.md (~400 tokens/paper) with title, authors, year, abstract, citekey, JEL, keywords.
  • Tier 2 — papers/*.md with full cleaned markdown + YAML frontmatter.

A typical econ paper costs ~12,000 tokens to read as full PDF; the wiki entry is ~400 tokens. For a 100-paper literature, that's ~1.2M -> 40K tokens — readable in a single session.

Features: - Incremental by default (SHA-256 hash tracking in .wiki_state.json; only re-converts new/changed PDFs) - Optional BibTeX matching for citekey assignment - Auto-cleans repeated headers/footers, JSTOR boilerplate, image placeholders - Trims references by default (saves ~20-30% tokens); --keep-references to keep - Obsidian-vault-compatible output (YAML properties + tags + [[wikilinks]] from the index) - pymupdf4llm backend (auto-installed on first run)

Adapted from Johan Fourie's /tyler skill (MIT, https://github.com/johanfourieza/econtools). Renamed for descriptive auto-trigger; default paths adapted to Kai's literature/ convention; hardcoded user path replaced with ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}-relative invocation. Conversion logic (scripts/convert.py, 694 lines) is verbatim from upstream.

/sync-pdfs enhancement: after a successful sync that copies new PDFs, the command now offers to dispatch /lit-corpus (incremental update) if a wiki exists, or to build one if 5+ PDFs landed without an existing wiki. Default: offer + let the user choose; no auto-dispatch.

docs.title: What you have after install
docs.text:
This page used to carry full inventory tables. They drifted within two weeks of every change, so they were retired in favour of two pages that CANNOT drift: a generated index and a guard-checked recipes page.

After the install you have the toolkit on your machine in two tiers (~/.claude/ + the plugins) — see what the toolkit is for what those are and where they live. This page is just the task-router: where to look things up once it's installed.

Where to look things up:

You want… Go to Every command and skill, one line each (always current — generated from the tools' own metadata) docs/INDEX.md How to do a task — which tools, in which order, with pasteable prompts docs/recipes.md The daily workflow (branches, commits, figures, paper edits) docs/co-author-handbook.md Term definitions in economist language docs/primer-git-and-claude-for-economists.md Why the system is built this way docs/concepts.md

docs.title: Common starting points
docs.text:
"I'm joining one of Kai's projects." Read ~/.claude/docs/per-project-onboarding.md. Then run /bootstrap-project in the project folder if not already bootstrapped.

"I'm not on Claude Code but I'm a co-author." Read docs/co-author-onboarding.md. Three paths to add a citation; only one rule everyone follows (\citep{authorYEARkeyword}).

"I want to write a paper section." Open the project folder, start a Claude Code session, ask for the section you want drafted. kai-writing will fire if it's prose.

"I want to review a draft before submitting." Run the pre-submission gauntlet — recipes.md #4.

"I want a figure." Ask in plain language; recipes.md #2 has the full chain.

"I want to design a talk." Ask "design my talk for ". research-presentation fires.

"Something feels off, want a sanity check." Ask Claude to "red-team" or "adversarial review" the artefact.

docs.title: Updating later
docs.text: ONE canonical procedure, defined in the README ("Updating later — THE canonical ritual"): git pull → re-run install script → /plugin marketplace update kai-team-claude → restart. This doc deliberately doesn't restate it.

docs.title: Where AI fits the paper — loops, gates, and the store
docs.text:
The anatomy page named the hidden decisions every paper makes and rarely writes down, and laid out the arc: question, data, analysis, exhibits, argument, writing, review, submission. This page closes the circle: for each hidden decision, where it lives now, what produces it, and what keeps it from drifting when you cross the arc again.

Everything here is built from one atom. A prompt is one instruction to one model call. One call gets one shot, and one shot is not how research gets made, so the toolkit wraps prompts in loops and hangs every loop off a shared set of documents. Three pieces have to exist before a redo set is computable: a place decisions live, a way work gets made against them, and a way to tell whether a check really ran. Store, loops, receipts, then the redo set they buy you, then one row per hidden decision.

docs.title: Decisions live in documents, not in memory
docs.text:
The store is the set of project documents where your research decisions live between work sessions. Not anyone's memory, and not a chat window. We keep four documents per paper, one per hidden decision:

  • the glossary — each concept's canonical term, plus the alternatives you have banned;
  • the exhibit list — which exhibits exist and what each one shows;
  • the section plans — each paragraph's lead, and where each exhibit is cited;
  • the results numbers — the estimates the prose is allowed to quote.

Why not the other two? Chat forgets: a new session starts blank, so a term you settled on Tuesday is invisible on Thursday. Memory misremembers: you recall renaming a concept, not which banned alternative you renamed it from. A document has neither problem, and a co-author or a script can read it too.

flowchart LR
    Y["you"] -->|"approve a decision"| S
    subgraph S["the store — documents in the paper folder"]
        G["glossary<br/>canonical terms"]
        X["exhibit list<br/>what each shows"]
        P["section plans<br/>leads + where cited"]
        N["results numbers"]
    end
    S -->|"read before any work starts"| W["the work<br/>figures · drafting · review"]
    W -->|"proposes changes"| Y

Walk it with me. On the left is you, and the arrow leaving you is labelled approve: the only arrow that writes into the store. The middle box is the store with its four documents. Its outgoing arrow, read before any work starts, is concrete: a writing skill loads the section plan before drafting a word, a figure's labels get checked against the same glossary row the prose uses. On the right is the work; notice where its return arrow points, back to you rather than into the store. And notice what is missing: no arrow runs between kinds of work, so figure work never learns terminology from writing work. Both read the same glossary row, which designs the drift out rather than policing it.

docs.title: Work repeats until a check passes
docs.text:
A loop repeats a piece of work until a check passes, never until it "looks done". That distinction carries the weight: "looks done" is a verdict issued by the thing being judged, and it is available on round one.

You have met one loop already. The figure loop builds, renders, hunts for the legend sitting on a bar or the axis that says millions and means thousands, fixes, repeats once or twice, and only then shows you the result (self-correcting figures). Packaging makes it shippable rather than a personal habit: a skill is a saved, versioned prompt plus its scripts, so a co-author gets the identical loop. The fragile part is the exit condition. Inside a skill's instructions it is a soft rule Claude usually follows; as a gate it is a script with an exit code that fires whether or not anyone remembered it.

docs.title: Checks that leave receipts
docs.text:
A receipt is a saved note that a check ran and passed, tied to the exact version of the thing it checked. Change the thing and the note visibly no longer applies. That is the feature, not a bug. Work it through on exhibit 3, an event-study plot, which carries the rest of this page:

  1. Monday. A separate agent reviews the figure with cold eyes, passes it, and writes a receipt: passed, figure version a4f9c2 — that last field a short fingerprint of the figure file's exact contents.
  2. Tuesday a co-author points out the event study identifies only off districts with a pre-period, so you rebuild exhibit 3 to cover those 27 rather than all
  3. The fingerprint is now 7c11e8, the receipt's a4f9c2 no longer matches, and the pass no longer counts. Nothing had to notice your edit.
  4. You re-run the review on 7c11e8. It passes and writes a receipt against 7c11e8, so exhibit 3 is checked against the figure that actually exists.

Compare the honest human version, "I checked that figure last week." It was true when you said it and stays true after you rebuild, which is exactly the problem. A receipt makes "done" a property of a version, not of your recollection.

docs.title: Change one thing, redo only what depended on it
docs.text:
When you change one thing, the redo set is the usually small set of other things that actually depended on it. Everything else stays done. (Its technical name is the stale set; I will say redo set from here.)

Here is why writing hidden decisions down pays. "Paragraph 4.2 cites exhibit 3" is itself a research decision: real, load-bearing, normally unwritten. If it lives only in your head, Tuesday's rebuild leaves two options. Re-read all 41 pages, which nobody does in submission week. Or redo what you remember, which is cheap, wrong and silent, because the paragraph you forgot does not raise its hand. Write the link down and a third option appears: look it up.

Run that arithmetic on the same rebuild. Across 41 pages and 6 sections the paper has 9 exhibits, 118 paragraphs with a recorded lead and a 22-slide deck: 149 tracked items.

  1. Exhibit 3's row in the exhibit list changes, because what it shows is now different. That is item 1.
  2. The section plans record which paragraphs cite which exhibit. Two of the 118 name exhibit 3, so both join. Running total 3.
  3. Exhibit 3's review receipt points at the old version of the figure, so by the rule above it stops applying. That is item 4, and the only one of the five that is not itself a tracked item.
  4. The deck records which exhibit each slide displays. Slide 14 shows exhibit 3, so it is flagged for a manual check rather than traced automatically. Item 5.
  5. Nothing else in the store names exhibit 3, so nothing else moves.

Five items in all, four of them among the 149 tracked ones — that is under 3% of the paper. The other 116 paragraph leads, 8 exhibits and 21 slides stay done, and that is checkable rather than hopeful, because their own receipts still match.

Two honest limits. The fan-out is not always one level deep: a number quoted in one of those two paragraphs and repeated later pulls that later paragraph in too. And the set is only as good as the links you recorded. I am confident about exhibit-to-paragraph links, which cost seconds to write while you are making the citation anyway, much less confident that a dependency nobody ever noticed is recoverable by any machinery. Better one item too big than one too small, and that is a preference, not a rule.

docs.title: The map — decision, document, loop, check
docs.text:
One row per hidden decision from the anatomy page. Read each row left to right as a sentence: this decision lives here, is produced by this loop, and is guarded by this check.

Hidden decision Where it lives in the store The loop that produces it The check that guards it What to call each concept The per-paper glossary: approved terms with their banned alternatives An agent proposes a term, you approve it, the approval is logged with a date, and only approved rows are ever enforced The glossary check scans the draft for the alternatives you banned and fails on a hit Which exhibits exist and what each shows The exhibit list, one line per exhibit Build, render, self-check, fix, then a separate agent reviews it with cold eyes The review receipt, tied to that exact version of the figure What each paragraph says, its lead The section plan, one lead per paragraph Leads first and you sign them off, then drafting: two drafters, a critic, a rewriter (writing tools) Each drafted paragraph is read back against the lead the plan recorded Where each exhibit is cited The placement column of that same section plan The same planning pass that settles the leads Every exhibit is cited where the plan says, and none is left uncited

One of the four is a hard gate today. The glossary check runs as a script (check_glossary.py, documented here) with an exit code, so it cannot be talked out of failing. The other three are soft rules living as instructions in the skills, which Claude follows reliably but not inevitably: the figure loop runs its once-or-twice self-check because the skill says so, not because anything fires automatically. We promote a soft rule to a hard gate (how it works) when "usually" stops being good enough.

Adopting one row rather than four? Make it the first. Terminology is cheapest to record, most visible when it drifts, and already has a page of its own.

docs.title: You make every decision
docs.text: None of this invents a research decision. An agent may propose a term, an exhibit or a lead, and a proposal has no force until you approve it. What the toolkit adds is memory and stubbornness: the store remembers the decision you made in March, the loops run until your check passes rather than until the output looks plausible, and the redo set hands you the honest list of what your change broke.

docs.title: Where to put things
docs.text:
A quick lookup. For the why, examples, and anti-patterns per topic, follow the link in the right-hand column.

The full canonical layout lives in project-structure; this page is the answer to "I have this thing — where does it go?".

Most topic groups have a dedicated page for the why, examples, and anti-patterns: data-provenance, notes-and-feedback, submissions, literature, experimental-organization, grants, and the full folder layout (which covers the IRB, admin, and presentations conventions). Each table below is the quick lookup; the linked page is the deep dive.

docs.title: Why collaboration is hard (and what we do about it)
docs.text:
Where to start. This is the conceptual page — the why behind the collaboration workflow. If you're on a team already using this, you can skip straight to the co-author quickstart. If you're sizing this up for your own team, you're in the right place. New to git? The terms clone, branch, commit, repo are defined in the 10-minute primer — or just read on and trust the conclusions; the mechanics come later.

Collaborating on a shared paper — text, code, data, and figures, all changing at once across several people and machines — has a handful of failure modes that every team hits. The point of this page is to name them, because the whole structure exists to make exactly those failures impossible or cheap to undo. In short, the bad days it prevents are:

  • lost edits (two people save the same file; one version quietly wins),
  • "which version is current?" (paper_final_v3_REALLY.tex),
  • "it works on my machine" (code that depends on one person's paths/data),
  • drifting data copies, and no real project-wide history.

If the structure ever feels like overhead, it's almost always preventing one of these. The rest of this page walks through them and the options for solving them.

These aren't new problems — they're the general challenges of organizing a research project, amplified. Keeping raw data safe, knowing which file is current, making results reproducible: every researcher faces these alone. Collaboration doesn't add a different category of problem — it takes the same ones and makes them harder, because now several people and machines change the same project at once. So the collaboration workflow isn't a separate discipline; it's the same discipline, scaled up with a few extra guardrails.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Here is what actually goes wrong, in roughly the order teams hit it:

  • Silent overwrites. Two people edit the same file; Dropbox keeps the last save and quietly makes a "conflicted copy" of the other. Hours of work vanish into a file nobody opens.
  • "Which version is current?" paper_final_v3_KG_REALLY_final.tex. When there's no single source of truth, everyone hedges by copying, and the copies multiply.
  • "It works on my machine." Code that depends on one person's folder paths or one person's data download. Nobody else can reproduce the table.
  • Data duplication and drift. The 4 GB raw dataset gets copied into everyone's folder. Then someone re-cleans their copy and the numbers stop matching.
  • No real history. Dropbox versioning is per-file and shallow. You can't ask "what changed in the whole project between the submission and now?"

A good setup has to beat all of these at once — fixing one by making another worse (the usual trap) isn't good enough.

docs.title: What we actually want
docs.text:
Five things, and the tension between them is the whole design problem:

  1. Everyone has the files locally and backed up automatically.
  2. No one can silently overwrite someone else's work.
  3. One canonical copy of the data — never N drifting copies.
  4. Full project history you can read, diff, and roll back.
  5. It has to work for people who don't know git — the structure can't assume everyone is a power user.

Dropbox is great at (1) and terrible at (2) and (4). Git is great at (2) and (4) and indifferent to (1). Neither alone gives you all five. The options below are really different ways of combining them.

docs.title: Option A — Everyone works in a local git clone outside Dropbox
docs.text:
Each person git clones the repo to a normal folder on their laptop. Git handles merging; Dropbox isn't involved.

flowchart TD
    GH[("GitHub<br/>main — the shared truth")]
    A["Ann's laptop<br/>~/projects/paper (git clone)"]
    B["Ben's laptop<br/>~/projects/paper (git clone)"]
    A -- "push / pull" --> GH
    B -- "push / pull" --> GH
    GH -. "no automatic backup<br/>of unpushed work" .-> X{{"if you forget to push,<br/>it's only on your laptop"}}

Honest assessment: this is the "correct" software-engineering answer and it nails (2), (3), (4). It fails (1) and (5). Unpushed work isn't backed up — forget to push before your laptop dies and it's gone. And it asks everyone to live in git fluently, which is a real barrier for co-authors who just want to edit prose. Great for an all-engineer team; rough for a mixed one.

docs.title: Option B — Shared Dropbox container + one git clone per person inside it
docs.text:
This is what we use. The Dropbox folder is a plain container — it is not a git repo. It holds the single shared data copy and one nested git clone per person (clone_AB/, clone_CD/, …). Each person works only in their own clone; git lives inside each clone, never at the shared root.

flowchart TD
    GH[("GitHub · main<br/>owned by no one")]
    subgraph DBX["Shared Dropbox container (NOT a git repo)"]
        DATA["data/ — one canonical copy<br/>literature/ · project_management/"]
        CA["clone_AB/ (Ann's git clone)<br/>on branch AB/..."]
        CB["clone_CD/ (Ben's git clone)<br/>on branch CD/..."]
    end
    CA -- "push → PR → merge (anyone)" --> GH
    CB -- "push → PR → merge (anyone)" --> GH
    GH -- "pull" --> CA
    GH -- "pull" --> CB
    CA -. "scripts read shared data via<br/>.data-in-parent re-anchor" .-> DATA
    CB -. ".data-in-parent" .-> DATA

How this hits all five:

  • (1) local + backed up — every clone lives inside Dropbox, so unpushed work is still synced and recoverable. You get git and Dropbox backup.
  • (2) no overwrites — you only ever edit inside your own clone. Two people can't touch the same working file, and merges happen deliberately through git, not by Dropbox guessing.
  • (3) one data copy — the heavy data sits once in the container; each clone's scripts reach it through a tiny .data-in-parent marker instead of copying it.
  • (4) full history — each clone is a real git repo; main on GitHub is the shared, diffable, roll-back-able truth.
  • (5) works for non-git people — Claude Code can drive the git parts; the human just stays in their own folder. The manual workflow spells out the by-hand path for those who want it.

There's exactly one cost, and we don't hide it — see The one honest cost further down.

docs.title: Not an option — one shared Dropbox folder that is itself a git repo
docs.text:
This is the move almost everyone reaches for first, so it's worth saying clearly why it is not on the list above: put the git repo straight into the shared Dropbox folder, so everyone sees the same files and gets Dropbox backup. It looks like it gives you everything — and it breaks.

flowchart TD
    GH[("GitHub<br/>main")]
    D["Shared Dropbox folder<br/>= ONE git repo (.git at root)"]
    A["Ann edits here"] --> D
    B["Ben edits here"] --> D
    D -- "Dropbox syncs the .git folder too" --> CONFLICT{{"two people, one .git →<br/>corrupted history,<br/>HEAD flips under your feet"}}
    D --> GH

A git repo's internals (.git/) are a live database. When Dropbox syncs that between two people working at once, it corrupts. Worse, one person switching branches flips the shared HEAD (git's pointer to "which branch you're on right now"), so a teammate's next commit silently lands on the wrong branch. This is not hypothetical — it's exactly the incident this kit was hardened against. It fails (2) and (4) in the most damaging way: it looks fine until it isn't. Option B above exists precisely to get the same benefits without this failure — which is why it's a real option and this is not.

docs.title: Why "leaderless", and why that matters
docs.text:
Option B has a tempting shortcut: make one person's clone the "main" one at the container root and have everyone else nest under it. We deliberately don't. There is no lead and no root clone. The container root is just a folder; every co-author's clone_<XX>/ is equal; main lives on GitHub, owned by no one.

Two reasons. First, social: a paper's co-authors are peers, and baking a "lead's canonical copy" into the folder structure creates a hierarchy that doesn't reflect how the work actually happens. Second, technical: the moment the root is someone's clone (a .git at the root), you've quietly slid back into the shared-repo trap above — a shared repo whose HEAD can flip. Keeping the root a plain container makes that specific incident — the shared .git two people fight over — structurally impossible: there's no shared repo at the root to corrupt. (Each person's own clone_<XX>/ still has a live .git; that can rarely corrupt if you run the same clone from two machines at once, but it's single-writer and re-cloning from GitHub fixes it in ~30 seconds with zero loss of pushed work.) Equality and safety turn out to be the same design choice.

docs.title: The one honest cost
docs.text: Because git lives inside each clone, you open your tools in your clone folder, not at the shared root. In Claude Code that means opening the session in clone_<XX>/ (and only adding the parent folder when you need a shared file like the data). It's one extra habit at setup time. That's the whole price — and in exchange the five failure modes above stop being your problem. We think that's a good trade; the handbook makes the habit concrete.

docs.title: Bringing this to your own team
docs.text:
If you're not on a team that already uses this and want to adopt it, two practical notes:

  • You don't need Dropbox. The happy path is Claude Code + Dropbox (every safety rail on automatically), but the workflow also runs on pure GitHub — the clones just live in an ordinary folder instead of inside a Dropbox container, and you take on a bit more manual care (Dropbox no longer backs up your unpushed work). The mechanics of that variant are flagged in set up your working clone and the manual workflow.
  • Explaining it to co-authors. The argument that lands is the one above: not "use this tool," but "here are the five bad days every paper has, and here's the cheapest way to make them impossible." Lead with the failure modes they've personally lived. One person sets the project up once (anyone can — there's no lead) and invites the others as collaborators; the one constraint is that Overleaf's git integration can only be configured by the Overleaf project owner.

docs.title: Good habits: permissions & planning
docs.text: The toolkit makes Claude Code capable; this page is about the habits that make it save you time without surprises. Two matter most: the permission mode you run in, and planning first, then having the plan checked before any code runs.

docs.title: Permission modes — which to use
docs.text:
Claude Code asks before it acts, and you control how often. Pressing Shift+Tab cycles through the modes; pick by how reversible the work is:

  • Plan mode (read-only). Claude can read and think but cannot edit or run anything — it produces a plan and waits for your approval. Use this for anything non-trivial: a multi-file change, a refactor, a new analysis. You catch a wrong approach before it touches a single file, which is far cheaper than undoing it afterwards.
  • Default (ask each time). Claude proposes each action and you approve it. The safe baseline; right when you're learning what a task involves, or any time the work touches something sensitive (raw data, a push, an external send).
  • Auto-accept edits. Claude makes file edits without pausing. Useful for speed, but only where a mistake is free to undo — inside your own clone_<XX>/ where git can revert anything, on a scratch branch, or for mechanical work you'll review as a diff. Don't run auto-accept against shared master content or data/raw/.

A simple rule of thumb: plan mode for non-trivial work, auto-accept inside a git sandbox, default-ask for anything irreversible or sensitive. Whatever the mode, the safety rails still apply — the raw-data guard and the "ask-before-pushing" rule fire regardless of how fast you've set things to go.

docs.title: Plan first, then have the plan checked
docs.text:
The habit that saves the most time: don't let Claude run straight at a big task. Put it in plan mode, get the plan, and then — before you approve — have an independent agent poke holes in it. A flawed plan caught on paper costs seconds; the same flaw caught after Claude has written ten files costs an afternoon.

In practice:

  1. Shift+Tab into plan mode and describe the task. Claude returns a plan instead of acting.
  2. Before approving, ask for an adversarial check — for example: "Before I approve this, spawn two independent agents to find the weakest points in this plan — wrong order, missed dependency, risky step — and report back." (Or run adversarial-review on the plan.)
  3. Read the critique, fix the plan, then approve. Now execution runs against a plan that's already survived scrutiny.

This is the same independent-reviewer logic the toolkit uses everywhere; see Reviewing with adversarial agents for why a fresh agent catches what the planning agent can't.

docs.title: A few more habits that pay off
docs.text:
• Work in small steps and read the diffs. Claude is fast; the bottleneck is your review. Small, reviewable changes beat one giant edit.
  • Commit at clean checkpoints. Each commit is a save point you can roll back to — which is also what makes auto-accept safe.
  • Let it verify its own work. Ask it to run the tests / recompile / re-read the output before declaring done — and for figures, to self-check before showing you (Self-correcting figures).
